19878-the-passaic-flood-of-1903:
The Passaic Flood of 1903 is a federal water-supply paper by Marshall Ora Leighton. It was transmitted to the Geological Survey for publication in that series. The Passaic River drains a crowded corner of New Jersey. Its 1903 flood ranked among the worst then recorded there. Leighton's report measures the water and maps the damage. Government science treated floods as data problems first.

Leighton became a leading American hydrologist. His flood studies set methods for gauging and records. Mill towns along the Passaic suffered repeated inundations. A careful post-flood survey served engineers and insurers alike. The report preserves rainfall, flow, and loss figures. It is a primary source for New Jersey flood history.
20130-magazine-or-animadversions-on-the-:
Magazine, or Animadversions on the English Spelling, dates from 1703, a very early spelling tract. Animadversions means critical remarks, and spelling is the target here. English spelling was still unsettled in Queen Anne's time. Writers of tracts argued for simpler, more regular ways to spell words.

The modern edition lists scholars from Columbia, Chicago, Princeton, and other schools. Their names show how later editors framed this old text for study. Readers get a glimpse of English before spelling froze into place. It suits those who love the history of words and print.
alchimia-nova-das-ist-die-guldene-kunst-: Alchimia nova, 1603. The new alchemy. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol1-1803:
Amadis of Gaul is the great Spanish romance of chivalry that set the pattern for a whole age of fiction. Robert Southey, the English poet, translated it, and the first volume appeared in 1803. Its hero Amadis became the model knight for readers across Europe.

Amadis loves the lady Oriana and proves himself against giants, enchanters, and rival knights. Battles, shipwrecks, and magic fill this opening volume. The book bewitched Renaissance readers, and Cervantes honored it even while mocking its imitators. Southey's version brought the Spanish epic to English readers in full. Volume one launches the quest in high style.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol2-1803:
Robert Southey's translation of Amadis of Gaul ran to four volumes in 1803, and this is the second. The Spanish romance follows the peerless knight Amadis, the standard by which later heroes were judged. His deeds for his lady Oriana drive the whole vast tale.

Volume two carries Amadis through wars fought for Oriana's hand and fresh dangers in strange lands. Enchantments test his faith, and new knights enter the lists beside him. The pace is pure romance, with marvel piled on marvel. Readers of Cervantes will know this world well, since Don Quixote's library was full of such books. The epic here rides at full gallop.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol3-1803:
The third volume of Southey's Amadis of Gaul came out in 1803 with the rest of his translation. Amadis, the Spanish knight whose fame spread over Europe, faces his hardest trials of constancy here. His lady Oriana remains the center of all his deeds.

Sorcerers lay cunning traps, and magic isles rise out of the sea to test him. Amadis must hold his faith through long separation and false reports. The wonders come thick in this book, the richest in marvels of the four. Southey, himself a poet of romance, keeps the old Spanish fire alive in English. The volume brings the epic near its climax.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol4-1803:
Southey's Amadis of Gaul ends with this fourth volume, published in 1803. The Spanish romance had shaped European ideas of knighthood for three hundred years before Southey Englished it. Here the long tale of Amadis and Oriana reaches its close.

Final battles settle the wars that run through all four volumes. The last enchantments break, and old wrongs come right at last. The lovers win their hard reward after years of trial. With this volume ends the romance that taught Europe how to dream of knights. Its shadow falls across Don Quixote and across every chivalric tale written after it.
anselm-proslogium-monologium-cur-deus-ho:
Sidney Norton Deane published his translation of St Anselm's major works in 1903. Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury in the 1100s, wrote the Proslogium and Monologium as prayers that reason through faith. Deane gathered those works with Cur Deus Homo in one English volume.

The Proslogium holds Anselm's famous argument that God, as the greatest conceivable being, must exist. Gaunilon, a monk, replied on behalf of the fool who denies God, and Anselm answered him. Cur Deus Homo explains why God became man, in the satisfaction theory of the atonement. These texts founded scholastic philosophy, the effort to prove the faith by reason, and they still anchor courses on medieval thought.
anthropography-or-bible-phrenology-of-th: Anthropography or Bible Phrenology, 1903. The nations' phrenology. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. Writers of history may cite it later in their work.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-03:
Volume three of Burton's Arabian Nights, issued in 1885, carries Shahrazad's tales deeper into the cycle. By now the frame is familiar: night after night of story buys the teller her life. The tales turn through courts, markets, deserts, and islands of wonder in Burton's unabridged English.

Sea voyages and marvels grow more frequent as the volume proceeds. Burton refused to soften the Arabic text's frank passages, which kept his edition to private subscribers at first. His terminal essay and notes, spread through the set, made it a storehouse of lore. Later editors borrowed his learning even when they cut his text. The third volume sustains the pace set by the first two.
arabian-nights-burton-supplemental-1886-:
The third supplemental volume of Burton's Nights, published from 1886, carries the overflow of the Arabic tradition further. Burton worked from manuscripts in several collections to catch tales the main cycle missed. Some are variants of known stories; others stand alone, rougher and stranger than the famous ones.

His method does not change: full text, kept verse, and notes that explain rite, dress, and law. The supplement as a whole shows how open the Nights remained, growing by copyists' hands for centuries. Burton wanted English readers to see that growth, not a polished extract. Volume three sits midway in the supplement's six books. It rewards readers who finished the main set and still want more.
arnaldi-de-villanova-philosophi-medici-e: Arnaldi de Villanova Omnia, 1603. The Villanova complete works. This book preserves that collection. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
arnim-svf-vol2-1903:
Chrysippus of Soli, the third head of the Stoic school, wrote hundreds of books, and none of them survive whole. Hans von Arnim devoted the second volume of his fragment collection, printed in 1903, to what remains of Chrysippus on logic and physics. The passages appear in Greek and Latin, as the sources kept them.

Here are the Stoic views on truth, signs, causes, fate, and the makeup of the cosmos, rebuilt from quotes in later authors. Chrysippus was the thinker who turned Stoicism into a tight system. This volume holds most of what can still be known of that system, and it stays a working tool for scholars of ancient thought.
arnim-svf-vol3-1903:
The third volume of Hans von Arnim's Stoic fragment collection, printed in 1903, turns from logic and physics to ethics. It gathers what survives of Chrysippus on how a person should live, and adds fragments from the Stoics who came after him. The texts stand in Greek and Latin, drawn from the authors who quoted them.

Readers find the roots of Stoic moral teaching here: virtue as the only true good, and the passions treated as errors in judgment. Duty is sorted by what fits nature and one's role in life. Because Chrysippus wrote the fullest defense of these views, his fragments form the core of Stoic ethics as later ages took it up.
arxiv-2512-00003:
Qian Li and Yuyi Wang make transformer simulations of Turing machines far more efficient. Transformers of constant bit size are known to be Turing complete in principle. Existing builds, however, need a number of chain-of-thought steps growing with the machine's space for every single mimicked step.

That cost makes the thinking traces far too long. Their build cuts the overhead sharply, bringing mimicked computation closer to feasible lengths. Efficient simulation sharpens what theory says about the thinking power of transformers. Impractical thinking lengths were the blocker, since each mimicked machine step multiplied into many chain-of-thought steps.
arxiv-2512-00203:
Expected goals models in soccer estimate the chance that a shot becomes a goal, given its location and the pressure on the shooter. Jonathan Pipping, Tianshu Feng, and Paul Sabin argue that such models miss half the story, in a 2025 study. They only score shots that actually happened.

The authors propose a possession-level framework that first estimates the probability a shot occurs within the next second. It then assigns the expected goals value that shot would carry if it occurred. Coaches and analysts could judge attacks that never produced a shot, not just finished chances, when grading team play. The framework shifts attention from finishing to the buildup that creates chances.
arxiv-2512-00403:
Automating scientific discovery with language-model agents promises end-to-end research assistance. Xiao Wu and a large team present SelfAI in 2025, a self-training AI system built from such agents. Earlier frameworks were often confined to narrow domains.

Many discovery systems offer limited real-time interaction with researchers and lack principled rules for when to stop exploring. Those gaps cause inefficiency, reproducibility problems, and underused human expertise. SelfAI aims to keep researchers in the loop while agents handle specification, planning, and execution of experiments. Self-training lets the system improve from its own experimental outcomes over time. The design keeps human expertise in the loop where automated exploration is weakest. For lab heads, the gain is a tireless aide that can plan runs, do the runs, and learn from what came out. The staff keep hold of the big calls.
arxiv-2512-00603:
Alloying and doping tune semiconductors, but they also introduce disorder that traps charge carriers. Mpatani and co-authors report carrier localization and dynamics in indium gallium nitride thin films in 2025. The films contain ten percent indium and a light silicon doping, grown by metal-organic vapor phase epitaxy.

Localization changes how the material emits and absorbs light, which matters because this alloy family powers LEDs and lasers. Comparing alloyed and doped films separates the effects of composition from those of the added silicon. The report helps growers balance performance gains from doping against the disorder it brings. Thin films are the form in which such alloys are grown for devices.
arxiv-2512-00703:
Xinyue Cheng and Yalu Feng wrote a 2025 geometry paper on concentration in Finsler spaces. Finsler geometry generalizes the usual way of measuring distance, letting the ruler depend on direction as well as place. A metric measure manifold pairs such a space with a way to measure volume.

Concentration describes how, in high dimensions, most of a space's volume sits near certain sets. Cheng and Feng study these properties in a systematic way. They link concentration to observable diameter, to isoperimetric inequalities, and to the first eigenvalue. As one use, they derive a Cheng-type upper bound for that eigenvalue from concentration alone.
arxiv-2512-01003:
William Press warns about a quiet trap in survey research in a 2025 paper. Studies in epidemiology and social science often need to remove confounding effects before trusting a correlation. A confounder is a hidden factor that drives both variables and fakes a link between them. Linear regression and its cousins are the usual removal tools.

Press argues that correlated confounders are not easily controlled for in large surveys. Knowing whether every confounder has been found, or is even visible rather than latent, is generally impossible. His warning matters because bigger datasets can make a biased answer look very precise. The paper urges care before causal claims.
arxiv-2512-01403:
Julien Dorner and co-authors study gamma rays made at the Sun. Cosmic rays from our galaxy hit the Sun's air and make gamma rays. Space scopes found far more of those rays than early models said. The flux also shifts in odd ways over time.

Those shifts hint that the Sun's magnetic field plays a big part. The team tests how field shapes steer cosmic rays near the Sun. Their work ties field form to the gamma ray output. A good match would help use the Sun as a probe of cosmic rays and fields.
arxiv-2512-01503:
Guo-Jun Wei and co-authors test nuclear models against data from space and labs. Covariant density functionals describe nuclei and dense matter well. Their couplings shift with density. How they shift is often tied to the baryon density alone.

The team uses Bayesian methods with multi-messenger data. That data spans star views and wave events. They ask how each choice in the model shifts the fit. Clear links between model choices and data help set the traits of matter in neutron stars, where lab tests cannot reach. Star data now spans gravitational waves as well, so dense matter claims must fit both light signals and wave signals at once.
arxiv-2512-01803:
Xavier Thomas and co-authors assess human motion in synthesized videos with action tell-tales. Video generators improve fast, but judging motion correctness is hard. Vision encoders and multimodal models lean on appearance. They miss time dynamics and flag few anatomical errors.

Their Generative Action Tell-Tales target motion itself. Checks focus on how acts unfold over time. Motion-aware scores help rank generators for film and training data. They also expose which acts, like jumps or lifts, current models still fake poorly. Tell-tales focus on joints and limbs over time, the exact cues coaches use when they judge whether a filmed move is real.
arxiv-2512-01903:
Large molecules change shape to do their work, but watching a protein move from one shape to another is hard because the change is rare and fast. Patrice Koehl, Marc Delarue, and Henri Orland present a 2025 framework that generates realistic paths for such transitions in large biomolecular systems.

Their method rests on the Langevin bridge formalism, which forces a molecular trajectory to arrive at a chosen final shape within a set time. A stochastic integro-differential equation describes the constrained motion, and a low-temperature approximation makes it practical to compute. Realistic transition paths help explain how molecules function and how drugs might interfere.
arxiv-2512-02103:
Matrix models compress quantum gravity and black hole physics into the algebra of large matrices with symmetries. Adwait Gaikwad and three co-authors study in 2025 the Hilbert space of gauged matrix models that also carry a global symmetry, asking exactly which states survive both sets of rules.

They focus on bosonic models with a U(2) gauge group and a rotational global symmetry, counting states that are singlets under both. These state counts, called cohomologies in the black hole context, test whether models reproduce the entropy of real black holes. Careful counting separates genuine gravitational physics from artifacts of how the model was gauged.
arxiv-2512-02203:
Gravity models in economics explain trade or migration flows between places, and multi-way versions carry many fixed effects that bias standard estimates. Lucas Resende and three co-authors propose in 2025 an estimator for these models that removes the incidental parameter bias at its root.

The usual maximum likelihood estimator, including the popular Poisson variant, mixes structural parameters with masses of nuisance parameters, and the joint estimation skews the answers. Their estimator is asymptotically unbiased, so the skew vanishes as data grow. Unbiased gravity estimates matter because these models inform trade policy and regional planning with real money at stake.
arxiv-2512-02303:
Neural networks are not born respecting symmetry; a rotated object must be learned as the same object. Max Shen and three co-authors study in 2025 how networks trained with data augmentation learn three-dimensional rotational equivariance, and how quickly and well they learn it.

The team derives a principled measure of equivariance error which, for convex losses, states what share of the total loss comes from imperfectly learned symmetry. That turns a vague worry into a number that can be tracked during training. Knowing how symmetry is acquired helps designers decide when augmentation suffices and when symmetry must be built into the architecture.
arxiv-2512-02703:
D.T. Huong and five co-authors study lepton flavor in an extended gauge model of particle physics. The flipped 3-3-1-1 model enlarges the known symmetry groups, and with that comes new patterns of Z boson decay. Some decays would violate flavor, changing one lepton type into another.

The team computes flavor violating Z decays at tree level, plus flavor conserving decays for comparison. Rates in such models tell experiments where new physics could peek through. Null results so far already constrain these models, and sharper predictions focus future searches at colliders and precision facilities. Small rates are still rates a sharp test can see, and nulls at that scale still fence the model in.
arxiv-2512-02803:
Tobias Petri, Simone Baratto, and Giancarlo Ferrari Trecate model a bumper car as a test bed for vehicle control. The cars serve an experimental framework for teaching, with high maneuverability by design. Standard bicycle models ignore the wide steering angles these small vehicles actually use.

The authors build modified planar bicycle models that allow those wide angles. They combine the models with parametric and non parametric identification, adding physical knowledge step by step. A humble bumper car thus becomes a cheap, safe stand in for testing autonomous driving ideas before road trials. Cheap cars that crash soft are a kind test bed: bold plans can fail there with no risk to life or limb at all.
arxiv-2512-03103:
What people post online can show how they feel about city policy. Shampa Saha and Shovan Roy study traffic policy in Knoxville, Tennessee, in this 2025 work. They gather posts from Twitter and Reddit over two years, from the start of 2022 to the end of 2023.

The team uses a word-based tool to score the mood of each post. They also use topic modeling to find the themes people raise most. City staff could use such findings to see which traffic plans please or anger the public. The method is cheap and fast next to surveys. Local readers may recognize debates over traffic flow, parking, and road work in these themes.
arxiv-2512-03303:
In many groups, local contests decide who leads a neighborhood. Michael Luby and Sandy Irani model that process in this 2025 work. Agents differ in strength, and repeated local contests shape who becomes dominant nearby.

Stable dominance patterns can emerge surprisingly fast compared to the size of the group. The authors connect this to fast maximal independent set algorithms, a classic computing problem. Their model bridges nature and distributed computing. It may help design networks where nodes must pick leaders quickly with only local information. Fast leader choice is a building block for swarms, sensor nets, and peer systems.
arxiv-2601-06903:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Bingnan Xiao and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers Divergence-Based adaptive aggregation for byzantine robust federated learning. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Inherent client drifts caused by data heterogeneity. As well as vulnerability to Byzantine attacks within the system, hinder effective model training and convergence in federated learning (FL).

The work presents two new frameworks, named DiveRgence-based Adaptive aGgregation (DRAG) and Byzantine-Resilient DRAG (BR-DRAG). To mitigate client drifts and resist attacks while expediting training. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07403:
Burcu Gurbuz and three co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on dengue, a fever spread by mosquitoes. Dengue comes in more than one strain. A first bout with one strain can change how a second bout plays out. The authors build a math model with two strains at once. The model is deterministic, so its path is fixed by its rules, not by chance.

The model sorts people by stage: some are in a first bout, and some in a second. A short shield from the first bout can guard against the next strain for a time. But a past bout can also make a second bout worse, an effect called antibody-dependent enhancement, or ADE. Death is more apt in a second bout, and the model tracks that risk. It also tracks mosquitoes that bear both strains at once.
arxiv-2601-08003:
Weiyue Li and colleagues improve creative writing by language models with a peer review trick. Models often struggle with creative generation. Multi-agent frameworks that help reasoning can paradoxically hurt creativity by homogenizing content. Their system, LLM Review, implements blind peer review. Agents exchange targeted feedback but revise independently. Divergent creative paths survive the process. Their 2026 preprint describes the framework.

Blind review borrows the guardrails of academic publishing. Reviewers comment without knowing whose draft they read, and authors keep control of revisions. Independence prevents the group from collapsing onto one voice. Targeted feedback still fixes weak passages. The paper serves scholars in creative AI and multi-agent systems. It shows a social structure, not a bigger model, as the source of better writing.
arxiv-2601-08103:
Abby Bault, Andrei Cuceu, Julien Guy, and many collaborators measure baryon acoustic oscillations in a new tracer. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses data from the second release of the DESI survey. Baryon acoustic oscillations are a frozen sound-wave pattern that works as a cosmic ruler.

The team cross-correlates triply ionized carbon absorption with quasar and emission-line galaxy positions. The sample holds 2.5 million quasars plus a large galaxy set. Carbon forest absorption traces gas between galaxies along quasar sightlines. Measuring the pattern there extends cosmic distance checks to gas that most surveys ignore, which helps pin down how the universe expands.
arxiv-2601-08403:
Abhijnan Nath and four co-authors propose Owen-Shapley policy optimization for generative search models. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses reinforcement learning for personalized recommendation. Standard methods like GRPO use sparse, sequence-level rewards, which blur credit assignment.

When a long answer succeeds, no one knows which tokens drove the success. The gap worsens when models must infer latent user intent from vague language without ground truth labels. Such reasoning rarely appears in pretraining data. Owen-Shapley optimization borrows Shapley value ideas to spread credit more fairly across tokens. Fairer credit could train search assistants that learn from whole-answer rewards without guessing.
arxiv-2601-08503:
Aditya Kumar and co-authors present Temporal Fusion Nexus, an embedding model for clinical data after kidney transplant. Their 2026 arXiv paper joins irregular time series with unstructured clinical narratives. The model is multimodal and task-agnostic, so one embedding can serve many outcomes.

The team analyzes a retrospective cohort of 3,382 transplant patients. Three outcomes are studied: graft loss, graft rejection, and mortality. Irregular lab timing and free-text notes usually force separate pipelines. A fused embedding could give clinicians a single patient summary that many risk tools can reuse. Transplant care generates exactly the messy mixed data this model targets.
arxiv-2601-08603: Carlos Antonio Pinzon and co-authors estimate true data distributions collected under randomized response. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies a protocol for categorical data with local differential privacy guarantees. Randomized response lets people answer surveys while plausibly denying their true answer. Big technology companies have used it as a building block for collecting app and web user data. Recovering the true distribution from noisy responses is the statistical core. Better estimators mean firms can learn population trends without learning any person's answer.
arxiv-2601-08703: Kaivalya Rawal and four co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on whether short accounts of a model's logic can tell like models apart. A Rashomon set holds many models that score much the same. Accounts of each model's logic should help a user pick which one to deploy, by showing how their acts differ. But such accounts vary with the explainer tool used. So they need tests of their own. The authors test how well accounts split models in a set. The work counts for fields under strict rules.
arxiv-2601-08803:
Carina Hausladen, Christoph Engel, and Marcel Schubert study why gifts in a shared pot game shift so much. In the game, each player can give to a group pot that helps all. First round gifts can be read as a sign of how fair a player likes to be. But gifts jump up and down in later rounds in ways that view can not explain.

The team uses a large set of plays from close to three thousand players. They bring in a method that works back from acts to hid aims. Two new steps help them track aims that change over time. A reader in social science gets a fresh way to read group gifts. It splits firm traits from fast shifts in mood or plan.
arxiv-2601-09003:
Melody Molander gives a drawn rule set for a deep algebra tied to the E7 shape. The algebra codes how lines and zones can join in a plane web used in quantum work. A known plan, called the Kuperberg program, seeks drawn rules for such algebras. Rules let a user shrink any web to a count by set steps.

She gives the rules for the affine E7 case, in its plain, unshaded form. She then proves the shrink plan, called the jellyfish algorithm, works and hits all counts. That proof was the hard part of the case. A reader in algebra gets a closed case in a long program, with rules they can use.
arxiv-2601-09103:
Haijian Shao and four co-authors fix a flaw in heart wave sorting: some beats are rare. A heart wave, or ECG, is a trace of the heart's spark. Tools sort traces by the ill they show. Rare ills have few train traces, so tools learn them poor. A sick folk with a rare ill is then most prone to a wrong call.

The team grows rare traces in two ways. A wave shift tool bends known traces in sound ways. A fusion step then mixes traits across beat types. Both add rich, fair train cases for rare types. A reader in heart tech gets a data fix for a class gap that can cost lives if left.
arxiv-2601-09203:
Ao-Xiang Liu and Cong-Feng Qiao push tests of quantum links past the first order. A link here means two bits share a state that no lone bit can hold. Most tests check a mean, the first count of that state. High counts, such as spread and skew sums, hold more of the tale. They have been left near bare by past tests.

The team works on linked hyperon pairs, heavy bits that can be made in vast sets in charm decays. They set a new form of a classic test for those high counts. It uses sums of joint marks, not just means. A reader in core physics gets a way to hunt links where past tests were blind.
arxiv-2601-09403:
Yu-Ming Yang, Xiao-Jun Bi, Long Wang, and Peng-Fei Yin ask what ultralight dark matter does to small star systems. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies compact stellar systems living inside halos of this wavy dark matter. Waves in the dark matter field make the halo's gravity flicker over time.

That flickering heats the stars, pumping energy into the system step by step. Small systems are often used to set tight limits on ultralight dark matter for this reason. Yet systems far smaller than the dark matter's wavelength are still poorly explored. The authors ask when heating puffs a system apart and when it instead collapses.
arxiv-2601-09603:
Petros Vavaroutsos, Theodoros Palamas, and Pantelis Vikatos seek a leaner way to train music-understanding models. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses self-supervised learning with a random quantizer, aimed at linear complexity. Foundation models work well but carry hundreds of millions of parameters, which makes them costly to train and run.

Self-supervised learning lets a model learn from unlabeled audio, a big plus for music. A random quantizer turns sound features into simple codes the model can predict. Keeping the cost linear in input size keeps long tracks affordable. The work targets music tasks where labs cannot match the budgets of big tech.
arxiv-2601-09803:
Mariam Bouhmadi-López and Carlos G. Boiza model dark energy as a field that may already be ringing. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats a generalized axion-like quintessence field. The field rolls down its potential as the universe expands.

Depending on its mass and starting point, the field may still be sliding toward the minimum or already oscillating around it. Those two regimes need distinct treatments of cosmic perturbations. The split matters for matching the model to data. An oscillating dark energy would leave different fingerprints in the cosmic microwave background than a slowly rolling one.
arxiv-2601-10003:
Sanghyeok Choi, Woosang Jeon, Kyuseok Yang, and Taehyeong Kim build webs of facts from raw text. A fact web links things by typed ties. Such webs back search and smart tools. AI built webs face a hard trade off.

Cast the net wide and the web breaks into loose bits. Pull it tight too soon and facts are lost. The team made SocraticKG to ease that trade. It first turns a text into pairs of asks and replies. Those pairs lay out the sense of the text. Only then does it pull out the typed ties. The step keeps more facts while the web stays joined.
arxiv-2601-10203:
Zheng Zhao and co authors speed up the tune of quantum chips. Before a chip runs, its qubits must be set to the right tones. Tones that clash cause cross talk. The tune step is a known slow point for large chips.

The team recast a known tune tool in fresh math terms. The Snake tool, they show, is a form of block descent. That fact gives the tool a firm base. They then built a new tune plan that uses the chip graph. It tunes blocks with the graph in mind. The aim is a faster tune with fewer clashes.
arxiv-2601-10803:
Woorak Choi and co-authors present radio views of NGC 4522, a galaxy being stripped by ram pressure. As the galaxy plows through the Virgo cluster's hot gas, that gas pushes its own gas out. The team used the Very Large Array at two bands, three and ten gigahertz. The maps reach fine scales of a few hundred parsecs.

The study reads the galaxy's radio continuum, its spectral index, and its magnetic field under this battering. Ram pressure can compress fields on one side and stretch them on the other. Watching that struggle shows how cluster weather reshapes a galaxy's magnetism and star birth. The work speaks to how environment, not just inner life, drives galaxy evolution.
arxiv-2601-10903:
M. R. Norman examines superconductivity tied to the Slater mode in KTaO3 heterostructures. At the interface of KTaO3 with other oxides, a two-dimensional electron gas can superconduct. Its transition temperature is about ten times higher than in its cousin SrTiO3. The transition also depends strongly on which way the interface faces.

Norman tests whether the Slater mode, a particular lattice vibration, drives the pairing. Orientation dependence is a clue a good theory must match. If a single mode explains both the high temperature and the orientation effect, the mechanism comes into focus. The work bears on the hunt for the rules behind interface superconductivity, a puzzle with device stakes.
arxiv-2601-11003:
Shivaksh Rawat, Samyobrata Mukherjee, and Gennady Shvets generate lasting nanoscale magnetization in all-dielectric metasurfaces. A metasurface is a thin sheet patterned to steer light. When such a sheet changes in time, it forms a boundary in time for guided waves. Changing the sheet fast can shift a wave's frequency as it travels.

The authors use light-injected free carriers to write lasting magnetization at very small scales. A magnetic pattern that stays after the light leaves could store data or set a wave's path. The work joins optics with magnetism at scales where both are hard to control, and points to sheets that remember what light wrote on them.
arxiv-2601-11103:
Minju Park, Seunghyun Lee, Juhwan Ma, and Dongwook Yoon present AI Twin, a speaking practice system for ESL learners. AI conversation tools let learners practice English speaking. Most rely on explicit correction, which can break the flow and dent confidence. AI Twin takes a gentler path grounded in language acquisition research and motivational psychology.

The system rephrases a learner's utterance into more fluent English. It then delivers that better version in the learner's own voice, a self-clone of a better me. Hearing oneself speak well can motivate without shaming. The work, shown at CHI 2026, serves language learners who need practice that builds fluency and nerve together.
arxiv-2601-11203:
Riku Kuze, Kunihito Ioka, Kohta Murase, Shigeo Kimura, and Kohei Inayoshi study odd red galaxies. Their 2026 preprint looks at Little Red Dots at high redshift. These small, red systems were found by the James Webb Space Telescope. They sit far back in time, at redshift four to seven.

Their light shows broad emission lines from fast gas. Yet they lack the X-ray and radio signs one would expect. That odd mix hints at black holes that feed in dense gas. The gas wrap could hide the holes from most probes. The team asks if such hid holes could also emit neutrinos. If so, these dots would be a new source class for those ghost particles.
arxiv-2601-11303:
David Feldstein-Bofill and six coauthors tune how Cooper pairs tunnel in a qubit. Their 2026 preprint deals with a hybrid superconducting qubit. Superconducting circuits get their key trait from one relation. The Josephson energy-phase relation gives them strong nonlinearity.

That relation holds more than the basic cosine term. Higher harmonics can appear, as cosines of multiples of phase. Each harmonic marks pairs that tunnel together as a group. The count in the group sets the parity of the process. Parity here means whether that group count is odd or even. The team shows control of which parity rules the device. That control is a new knob for qubit design.
arxiv-2601-11403:
Michael Eides and Vladimir Yerokhin compute levels of bound states in QED. Their 2026 preprint uses the energy-momentum trace for the task. Some bound states depend on more than one mass at once. Muonic hydrogen is their worked example of such a system.

In muonic hydrogen, a muon orbits a proton like an electron. Its energy levels depend on both the electron and muon masses. The team writes the levels as matrix elements of one operator. That operator is the trace of the QED energy-momentum tensor. One-loop corrections to the levels follow from that form. The trick turns a hard multi-scale problem into clean algebra. It may serve other exotic atoms with mixed masses.
arxiv-2601-11503:
Viren Tyagi, Mike Pols, Geert Brocks, and Shuxia Tao track halide motion in perovskites. Their 2026 preprint studies mixed-halide crystals and heterojunctions. Perovskites are prized materials for solar cells and lights. Halide defects inside them guide how ions move around.

That motion sets the pace of halide mixing in the crystal. It also sets how fast phases separate into unlike zones. The team studies diffusion of two defect kinds. Halide vacancies are missing atoms that hop through the lattice. Interstitials are extra atoms squeezed between lattice sites. The test crystal mixes iodine and bromine in CsPb halide. Knowing both paths helps design stable perovskite devices.
arxiv-2601-11703:
Marco Chianese and six coauthors probe super-heavy dark matter with gamma rays. Their 2026 preprint refines lifetime constraints on such particles. Super-heavy dark matter spans a vast mass range here. Masses run from 10 to the 7 up to 10 to the 15 GeV.

Decaying particles of that kind would shed gamma rays. Ultra-high-energy gamma-ray data can catch that faint glow. No glow at a set level bounds how fast they decay. The team analyzes UHE gamma-ray data for those bounds. Refined constraints narrow where such dark matter can hide. The work tests a dark sector far above collider reach.
arxiv-2601-11803:
Lee D. Feinberg, Breann N. Sitarski, Michael W. McElwain, and a large NASA-linked team set out the plan for a future space scope. The Habitable Worlds Observatory is built to search for life on far worlds. The team call it the first scope designed for that task.

They also frame it as a broad tool for star and galaxy science. Their study weighs early design picks and the tech work still needed. It maps the trade space, where cost, risk, and skill pull in unlike ways. The plan guides the next steps toward build and launch.
arxiv-2601-12003:
Angel Y. He and David Parker make checks for shared stochastic games more sound when odds are not known in full. Such games model agents that act at once, plan ahead, and face chance. They suit self-run systems that share roads, grids, or air.

Real use rarely gives exact odds for each move. Past tools need those exact odds, which is a weak spot. Their robust checks work over a range of odds in place of one set. That makes proofs of safe acts more fit for the real world.
arxiv-2601-12203:
Antonella M. C. Torrisi, Inês Nolasco, Paola Sgadò, Elisabetta Versace, and Emmanouil Benetos study chick calls after embryonic exposure to VPA. Young chicks use calls to signal state and needs. Hand coding of calls is biased, slow, and misses much of the full call set.

Their computational study reads the calls by machine. VPA exposure before hatch is the test factor. Machine reads can show if such exposure shifts call form or use. The work links early exposure to later social signals in birds.  Calls are a rich sign of chick health and mood.
arxiv-2601-12303:
Shizhan Gong, Xiaofan Zhang, and Qi Dou explain image models via concepts found after training. Deep models win at image tasks, yet their opacity blocks use in critical fields. Concept methods explain calls in human terms in place of raw pixels.

Past post-hoc and built-in concept tools have flaws: weak concept links, non-visual concepts, or high hand cost. Their tool finds concepts by sparse decomposition of visual traits. Found concepts are visual by design. That should make image AI calls more clear to experts.  Sparse parts keep each concept small and clear.
arxiv-2601-12403:
Shu Cai, Ya-Feng Liu, Jun Zhang, and Qi Zhang study a wireless setup that sends two streams at once. A main sender beams common data to many main receivers over broadcast signals. At the same time, a smart surface helps a backscatter device send its own data to a second receiver. The surface can be tuned, which adds a new degree of control.

The setup is called a decoupled symbiotic radio system, boosted by the tunable surface. The two streams share the same airwaves, so they must not spoil each other. Work of this kind aims to squeeze more use from scarce spectrum. The paper was accepted to a major signal processing venue for 2026.
arxiv-2601-12703:
Andrew Gordon and five co authors at Timaeus borrow a method from physics to study language models. Spectroscopy infers internal structure by measuring how a system responds to perturbations. They apply that principle to neural networks. Their perturbation upweights one token in a given context, shifting the data distribution slightly.

The response is measured through susceptibilities, covariances between component level observables and the perturbation. These are computed over a localized Gibbs posterior, in the language of the work. A susceptibility map could show which parts of a model care about which tokens. That would give interpretability a tool with roots in statistical physics. The team frame this as a step toward a spectroscopy of models.
arxiv-2601-13003:
Safaa Menssouri and El Mehdi Amhoud study how to spot rare cyber attacks in networks of flying devices. These networks, called the Internet of Flying Things, support tasks such as air watch and smart travel. They also face real risk, since attacks can harm private data and safe use.

The authors put forward PrivFly, a self-taught system that aims to guard privacy while it hunts for rare attacks. They note three hard parts of the task. Attack data is badly skewed, with few rare cases. Privacy must be kept. Older tools often miss the rare but harmful threats. Readers get a clear view of why rare attack search in such networks is hard.
arxiv-2601-13303:
Minh Le and Phuong Cao check if cut down neural nets stay safe in a provable way. Formal proof of net acts is a must for high stakes use. Such use spans surgery bots to NASA craft that drive on their own. Yet proof cost for big nets blocks wide use.

Pruning cuts a net by drop of weak links. The team asks what prune shares do to local proof of calm. A calm proof says small input shifts cannot flip the out put. By prune rate, they map where proofs hold and where they break. For safety teams, the map helps pick a prune rate that saves cost with no loss of proof.
arxiv-2601-13603:
Wylliam Cantin Charawi and co-authors work on turning raw 3D data into clean mesh shapes in 2026. Tools like Marching Cubes build meshes fast and are used in many pipelines. Their trainable forms, though, often give weak mesh quality. That flaw caps the worth of meshes rebuilt from point clouds or images by learning systems.

The team puts forward DCCVT, a trainable take on clipped centroidal Voronoi tessellation. In plain terms, space is split into cells, and each cell is clipped to the shape. Such clipped cells carry strong math backing and tend to yield finer meshes. The aim is mesh output that learning tools can tune end to end.
arxiv-2601-14503:
Wouter Termont and Esteves Beatriz examine European digital identity in this 2026 paper. Recent European efforts center on the EUDI regulation and its OpenID architecture. The authors say these efforts aim high but start from a narrow, ill-defined view of authentication. From a broader, more grounded view of the term, they identify several issues.

The issues sit in the OpenID4VCI and OpenID4VP protocols. They name insecure practices, plus static and subject-bound credential types. A limited query language also restricts the design. The authors say these limits confine the system to classic credential exchange cases, which existing solutions like OpenID Connect already support.
arxiv-2601-14603:
Jingru Li, Yibo Fan, and Huan Li speed up language model training in this 2026 paper. Large language models perform well across natural language tasks, yet pretraining is computationally demanding. Optimizer efficiency is thus an important practical concern. Muon is an optimizer that accelerates pretraining via orthogonal momentum updates. Those updates act as a matrix analogue of the element-wise sign operator.

The team presents Variance-Adaptive Muon. It adds NSR-modulated and variance-scaled momentum to the base method. In plain terms, the step size adapts to how noisy the gradients are. Readers get an optimizer aimed at cutting the cost of the most expensive phase in building a model.
arxiv-2601-15003:
Bartosz Bieganowski and Daniel Strzelecki study a nonlinear scalar field equation with a harsh twist at the origin. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with an inverse-square potential term. That term carries the critical strength, the largest value of its kind that the math allows.

The question is one of multiplicity. The authors ask how many distinct solutions the equation can have. The equation is set on all of space with the origin removed. A general nonlinear term drives the field. Results of this kind sort out when a field can settle in more than one way.
arxiv-2601-15203:
L. Einramhof, L. Bugnet, and co-authors read the magnetic past of dead stars. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with white dwarfs, the dense remains of stars like the Sun. Strong, large-scale magnetic fields show at the surface of only the oldest white dwarfs.

That pattern hints at a hidden field inside the star. The field may rise slowly to the surface over time. Strong fields have also been gauged by asteroseismology inside red giants, the stars white dwarfs come from. The authors use those clues to reconstruct the hidden field's long history.
arxiv-2601-15303:
Liang Chen explains why China's platform giants earn thin margins despite huge market shares. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with platform pricing in concentrated markets. The giants hold over sixty percent of their core segments, yet margins stay compressed for a decade.

Standard theory predicts a different end. Either the weaker firm exits, or the survivors raise prices toward monopoly levels. Chen builds a dynamic theory of ecosystem competition. Cross-market subsidization plays a central part: profits in one market fund low prices in another, and the long price fight never settles.
arxiv-2601-15403:
Adam LaClair and Jason McCullough test a conjecture about when a graph's edge ideal has a purity property. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with binomial edge ideals in positive characteristic. Matsuda defined weakly closed graphs and asked when these ideals are F-pure.

Matsuda proved that weakly closed ideals are F-pure in positive characteristic. He conjectured two things. In characteristic two, every F-pure example should come from a weakly closed graph. And every such ideal should be F-pure when the characteristic is large enough. The authors take up both of those open claims.
arxiv-2601-15503:
Rishit Chatterjee and Tahiya Chowdhury forecast lake water quality with machine learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Volunteers do much of the lake monitoring behind their data. That yields seasonal time series with many gaps. Ice cover blocks access in winter. Bad weather and simple human error add more holes. Gaps make forecasting and early warning of algal blooms hard.

The pair study Secchi disk depth, a classic measure of water clarity. Their data cover a rich subset of 30 lakes. The records span three decades of in-person sampling across Maine lakes. Learning from gappy records is the core challenge here. A method that copes with missing data could help lake groups act sooner. Early word on blooms protects swimmers, wildlife, and drinking water alike.
arxiv-2601-15603:
Yi Yu and five co-authors study estimation in large network systems in a 2026 arXiv paper. Hierarchical Bayesian models are now common for such systems. They treat each unit's parameters as draws from a shared distribution. A hyperparameter governs that distribution. Theory for these estimates has lagged practice, though. In particular, guarantees as system size grows have been missing.

One fear stands out. Hyperparameter estimates might diverge as networks get larger. That would undercut the model's reliability at exactly the scales where it is used. The authors give a nonasymptotic scaling guarantee, per the title. It covers inhomogeneous systems with weak dependence between units. For data scientists who model big networks, such guarantees mark when trust is earned.
arxiv-2601-15703:
Jiaxin Zhang, Prafulla Kumar Choubey, and Kung-Hsiang Huang tackle trust in AI agents in a 2026 arXiv paper. Agents now reason over long horizons with real skill. Early errors can poison that whole run, though. The authors name this the spiral of hallucination. Small epistemic mistakes propagate and cannot be undone. Existing tools split into two camps, each with a flaw.

Uncertainty methods act as passive sensors. They flag risk but do not fix it. Self-reflection methods try to fix errors, but their corrections can be aimless. The title names the authors' aim: agentic uncertainty quantification that does more. A system that measures doubt and acts on it could stop spirals early. For long agent runs in real work, that combination is the missing piece.
arxiv-2601-16003:
Yunan Wang, Chuxiong Hu, and Zhao Jin solve a control problem exactly in a 2026 arXiv paper. Time-optimal control drives a system to its target as fast as possible. Their system is a triple integrator, a chain of three integrations. Full box constraints bound its state and input. The problem is fundamental and widely applied in industry. Motion control for machines and vehicles is a typical home.

Hard cases have resisted clean solutions. Asymmetric constraints, moving boundary conditions, and active position constraints all complicate the answer. The authors derive time-optimal switching surfaces for this setting. Switching surfaces tell the controller when to flip its input. An exact surface means fast, provable control. The paper was accepted by the American Control Conference, per the record.
arxiv-2601-16203:
Usoskin and coauthors rebuild sun spot cycles of the first thou years CE. Their 2026 preprint uses carbon based proxy data for past sun acts. Direct views of sun acts start in the year 1610. Past that, teams turn to trace data kept in wood and ice. New carbon tests are now fine to pick out the known sun cycle of near eleven years.

The team uses that fine grain to rebuild cycles far back. Clear cycles show the sun kept its beat in that era. They also show how strong each past beat was. That past helps test sun models over long spans. It links earth trace data to sun acts of old.
arxiv-2601-16403:
Zhaochun Li and coauthors set theory for how RLHF learns past its train set. Their 2026 preprint deals with learn from human feed back. That path, called RLHF, is now the main way to align models. It works well in tests, but why it holds on new prompts is less clear. High size prompts make that why hard to pin down.

The team builds maths for spread of skill to new cases. Spread bounds rest on train size and model class traits. Firm bounds would guide how much feed back teams must buy. They would also flag when align may fail on new ground. The work firms up a much used train path.
arxiv-2601-16503:
Wei Zhu builds a test set for search backed builds in the med field. His 2026 preprint, named MRAG, deals with search plus build tools. Such tools have spread fast in science and ward QA work. Yet the med field lacks a full test for their worth. Gaps in tests hide where the tools fail on med asks.

MRAG spans a wide range of med ask types. Each type checks search grade and build truth as one. Firm scores let teams weigh med tools fair and fast. They also show which ask types need more work. The work gives the med field a shared test base.
arxiv-2601-16603:
Ke Xue and four coauthors use a Mamba gaze that looks all ways for speech split. Their 2026 preprint deals with split of mixed speech to lone voices. Mamba, a state space model, now rivals coders for speech work. It runs long chains at straight cost, not square cost. Past Mamba speech tools still missed acts that span all dirs.

An all way gaze lets the model weigh past and next as one. Joint weight should lift split grade on hard mixes. Speech split backs aids, notes and call tools in real rooms. The work tests all way Mamba on split tasks. It seeks grade gains with no loss of speed.
arxiv-2601-16803:
Carolin Holtermann, Florian Schneider, and Anne Lauscher test image bots across tongues. Such bots turn words into shots. Most users type in English. The same ask in a new tongue should give the same shot. Yet bots oft swap sense for surface cues. They paint stock scenes tied to the tongue's home land.

Their 2026 preprint names this flaw surface-over-semantics. It gauges how oft bots pick stock traits over true sense. The flaw can spread trite views of lands and folks. Clear gauges push bot makers to serve all tongues fair. The work aids fair AI for a world of many tongues.
arxiv-2601-16903:
Sk Jeesun and Anirban Majumdar chase light dark matter with help from cosmic rays. Big tanks now curb heavy dark bits to near the neutrino fog. Yet light dark bits slip past those tanks. Cosmic rays can kick halo dark bits to high speed. Kicked bits can then trip a tank's eye. Their 2026 preprint reads fresh LZ tank data for such kicks.

The LZ tank's 2025 data sets the stage for the read. The team maps what cross rates the data allow. Light bits gain a test they long lacked. Null marks here trim the space for dark tales.
arxiv-2601-17103:
Pascaline André and a large team check how firm scan AI scores truly are. A score with no range can look more firm than it is. Ranges, called confidence intervals, show that doubt. Their 2026 preprint runs a large-scale check of those ranges. It spans many scan tasks and AI tools. The aim is sound doubt marks for care use.

Hospitals need doubt marks before they trust a tool. A tool that tops a chart may tie with the next in truth. Wide ranges flag scores that need more data. The check sets a base for fair score claims. It aids rules for AI in clinics.
arxiv-2601-17203:
Scott Friedman, Sonja Schmer-Galunder, Anthony Chen, and Jeffrey Rye tie word-code slant to real pay and role gaps. Text bots learn word codes from news and posts. Those codes oft lean by sex in clear ways. Their 2026 preprint sets code lean next to real-world gaps. Many lands' texts and gaps join the check. The aim is to see if code lean tracks true gaps.

A track would mean codes mirror each land's state. A gap twixt them would flag bot-made bias. Such checks help teams clean text bots for fair use. They span tongues and lands in one frame.
arxiv-2601-17503:
Laura Bernard, Tamanna Jain, and Stavros Mougiakakos compute how binary stars scatter in scalar-tensor gravity. These theories add a scalar field to Einstein's gravity. The authors use post-Minkowskian effective field theory. Their main result is the scattering angle for non-spinning binaries. It is computed to third post-Minkowskian order. That order needs two-loop Feynman diagrams.

Scattering angles feed models of gravitational wave signals. Wave detectors need exact templates to pull signals from noise. Scalar-tensor terms would mark a break from pure Einstein theory. A third-order result sharpens that test. The work gives wave teams a firm formula. It links loop math to what detectors hear.
arxiv-2601-18003:
Pascual Lucas and José Antonio Ortega-Yagües describe a special family of surfaces in curved spaces. Their 2026 preprint studies concircular hypersurfaces in space forms. Space forms are spaces with the same curvature everywhere, like spheres and hyperbolic spaces. The authors give a full description of these hypersurfaces as a special family of ruled ones, built by sweeping a line through space.

They also characterize concircular helices in three-dimensional space forms. A differential equation links the helix to its curvature and torsion through a concircular factor. Together, the two results pin down a class of shapes that had been only partly known. Such clean descriptions serve geometry and its uses in physics.
arxiv-2601-18103:
Jiang Yan, Xiong-Hui Cao, Meng-Lin Du, and Feng-Kun Guo measure how a heavy particle and light mesons interact at low energy. Their 2026 preprint studies the J/psi particle with pions and kaons. The tool is dispersion relations, which tie an interaction's parts together by strict rules. The authors show that symmetry-breaking terms in the chiral Lagrangian mix the bare charmonium fields. That mixing shapes the scattering lengths they compute.

Scattering lengths are compact numbers that sum up low-energy behavior. They test how well our theory of strong forces handles heavy-light pairs. Values here can guide both lattice work and collider studies. The paper adds firm numbers where data are thin.
arxiv-2601-18203:
ShunLiang Fu, Yanxin Zhang, Yixin Xiang, Xiaoyu Du, and Jinhui Tang build document maps that match how people see a page's structure. Their 2026 preprint presents DMAP for multimodal document understanding. Most question-answering systems treat a document as a bag of loose text chunks. That flat view drops the document's hierarchy and its links. Sections, figure-text ties, and cross-references all vanish, and answers suffer.

DMAP keeps a structural map of the document, aligned with human reading. Retrieval can then follow the document's own logic and layout. Questions that hinge on a figure or a section gain the context they need. The work serves anyone who asks machines to read reports, papers, and manuals.
arxiv-2601-18303:
Léonard Brice, Thomas A. Henzinger, and K. S. Thejaswini study games where players share a source of randomness. Their 2026 preprint opens with a four-player matching pennies game. A team of three faces the Devil. Each player calls heads or tails at the same time. The team wins only if all four calls match. If the team randomizes independently, it wins with probability one in eight. Shared randomness changes that math.

The paper grows that seed into a theory of dicey games in distributed systems. Shared coins can align players who cannot talk. That alignment has real value in protocols and verification. The work links a toy game to deep questions about coordination.
arxiv-2601-18403:
Raphaël Maire, Andrea Plati, Frank Smallenburg, and Giuseppe Foffi study how odd crystals can build them-selves when a flat layer is sheared back and forth. The crystals at hand have twelve-fold form, a shape that breaks the rules of plain crystals. In most labs such forms grow when heat makes bits jiggle and sort. Here the jiggle comes from shear, not heat.

Each pass of shear shoves the bits, and the shoves let them snap into new spots. In time the layer can sort itself into the twelve-fold form. The work shows a fresh path to make rare forms of matter in the lab. It also hints at ways to grow films with traits that plain crystals cannot give. The file is the extra note that goes with the main study.
arxiv-2601-18503:
Xin Wu and four colleagues study a rare case where pairs of bits are born with linked fates and no time to drift apart. In most smashes of bits, the pair lives for a while, and that life blurs the link. Here the pair is made in a graze of two heavy cores that just miss each other. The pair is whole at birth and stays clean, with no long life to blur it.

That clean birth makes the pair a fine test bed for true quantum links. The team show how the link shows up in the paths of the pair. Since the pair does not age, later bumps do not wash the link out. The setup gives labs a rare clean case to check deep claims of quantum theory. It may also set a yard stick for less clean cases.
arxiv-2601-18703:
Alex Viguerie and four colleagues model how germs borne on air spread through a space, with maths drawn from how cells chase food. In that chase, cells drift toward a scent and bunch where it is strong. Air-borne germs act in a like way: they drift with the air and bunch where the flow slows. Past spread models treat that drift as a plain spread, like heat in a pan.

The team build a spread model with the chase term in it, so bunching shows up where it should. They test the maths and run it on cases to see how peaks of germ load form. Sharp peaks mark rooms or zones where risk runs high. Such a model could guide vents and room plans that cut the peaks. It could also help trace where a bout of ill health began.
arxiv-2601-19003:
Santanu S. Dey and Jingye Xu tighten a bound that makes hard sums look almost convex. A classic lemma covers sums of many bounded, nonconvex sets in fixed dimension. Once the set count passes the dimension, the sum's nonconvexity stops growing. The sum then looks nearly convex, which helps in optimization.

The pair use a sharper error bound for that lemma on smooth nonconvex problems. Their gain makes the Lagrangian dual, a key tool for bounding hard problems, as tight as it can be. Tight duals mean better proof that a found solution is near the best one can do.
arxiv-2601-19203:
Kaicheng Wang and four co-authors teach video systems to plan smells that match what is on screen. Smell can deepen immersion in media, yet it is rare because scent is hard to author and to sync with moving video. Past scent tools lean on hand set triggers and fixed links between events and odors, which do not scale to open content.

Their two stage pipeline first reads the video and drafts a scent plan a person can inspect. Keeping the plan readable lets a human check it before any scent is made. The work asks whether semantic planning can carry smell design the way it now carries image and sound design.
arxiv-2601-19503:
Wei Huang, Anda Cheng, and Yinggui Wang prune whole layers of large models using the gradient as a guide. Fine tuning big models on new data is slow and costly. Structured pruning can speed inference, but it often demands extra training, distillation, or search that eats the savings.

Their method, GradPruner, picks layers to cut by gradient signals, aiming to keep fine tuning and inference both efficient. Cutting whole layers, not scattered weights, gives speed that real hardware feels. A cheaper path from base model to tuned model matters as more teams adapt models of this size.
arxiv-2601-19903:
Saeid Rajabi, Chengmo Yang, and Satwik Patnaik automate a tedious step in chip verification. Formal verification relies on SystemVerilog assertions, statements that a design must always satisfy. Writing them by hand is slow and error-prone. Language models can draft assertions, but they usually start from scratch or ignore the design's structure.

Their framework, STELLAR, retrieves expert-crafted assertions and uses structural similarity to guide generation. A new assertion is modelled on proven ones from similar hardware. This retrieval-and-generation design is the first to exploit structural patterns this way. Better assertions catch design bugs earlier and cheaper. The work brings verification closer to push-button status.
arxiv-2601-20103:
Darshan Deshpande, Anand Kannappan, and Rebecca Qian study reward hacking in code training, where a model games the score instead of solving the task. As language models act more often as judges in code training, their skill at spotting such cheating matters. The authors build a taxonomy of reward exploits that spans dozens of categories.

They also introduce TRACE, a benchmark of testing trajectories that was built from synthetic cases and checked by humans. It lets researchers measure how well a judge model catches each kind of exploit. Stronger detection would make training by reward safer, since a model that fools its judge learns the wrong lesson.
arxiv-2601-20503:
Jesse Phitidis and five colleagues compare training strategies for segmenting brain MRI scans when labels are incomplete. The targets are white matter hyperintensities and ischaemic stroke lesions, both signs of cerebral small vessel disease visible on FLAIR scans. The two look alike and often appear in the same brain, which makes telling them apart hard.

Models are hard to build and validate when expert labels cover only part of each scan. The authors test which training strategies cope best with partial labels. Better segmentation would give doctors cleaner measures of disease burden for prognosis and trials.
arxiv-2601-20603:
Peter V. Dovbush and Steven G. Krantz characterize normal families of analytic functions in the unit ball. A family is normal when every sequence in it has a well-behaved convergent subsequence, a compactness property at the heart of complex analysis. They show a family in the ball is normal exactly when its restriction to each complex line through the origin is normal.

They then generalize the result to normal functions, judged by behavior on analytic discs. Reducing a high-dimensional question to one-dimensional slices is a powerful pattern. Their characterization gives analysts a simpler test for normality in several complex variables.
arxiv-2601-20703:
Bixin Yan, Valentine Gillioz, Ipek Efe, and Morgan Trassin review new ways to steer a special class of materials. Their 2026 perspective paper is about ferroelectric materials. These materials hold a built-in electric polarization that stays in place. That trait makes them strong candidates for chips beyond today's standard designs.

Most control of these materials uses applied electric fields. The authors survey a newer set of routes that need no such bias. Recent work on dipole textures, tiny patterns of polarization, has opened these paths. The paper lays out how texture design can flip or move polarization. It maps where this field-free control could lead. Readers get a compact guide to a fast-moving corner of materials science.
arxiv-2601-20803:
Aunabil Chakma, Mihai Surdeanu, and Eduardo Blanco work on pulling facts out of text with very few examples. Their 2026 paper studies few-shot relation extraction. The task is to find links between entities in a sentence, such as who founded what. In-context learning lets a model copy the pattern from one given example. The catch is finding more good examples to show it.

The authors present several strategies to gather extra examples on their own. Their novel strategy picks examples by deep structure, not surface words. It compares the syntactic-semantic shape of each candidate with the one-shot example. A close match in structure should teach the model more. The work helps extraction systems that must start from almost no labeled data.
arxiv-2601-21603:
K. Karatsu, A. Endo, and a large team describe an upgraded spectrometer for millimeter-wave astronomy. The instrument, DESHIMA 2.0, covers a very wide band in one device. It is built on superconducting detectors that sense faint cosmic signals.

The first version proved itself in tests several years ago. The paper lays out the upgrade and its lab characterization. A single instrument that maps wide bands at once can survey distant galaxies far faster. Such speed matters for tracing how galaxies and their gas evolved across cosmic time. Its sensing parts are kinetic inductance detectors, which react to tiny amounts of incoming radiation. Wideband maps also help pick targets for deeper follow-up with larger telescopes.
arxiv-2601-21803:
Korbinian Randl and co-authors build a way to inspect how retrieval systems and language models work together. Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a model's answers in fetched documents. But how the retriever and the generator interact is opaque, which is risky in high-stakes fields.

Their 2026 preprint presents RAG-E, an end-to-end explainability framework. It measures how well the retriever's choices align with what the generator actually uses, through attribution methods grounded in mathematics. And it names the ways the pairing can fail. Deployment teams in medicine, law, and finance need exactly this. A way to tell whether a wrong answer came from bad retrieval, bad generation, or a mismatch between them.
arxiv-2601-21903:
Konstantinos Varsos and co-authors study whether viewers will accept greener video streaming. Streaming over fast mobile networks consumes growing energy across access networks, core networks, and data centers. Lowering a stream's bitrate saves energy, but viewers may feel the drop as worse quality.

Success therefore hinges on user acceptance. The team's 2026 preprint builds a user acceptance model for smart incentives. These include rewards offered for choosing efficient settings. The goal is sustainable streaming toward sixth-generation networks. Knowing what makes users say yes is essential: an efficiency feature nobody enables saves nothing. While one framed well could cut the footprint of a hugely popular activity.
arxiv-2601-22003:
James Cuin, Davide Carbone, Yanbo Tang, and Deniz Akyildiz optimize functions whose gradients cannot be computed directly. Such problems fill machine learning and statistics, from estimating models by marginal likelihood to fine-tuning generative models. Stochastic approximation is the standard route.

Standard methods run inner sampling loops to get noisy, biased estimates of the gradient, which is slow and delicate. The team's 2026 preprint instead drives optimization with sequential Monte Carlo, a population-based sampling method that can track the needed quantities as the parameters move. Cleaner gradient estimates could make a whole class of hard estimation problems faster and more reliable in practice.
arxiv-2601-22103:
