The memo adds one more veiled page to the case file. Its redactions are part of its record, marking what still cannot be said. For readers, it stands among the secrets behind the secrets, the guarded routine of the spy business.
cia-0000012403:
The day's second sitting gets its own record: meeting number fifteen, London, May 4, 1961. Penkovsky is named in the title this time. Double days were becoming the pattern that spring in London. The pattern showed how much the colonel carried in his memory. It also showed how hard his handlers pressed to draw it out before his trip ended and the door closed.

The fifteenth session's record sustains the debriefings' intensity. Morning's questions bred afternoon's, as each answer opened new ground. For readers, the page measures a source who seemed, to the men questioning him, inexhaustible.
cia-0000012803:
Small observations from Hanoi fill a CIA paper from May 1967, a notebook of the enemy capital's details. American planes bombed the north, but Americans could not walk its streets. What reached Langley came through travelers, defectors, and watchers abroad. The miscellany collects their scraps: prices, moods, uniforms, shortages. Together they form the small change of a city at war, spent daily under the bombs.

Such trivia accumulated into a portrait no single report could give. The enemy's seat was observed at one remove, and honestly labeled as such. For readers, the paper shows intelligence at its most human scale: the small things, noticed.
cia-0000013603:
Subversion in Honduras is the danger weighed in a CIA paper from January 1964. The small republic's weakness was its exposure. Honduras sat between revolutionary Cuba's admirers and nervous neighbors, with an army that ruled as much as it guarded. Its strategic spot on the map belied its size, sitting astride routes and borders that mattered to every plan Washington drew for the region.

The paper weighs the left's chances and the regime's defenses. It treats the banana republic's red scare with the seriousness of the era. For readers, it shows how thoroughly the Cold War graded even its smallest stages.
cia-0000013903: Two American prisoners were observed in Binh Dinh Province, in a CIA note dated November 5, 1967. The note is brief and gives no names in its title. Even so, a count of two at a known place helped track the southern camps. Reports like this piled up into the full prisoner picture officials worked from.
cia-0000014803: Testimony before a federal grand jury anchors an untitled CIA file dated May 2, 1950. The witness is unnamed in the title, and the case is left unsaid. Grand jury words built the spy cases in secret that spring. A scrap like this marks one step in the quiet march toward the Rosenberg arrests.
cia-0000015303: A letter to Donald Keyhoe from J. S. Harman fills a CIA file dated March 4, 1958. Harman wrote that he found nothing reflecting the point raised, per the title. Keyhoe was the loudest saucer author of the age, pressing the government for answers. A flat reply like this was the standard wall he met.
cia-0000037103: Disbursements for travel and other expenses are listed in a CIA record dated October 3, 1942, naming Cook, Dulles, Nelson, Rado, Tyler, and Foss. The page comes from the first year of the OSS, the wartime office that grew into the CIA. It sets out payments in the dry form of a ledger, name by name. Bookkeeping like this tracked the cost of building a secret service from scratch.
cia-0000045203:
Salvadoran officials reportedly negotiated the kidnapping in Panama, in a CIA record dated September 1, 1985. Panama offered neutral ground away from San Salvador's dangers. Secret talks abroad were the crisis's hidden second track.

Inside, the reported Panama channel is recorded as it leaked out. Back channels work only while they stay unspoken and unseen. Once reported in the press, they become part of the public bargaining too, whether the negotiators in Panama wished it or not at the time. The file preserves the moment the secret track surfaced, when a negotiation meant to be invisible became one more headline in a watched and worried country.
cia-0000046503: Sources in Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam, their names blacked out, spoke to the prisoner and missing-men question in a CIA item dated March 6, 1988. What people inside those countries said was the hardest kind of evidence to get and to judge. The item gathers regional voices on an issue Washington usually heard about secondhand.
cia-0000049003: A strong movement among right-wing Salvadoran officers aimed to overthrow the revolutionary government in 1980, and a CIA item from that year tracks it. The junta then ruling in San Salvador sat between a rebellious right and a rising guerrilla left. The item preserves the coup danger as watchers saw it then, from inside the files.
cia-0000049203: Senior officers of ESAF, the Salvadoran armed forces, met at a high level in 1991 to discuss the Jesuit case. A CIA item from that year preserves the meeting, kept with the Truth Commission records. By then the case was the single greatest danger the institution faced, greater than the guerrillas that year.
cia-0000049303: San Salvador, the capital, stood tense in a CIA item from 1989, kept with the Truth Commission records. Capital tense was a headline built from mood: rumors, troop movements, and a city listening for the offensive everyone expected. The item preserves the held breath of a city that had learned to read its own danger.
cia-0000049403: El Salvador Situation Report number fourteen is preserved as declassified CIA document 0000049403, dated February 3, 1983. Marked for the Truth Commission, it belongs to a numbered situation report series. The file's chief interest is serial: one dated installment in a running sequence of Salvadoran situation reports, showing the routine form of the agency's wartime updates.
cia-0000096503: Third Report to the President by the President's Board of Consultants on Foreign Intelligence Activities appears again as declassified CIA document 0000096503, dated January 1, 1959. The catalog holds several records of this same board report with different dates. Readers get another dated copy in that run, useful mainly for showing how often the report was filed.
cia-0000119203:
In August 1968 the CIA compared an unidentified prisoner photograph, numbered 109, with known photos of Roy F. Townley. The task was simple to state and hard to do: decide whether the man in the prisoner photo was Townley. Work like this sat at the center of the prisoner accounting effort.

Photo comparison was painstaking work done from grainy prints and old service pictures. A match could bring a family long-awaited news, while a wrong call could do real harm. The document preserves one such comparison, showing how analysts tried to put names to faces when the prisoners themselves could not be asked.
cia-0000119703:
A September 1952 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in the Union of South Africa. The country was four years into formal apartheid, and its government was tightening racial rule. Analysts in Washington were asked to chart where the country was heading.

Forecast papers like this one weighed a government's strength, its opposition, and the pressures that might change it. South Africa posed hard questions, since it was both an anti-communist partner and a state building open racial rule. The paper records the agency's early read on that problem. It marks the start of a long American effort to judge a regime whose policies would trouble relations for decades.
cia-0000124303: A November 1962 CIA technical report works out the sizes of Cosmos series satellites from their mass, area ratio, and brightness, adding matching figures for American satellites. Analysts sized up Soviet craft from the light they reflected. The paper shows technical intelligence at its most careful. Brightness tricks let analysts estimate size for craft they could never inspect, a standard method of the years before spy satellites could settle such questions directly.
cia-0000132203: Situation report 520, from January 1991, reports Israeli fears that Iraqi chemical attacks are imminent, with Israel misspelled in the original heading. Fear of gas-tipped missiles drove the handing out of gas masks. The report records that anxiety as filed. Israel's fear had deep roots in the gas attacks of the Iran war, and the sitrep's misspelling survives as a fingerprint of reporting done at crisis speed.
cia-0000132403: Cuba and Latin America are paired in a CIA document carrying an estimated date of January 1, 1961. The invasion at the Bay of Pigs was still three months away. Havana's revolution was already sending its example across the hemisphere. The short document covers that regional picture, as analysts watched governments and rebel movements react to the Cuban model in the new year.
cia-0000132503: Dissension inside Ecuador over policy toward Cuba fills a CIA document dated February 3, 1961. It pairs with a warning from the same month that violence might break out there over the same issue. The Cuba question was dividing governments and parties across the region that year. The short document tracks the Ecuadorian dispute and the sides forming within it.
cia-0000133203: Eighty-three photographs marked with the code name JMTIDE fill a CIA paper carrying an estimated date of January 1, 1961. The paper itself is untitled in the record. JMTIDE was an agency code name, and its meaning is not given here. The photographs form the picture file of some covert program. The short paper keeps the set in the bare form the record gives it.
cia-0000136703: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade documents, cataloged at 1 January 1961 with the date flagged as estimated. The new year found the brigade of anti-Castro exiles in training for a secret invasion. The record states no subject for this item. It is preserved in Spanish in the declassified release, grouped with the other estimated New Year records in the brigade's file, and described on that basis.
cia-0000137003: Asylees sheltering in embassies create a dangerous problem in this June 1954 cable on extradition, signed under J. C. King. Through a channel, a request is made to resolve a tense and potentially explosive situation in Guatemala City, where diplomatic establishments including the Ecuadoran embassy hold asylees. If Ecuador refuses and insists on safe conduct, the asylees would have to be received by Ecuador, adding Iron Curtain trained communists and hardened criminals to its already alarming local communist situation. Prestige and precedent are both invoked.
cia-0000140403: Consultants for a hypnosis research project are recommended in this February 1952 memo. It discusses an unnamed psychologist known for his work in hypnosis. One researcher's ten-year experiments form a careful classic. His book is key reading for anyone serious in the field. He is now feeble and no longer interested. His two chief assistants remain active and valuable. Another man is very able and broad-minded. He has experience in research, lab, clinical, and business psychology. His judgment on hypnotism or drugs is trusted.
cia-03006503: THE COMMUNIST WINTER-SPRING OFFENSIVE IN SOUTH VIETNAM, a CIA assessment. The offensive analysis. This file preserves that declassified paper. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
cia-03192203: The sixth of January 1958 opened with this bulletin. Analysts briefed Washington on global events. The Cold War's new-year memo. The library keeps the document safe. This declassified bulletin is held. The text is preserved.
cia-06157003: LP OR MILITARY REGION 1 UPDATE FOR DECEMBER 1983: DELIVERY OF SOVIET-MADE CHEC, a CIA document. The Laos update. This file preserves that declassified paper. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
cia-06778003: SOVIET AND CUBAN DISAPPOINTMENT IN RESULTS OF 3-6 MAY 1984 INTERNATIONAL CONFE, a CIA document. The communist disappointment. This file preserves that declassified paper. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
coniston-volume-03: The third volume deepens the stirring political drama of Coniston. The hero's high ideals clash head-on with the party machine. New Hampshire politics turn personal, bitter, and fierce. The gathering story builds steadily toward its climax.
constitution-qatar-2003: Qatar's 2003 Constitution, passed by referendum, frames its emirate. The Emir rules. The Tower library holds the full text. It ordered gas wealth. Emir reigned. Riches flowed. Law framed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-romania-2003: Romania's 1991 Constitution, amended 2003, frames its republic. It buried Ceausescu. The Tower library holds the full text. It ended a tyrant. Crowds stormed. Dictator fell. Europe beckoned. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
crowley-equinox-vol-1-no-03:
March 1910 opened the second year of The Equinox with its third number. Crowley edited the journal as the organ of his order, and its bulk grew with each issue. The spring number mixes rite texts, essays, and reviews in the journal's settled plan.

New work from Crowley's pen stands beside pieces by his students and friends. The number carries the ongoing course of the order into print for any reader to test. Scholars mine these pages for first printings of the Thelemic canon. The issue is one solid block in the founding archive of the school.
cumont-mysteries-mithra-1903:
Franz Cumont, a Belgian scholar of the old faiths, wrote this study of Mithraism, and Thomas J. McCormack turned it into English in 1903. It was the first full book on the cult in English. Cumont had spent years on the shrines, stones, and texts of the cult.

Mithra, the bull slayer, was a god of the Roman ranks, with rites kept in cave like shrines. Cumont sets out the cult's myths, grades of rank, and spread through the Roman world. His book founds the study of Mithra in the West, and it still sets the frame.
dead-men-tell-no-tales-pg1703: E. W. Hornung's 1899 adventure novel opens with a shipwreck and a survivor who may not be who he claims. Hidden identities, buried secrets, and a villain unmasked drive this non-Raffles thriller. Full of suspense: ripping Edwardian adventure from a master storyteller.
delitzsch-babel-bibel-mccormack-1903:
Friedrich Delitzsch was a leading German Assyriologist who gave three famous lectures in Berlin on what Babylon gave the Bible. His Babel and Bible, in McCormack's 1903 translation, carries the Kaiser-era lectures to English readers. The talks set off the great Babel-Bibel controversy across Europe.

Delitzsch claims that stories of creation, flood, and law in the Hebrew Bible grew from older Babylonian roots. Churchmen attacked him for lowering the Bible to a copy, while scholars weighed the tablets he cited. The fight forced a wide public to face how deeply Israel's faith sat within its ancient world.
denon-travels-egypt-vol-1-1803:
Vivant Denon rode with the troops of France to Egypt, and Vol. 1 of his Travels, in English from 1803, shows what he saw. Denon was an artist at the court of France. He drew as the troops marched: camps, fights, towns, and the first grand views of tombs and shrines that most in Europe had yet to see.

Arthur Aikin turned the French text to English prose. The tome made Egypt a craze in the West at once. Its zest still leaps off the page. All the field's art starts near here.
denon-travels-egypt-vol-2-1803:
Vivant Denon pushes up the Nile in Vol. 2 of his Travels in Upper and Lower Egypt, in English from 1803. The first tome told of the march and the low lands. Here the troops reach the great shrines of the south. Denon draws each gate, hall, and carved wall while shells and heat press the camp each day.

His zest for the strange land fills each page. Old lore and new peril mix in his log. The tome holds some of the first true views of the south shrines. Fans still feel its thrill.
denon-travels-egypt-vol-3-1803:
Vivant Denon brings his trek to a close in Vol. 3 of his Travels, in English from 1803. The set as a whole is the first full drawn tale of old Egypt for the West. In this last tome the artist sums his finds, lists the sites, and gives the plates their full gloss in calm, clear words.

Denon went home to shape the great state book on Egypt. His own tale came first and reached more hands. It taught the West to see Egypt as grand, not just strange. The set ends here in fine form.
dieterich-mithrasliturgie-1903:
Albrecht Dieterich published his edition of the so-called Mithras Liturgy in 1903, in German. The ritual survives inside a great Greek magical papyrus from Egypt. Dieterich gave it a text, translation, and long commentary.

The rite guides a soul upward through the heavens toward the sun god. Prayers, secret names, and breath control mark the ascent's stages. Dieterich connected the text with the Mithras mysteries, a link scholars still debate. His publication changed study of ancient magic and mystery religion overnight. The liturgy remains one of the most discussed ritual texts from antiquity. Dieterich's commentary still frames the argument.
doe-osti-2588284-outgassing-screening-of: AE3030 adhesives got their outgassing screening, and this DOE report covers the LS variant too. The pages detail the test results. The materials folks get their data. The adhesives were AE3030. The screening was outgassing. The folks were material. The results were test.
dubois-souls-of-black-folk-1903:
W. E. B. Du Bois published The Souls of Black Folk in 1903, a book of fourteen essays on race in America. Du Bois was a scholar trained at Fisk, Harvard, and Berlin. He writes of the color line as the central problem of the new century. Chapters mix history, sociology, memoir, and fiction.

He describes double-consciousness, the sense of seeing oneself through white eyes. He honors the sorrow songs sung by enslaved people. He also disputes Booker T. Washington's call for patience on rights. Each chapter opens with lines of music and verse. The book is a cornerstone of Black American thought and American letters.
eddy-manual-mother-church-1903:
Mary Baker Eddy governed her church by a book of by-laws, the Manual of The Mother Church, seen here in its 89th edition of 1903. The Manual fixes the structure of Christian Science: officers, services, discipline, and the duties of members. Eddy revised it across her lifetime, and its text was set within her church's rules.

Small as it is, the Manual works as an organizational charter meant to outlast its author. Every branch church orders its affairs by these pages. Students of the movement read it beside Eddy's other writings to see how a charismatic founding became a lasting institution.
encyclopaedia-biblica-vol4-1903:
The fourth volume of the Encyclopaedia Biblica appeared in 1903, completing the set with Q to Z. Cheyne and Black closed their great critical dictionary four years after it began. It had drawn praise, outrage, and heavy use in equal measure.

Final articles cover the Resurrection debates, sacrifice, the Temple, and the writings of the New Testament. Indexes and additions tie the four volumes together. The encyclopaedia's method, treating the Bible as ancient literature to be tested, won the future of scholarship. Read today, it shows the moment when modern Bible study came of age in English.
engels-ludwig-feuerbach-lewis-1903:
Friedrich Engels reckoned with Hegel and Feuerbach in his Ludwig Feuerbach, first issued in 1886. Austin Lewis translated the work for Charles H. Kerr in 1903. Engels, Marx's lifelong partner, tells how German philosophy reached its end in their hands. Feuerbach had restored materialism, yet stopped halfway, in Engels's view.

Engels sets dialectical materialism against the mechanical kind he faults in others. Mind, nature, and history move through conflict and change, on his account. The book became a classic short statement of the Marxist worldview. Marx's Theses on Feuerbach appear as an appendix here, and also as a separate entry. Students still start with this text.
equality-pg7303: Edward Bellamy's follow-up to Looking Backward takes Julian West deeper into the year 2000 — its work, its play, its plain living. Less famed than the first book, it rounds out his dream of a fair world. A key work of old American socialist hope.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-03: Volume three of the Essays ranges across Montaigne's favorite themes. He muses on custom, cruelty, and the strangeness of human nature. The tone is honest, playful, and deeply personal. A master thinking aloud on the page.
europmc-pmc10024303:
Kitagawa and fellow experts present the 2022 practice guidelines for esophageal cancer from the Japan Esophageal Society, in this first part of the guideline set. Esophageal cancer is a serious disease of the food pipe, and care standards differ between countries. Japan's society updates its guidance as new evidence appears.

Part one sets out the shared base for care, including how the disease is classed and staged. It frames the choices doctors face on testing and treatment paths. Later parts go deeper into each treatment. Clinicians get an official, current statement of good practice from a leading national society.
europmc-pmc10202803:
Subbiah and a large trial team present final results of the phase two ROAR trial in a 2023 paper. The trial tested two drugs together, dabrafenib and trametinib, in rare cancers carrying a BRAF V600E mutation. That mutation appears across many tumor types and drives growth through a known pathway that both drugs block.

The basket trial enrolled patients by mutation rather than by cancer type, across eight groups. The paper reports how well the drug pair worked and how safe it was. The results support mutation-based treatment for rare cancers.
europmc-pmc10384403:
Aghababaei and Hadidi reviewed quercetin in 2023, a plant compound found in fruits and vegetables. People have eaten it in food for centuries. Lab work links it to a wide range of health effects. It can soak up free radicals, the unstable bits that damage cells.

Quercetin also calms swelling by blocking signals that drive it. Aghababaei reports that it slows cancer cell growth and can trigger their death. Heart gains may include lower blood pressure and lower blood fats. The review covers the compound's form, its uptake in the body, and ways to deliver it. The authors still call for more work on safe long-term use.
europmc-pmc10719103:
Zhang and a large team built a cell atlas of the whole mouse brain in 2023 at fine detail. The brain holds millions of cells in a dense web of types. The team imaged over 1,100 genes in about 10 million cells across the full adult brain. A second data set added whole gene profiles for the same cell types.

The atlas sorts cells into more than 5,000 clusters, grouped in over 300 major types. Zhang mapped how each type spreads across brain regions. Zones with set cell mixes emerged, plus smooth gradients of change between them. The map also flagged which cell pairs likely talk to each other, and by which signals. It lays a base for studies of brain circuits in health and disease.
europmc-pmc10777403:
Heid and co-authors describe a free software package for chemists in this 2024 paper. Chemists often need to guess traits of a molecule, such as how it mixes with water or fat, before making it. Deep learning, a type of AI that learns from examples, can make those guesses fast. Many chemists, though, are not AI experts and need tools that are simple to run.

Their package, Chemprop, builds on a neural network design that passes notes between atoms in a molecule. The new version handles pairs of molecules, reactions, single atoms, and light spectra, meaning how a substance absorbs light. It also offers ways to judge how sure a guess is. Tests on shared datasets show top scores on several tasks, the authors report.
europmc-pmc10949203:
GBD 2021 Nervous System Disorders Collaborators chart the global burden of brain and nerve diseases in this 2024 study. These disorders range from child development conditions to late-life nerve decay and new harms such as thinking problems after COVID. Past global counts covered only 15 conditions and left out many that damage nerves. This study widens the count to 37 conditions.

The team estimated deaths, case counts, and years of healthy life lost from 1990 to 2021. Counts cover 204 countries and split by age and sex. They also counted nerve harm that flows from birth defects, infections, and other ills. Risk factors tied to each condition were weighed as well. The authors say the fuller picture should guide where care and prevention funds go. It also shows how the burden shifts as populations age.
europmc-pmc1156903:
Martin and Rygiewicz develop DNA primers that pick fungi out of environmental samples in this 2005 paper. The internal transcribed spacer region of fungal ribosomal DNA varies greatly between species. Reading it identifies fungi, but primers must copy fungal DNA while skipping plant DNA from the same sample. Existing primers varied in success, and labs often needed several sets, which could create artificial distinctions.

The authors tested numerous primer sequences against the twin criteria of broad fungal reach and plant exclusion. A nested set of four primers performed well at amplifying fungal spacer regions. Extra primers in a conserved segment let the two spacer parts be amplified separately. The set was validated on a range of mushroom-forming fungi and cultured ascomycetes. The paper offers the set as a single standard assay.
europmc-pmc1190203:
Zuccato and co-authors tried a bold way to track cocaine use in 2005. Surveys and crime data give only rough, biased pictures. Drug traces in rivers and sewage offer direct field proof. The team sampled water in Italy with precise lab methods.

Cocaine and its main breakdown product both showed up in samples. The River Po alone carried about four kilograms per day. Flow and population data turned traces into use estimates. Those estimates topped what official figures suggested. Zuccato shows wastewater can reveal real drug use in a community.
europmc-pmc11993303:
Aroney and co-authors introduced a software tool called CoverM in 2025. CoverM serves metagenomics, the study of mixed microbe samples. Scientists match DNA reads to reference genomes. Coverage, how deeply each genome is read, guides the analysis.

Coverage helps sort genomes from mixtures and gauge community makeup. Each older tool defined coverage in its own way. CoverM unifies several coverage stats in one package. It streams alignment results to save time and disk use. Aroney wrote it in Rust, with add-ons for Python and Julia users. It appeared in Bioinformatics in 2025.
europmc-pmc1314903:
Barbosa, Tanus-Santos, Gerlach, and Parsons reviewed lead exposure markers in 2005. Blood lead is the primary measure for monitoring exposure. Health agencies set 10 micrograms per deciliter as the child concern level. Newer studies report harm below that line, suggesting no safe level.

A single blood reading cannot separate past from recent exposure. Lead cycles between bone, blood, and soft tissues for years. Serial measurements estimate outcomes better than one-off tests. The review weighs advantages and limits of each biomarker. Barbosa calls for tools that read stored lead, not just circulating lead.
europmc-pmc13155203:
van Amerongen, Bowman, and Nusse traced stem cells in the mouse mammary gland in 2012. The gland grows and remodels heavily in pregnancy. Which cells drive that growth in intact tissue was unknown. A genetic label marked cells responding to Wnt and beta-catenin signals.

Labeling revealed a signaling switch around birth. Marked cells fed different lineages depending on life stage. Behavior in transplants differed from behavior in place. In adults, marked cells built milk structures across repeated pregnancies. That proves a responsive adult stem cell exists. Timing and stage dictate what these cells become.
europmc-pmc1779303:
Zhao and co-authors used the small flowering plant Arabidopsis thaliana in 2007 to test a hard problem in gene hunting. When researchers link DNA markers to a trait, the link may reflect shared ancestry rather than a real gene effect. That mix-up is called confounding by population structure.

The group worked with a world sample of 95 plant lines and several traits tied to flowering time. They compared many ways to correct for shared ancestry, using both real data and altered test data. A newer mixed-model method, which uses genome-wide kinship between plants, cut false hits best while keeping real power. Adding results from F2 crosses confirmed one known true link and flagged new ones, but false hits and misses still remained.
europmc-pmc1796903:
Strobl and colleagues warned in 2007 that a popular machine learning tool can rank the wrong factors as most important. The tool is the random forest, an ensemble of decision trees used to pick which variables predict an outcome. Its importance scores guide choices such as which genetic markers to keep for disease prediction.

Simulations showed the scores mislead when candidate variables differ in scale or in how many categories they carry. Two flaws cause the bias. Trees tend to pick multi-category or wide-scale variables at each split, and resampling the data with replacement adds a second distortion. Weak variables can thus look artificially strong. The authors propose an alternate random forest implementation that removes the bias and restores fair variable selection.
europmc-pmc1904203:
Liang, Ridzon, Wong and Chen charted in 2007 the levels of microRNAs across normal human tissues. MicroRNAs are tiny regulators that tune gene activity, and knowing their healthy baseline is the first step to spotting disease shifts. Matched normal samples are the reference every disease study needs.

The team measured 345 microRNAs in 40 normal tissue types. Some microRNAs appeared everywhere, while several groups showed only in, or mostly in, specific tissues. MicroRNAs that rose and fell together often sat in the same genome clusters, hinting at shared control switches. Grouping tissues by their microRNA profiles reproduced their anatomy and function, suggesting a microRNA's job can be guessed from where it is active. In brain and blood cells, predicted targets of scarce microRNAs clustered in development genes for those very systems.
europmc-pmc1952203:
de Munter, van Dam and co-authors asked in 2007 whether eating whole grains, bran, or germ protects against type 2 diabetes. Weight control is the proven lever for prevention, but the role of specific foods was less settled. Whole grains keep the bran and germ that refining removes.

They followed 161,737 American women in two Nurses' Health Studies, all free of diabetes, heart disease, and cancer at the start. Over 12 to 18 years, 6,486 women developed type 2 diabetes. Median whole grain intake ranged from about four grams a day in the lowest fifth to about 31 to 40 grams in the highest fifth, depending on the cohort. Risk comparisons for the highest against the lowest intake were then adjusted for other lifestyle factors. A pooled review of other cohorts completed the analysis.
europmc-pmc1976403:
Stam and Reijneveld reviewed in 2007 how graph theory, the mathematics of networks, is being applied to the brain. Network science had recently revealed small-world and scale-free patterns across complex systems, plus rules linking a network's shape to the dynamics running on it. Neuroscience was a natural next target.

Graph analysis now serves in studies of model neural networks, anatomical wiring, and functional connectivity from fMRI, EEG, and MEG recordings. The evidence suggests the human brain works as a complex network with small-world structure in both its wiring and its activity. That layout may optimize rapid synchronization and information transfer at minimal wiring cost, balancing local processing against global integration. The authors note the functional network's shape is likely restrained by genes and anatomy, yet can shift with state and disease.
europmc-pmc2002403:
Bronchud and colleagues tested in 1987 a lab-made growth factor in patients with small cell lung cancer. The factor, called G-CSF, boosts neutrophils, white cells that fight infection. Chemotherapy often wipes those cells out. Twelve patients with advanced cancer first received the factor alone by continuous infusion for five days, at five dose levels.

No toxic effects appeared from the factor itself. Neutrophil counts rose fast in all 12 patients. The new cells moved and killed bacteria normally in tests. During later chemotherapy cycles, the factor cut the period of severe neutropenia by a median of 80 percent. Six severe infections occurred in cycles without it. None occurred in cycles with it.
europmc-pmc2077903:
Brueggemann, Pai, Crook and Beall documented in 2007 how pneumococcal bacteria evaded a childhood vaccine in the United States. The vaccine PCV7, introduced in 2000, sharply cut invasive pneumococcal disease. Yet disease from serotype 19A, a capsule type the vaccine misses, was rising. Part came from an older circulating strain. The team hunted for a newer genetic event, called capsular switching.

Sequencing 51 strains revealed a single swapped DNA stretch of 39,000 bases. It carried the capsule genes plus two penicillin-binding proteins. One swap therefore changed the capsule to 19A and reduced penicillin susceptibility at once. Since 2003, 37 such vaccine escape strains had been detected. Two new 19A escape types emerged in 2005. The authors warn this process could erode vaccine gains.
europmc-pmc2124703: A medical paper on tetany, the parathyroid glands, and calcium metabolism. The cramping disease. This article preserves that endocrine research. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2124803: A medical paper with studies in edema, the influence of nephrectomy and other surgical operations. The kidney-less swelling. This article preserves that nephrology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2125003: A medical paper with experiments on insect transmission of the poliomyelitis virus. The polio carriers. This article preserves that virology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc2125403: A medical paper on partial occlusion of the aorta with a metallic band and blood pressure observations. The banded vessel. This article preserves that vascular research. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2128503: A medical paper with studies on pneumococcus growth inhibition, the protective action of gelatin. The gelatin shield. This article preserves that bacteriology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2131403: A medical paper on the electrophoresis of the blood platelets of the horse. The horse platelets' charge. This article preserves that hematology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131603: A medical paper with further notes on the filtration of the virus of vaccinia. The filtered vaccine. This article preserves that virology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2140303: Cut a worm the wrong way and it regrows backwards, which is why this paper probed the physiological basis of polarity in regeneration. The researchers studied the first principles. The regrowth's direction, explained. The article preserves that developmental biology research.
europmc-pmc2140403: A biology paper on ion series and the physical properties of proteins. The protein ions. This article preserves that biochemistry. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2180203: A medical paper with studies on experimental pneumonia, pathology and pathogenesis. The lab pneumonia's damage. This article preserves that pathology. Coming generations can find it. It retains its place in time. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2267703:
Langfelder and Horvath presented eigengene networks in 2007 for studying relationships between gene co-expression modules. Genes working together form modules, groups whose activity rises and falls in concert. Plenty of methods detect modules, but few examine how modules relate to each other. The authors summarise each module by its eigengene, a representative activity profile. They then build networks whose nodes are those eigengenes.

Their method also detects consensus modules shared across two or more networks. Differential analysis tests whether network properties survive across data sets. Applications covered human and chimpanzee brains, four mouse tissues, and sex differences in mice linked to clinical traits. In some cases eigengenes grouped into higher-level clusters the authors call meta-modules. The approach reveals higher-order organisation of the transcriptome, the full set of gene messages.
europmc-pmc2361103:
Hiraoka and co-authors studied immune cells inside lung tumors in 2006. The cancer was non-small-cell lung carcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. They counted two kinds of T cells, immune cells marked CD8 and CD4, in tumors removed from 109 patients.

CD8 cells alone carried no link to survival. Patients whose tumors held high levels of both cell types lived significantly longer than all other groups. A combined analysis that adjusted for other factors still marked the double-high pattern as an independent sign of better outcome. The authors argued the two cell types cooperate. CD4 cells orchestrate the immune attack, while CD8 cells kill cancer cells directly, and together they mount a stronger response than either alone.
europmc-pmc2374903:
Wagner and co-authors tracked how lab-grown stem cells age in 2008. The cells were mesenchymal stem cells, adult stem cells from bone marrow that are prized for cell therapy. Before use, labs must grow them through many rounds of division, and the team asked what that growth does to the cells.

Within 43 to 77 days of culture, the cells grew large and odd-shaped, lost surface markers, and finally stopped dividing. Their ability to become fat cells fell, while their pull toward bone cells rose. Gene activity shifted steadily from the very first passage, not just at the end. Genes for cell division and DNA repair faded in late passages, and small RNA regulators changed too. The authors warned that therapy products change continuously during expansion, so passage number matters.
europmc-pmc2375003:
Kapsimali and colleagues charted small gene regulators across the zebrafish brain in 2007. The regulators are microRNAs, tiny RNA pieces that fine-tune how much protein genes make. Zebrafish are small fish widely used to study brain development, and the team mapped where each microRNA appears.

They profiled 38 abundant microRNAs that are shared, in near-identical form, across many animals. The mapping covered both growing embryos and adult fish brains. Patterns varied widely: some microRNAs filled the whole brain, while others lit up only in narrow cell groups or single brain regions. Some changed sharply as the brain matured. The authors said this diversity shows microRNAs help set the identity of brain areas, and they offered the atlas as a base for tests of each regulator's job.
europmc-pmc2481503:
Honeth and colleagues counted stem-pattern cells across 240 human breast tumors in 2008. The pattern, CD44 positive and CD24 negative, marks cells proposed to seed tumors and resist treatment. The team used double staining to locate both proteins in each tumor and matched results to tumor subtype and patient data.

The pattern appeared in 31% of tumors, anywhere from a few cells to nearly all of them. A full 35% of tumors lacked both proteins entirely. The stem pattern concentrated in basal-like tumors, the subtype lacking hormone receptors and HER2. It was near-universal in inherited BRCA1 tumors, 94% of which contained such cells. In HER2-positive tumors it was scarce, those tumors favouring the CD24-positive state instead. A gene signature built from the pattern ranked CD44 and the integrin CD49f at the top. The authors cautioned that tumor-seeding power may not live only in this cell type.
europmc-pmc2556103:
Wu, Bhat, Close, and Lonardi presented a new algorithm in 2008 for building genetic linkage maps, the charts that order DNA markers along chromosomes. Breeders and gene hunters depend on these maps, but high-throughput genotyping had flooded them with markers faster than existing methods could order accurately. Their approach rests on a mathematical property they prove about how correct marker order relates to a graph structure.

The method builds a graph from the data and computes its minimum spanning tree to order the markers. That is a classic network problem with fast solutions. Tested on three barley mapping populations and on synthetic data, it consistently beat the best available methods, especially when data were noisy or incomplete. The team released the software as a free web tool named MSTmap.
europmc-pmc2575403:
Peyron and colleagues studied in 2008 how the tuberculosis bacterium hides inside fat-laden immune cells in the lung. In TB, immune cells wall the bacteria into clusters called granulomas, yet some bacteria persist there for years. A granuloma cell type called the foamy macrophage, stuffed with lipid droplets, was a prime suspect for sheltering them, and the team recreated granulomas in the laboratory.

They found that long fatty acids from the bacterium's coat, called oxygenated mycolic acids, push ordinary macrophages to become foamy ones. Inside these cells the bacteria stopped multiplying and slipped into a dormant state. Microscopy showed the compartments holding bacteria migrating toward the cell's lipid droplets, then being swallowed into them while fats also accumulated inside the microbes. The authors propose foamy macrophages are the reservoir for dormant TB.
europmc-pmc2581603:
Mulcahy, Charron-Mazenod, and Lewenza showed in 2008 that the DNA bacteria shed into their biofilms is not just scaffolding but a chemical weapon and shield. Biofilms of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a lung pathogen, resist antibiotics up to a thousand times better than free-floating cells. Their matrix is rich in extracellular DNA, whose role was thought to be structural.

At body-realistic levels, that DNA kills bacteria by chelating cations, grabbing the charged mineral particles that stabilise the outer membrane, so cells burst within minutes. At lower levels, the same cation shortage switches on a resistance programme in surviving bacteria. Resistance to antimicrobial peptides rose up to 2,560-fold and to aminoglycoside antibiotics 640-fold, while other drug classes were unaffected. DNA-rich sites like the cystic fibrosis lung likely trigger this defence.
europmc-pmc2592803:
Hak and Choi examined in 2008 whether menopause and hormone use move uric acid levels in American women. They used NHANES III, the third round of the US national health and nutrition survey. High uric acid causes gout, which is common in older women, yet hormonal influences had never been comprehensively tested. The analysis covered 7,662 women aged 20 and over surveyed between 1988 and 1994.

After adjustment for diet, body size, alcohol, kidney function, blood pressure, and diuretic use, menopause was tied to higher uric acid. Women with natural menopause ran 0.34 milligrams per decilitre above premenopausal women. Surgical menopause ran 0.36 higher. Current hormone users among postmenopausal women ran 0.24 lower than non-users. The crude rise of uric acid with age vanished after adjustment, suggesting menopause and related factors, not age itself, drive it.
europmc-pmc2600703:
McCowan and colleagues followed 2,080 women treated for breast cancer in Tayside, Scotland, in 2008 to see whether sticking with tamoxifen affects survival. Tamoxifen, taken for five years after surgery, cuts breast cancer deaths, but how many women complete the course and whether adherence matters were unclear. The team linked cancer records from 1993 to 2002 with cashed prescription records.

Of the cohort, 1,633 women were prescribed tamoxifen, with a median use of 2.42 years. Only 49 percent of women followed for five years were still taking it at five years. Median adherence was 93 percent of doses, but women below 80 percent adherence faced a higher death risk, with a hazard ratio of 1.10 in that comparison. Longer use was tied to better survival, strengthening over time.
europmc-pmc2685803:
Revelli and colleagues reviewed in 2009 the search for chemical signs in follicular fluid that reveal how good a human egg is. In IVF, fertility treatment in a lab dish, doctors would love to pick the best eggs before fertilizing them. The fluid bathing each egg in the ovary is easy to collect during egg retrieval, making it a tempting place to look for clues.

Study after study had tested single molecules in the fluid: hormones, growth factors, sugars, and more. None proved reliable enough to judge an egg's power to fertilize, grow into an embryo, and start a pregnancy. The review then turns to metabolomics, the young approach of reading all small chemicals in the fluid at once. Patterns across many molecules may succeed where single markers failed. That work, the authors note, has only just begun.
europmc-pmc2691003:
Harismendy and colleagues compared in 2009 the three new high-speed DNA sequencing platforms then challenging the classic Sanger method. The newcomers, from Roche, Illumina, and ABI, produced thousands of times more sequence at far lower cost. The team tested them on the same job: targeted sequencing of chosen regions in four samples.

Each platform read the same 260,000-letter stretch using its maker's own preparation and software. All three worked, but their coverage was uneven in a telling way. Stretches with certain local sequence features were read deeply, while neighbors went thin, and the pattern differed by platform. Systematic bias, not random chance, explained the gaps. For studies sequencing many people's candidate regions, the authors warn, platform choice shapes which spots are trustworthy, and results across platforms are not simply interchangeable.
europmc-pmc2702403:
Zanobetti and Schwartz published a national study in 2009 on how fine and coarse dust in the air affects deaths in the United States. Fine particles are tiny bits of pollution that float in air and can enter the lungs. Coarse particles are larger, but still small enough to breathe in.

Working with data from 112 cities for 1999 to 2005, the authors linked daily particle levels to deaths from all causes and from heart and lung illness. A rise in fine particles was tied to more deaths overall, and to more deaths from stroke and lung disease as well. Effects were strongest in spring, and coarse particles also raised risk, though by less.
europmc-pmc2718703:
Calebiro and co-authors showed in 2009 that a hormone receptor can keep signaling after it is pulled inside the cell, against the standard model. G-protein-coupled receptors were thought to signal only at the cell surface, then switch off as they are internalized. They watched the thyroid stimulating hormone receptor in living native cells in real time.

The receptor kept producing cAMP, a key internal signal, well after internalization, in a persistent phase that surface signaling cannot explain. Internalized receptors thus stay active and may drive the long phase of the response. That finding reshapes how this huge receptor family, a major drug target group, is understood to work in space and time.
europmc-pmc2745803:
Bennett and co-authors revised in 2009 the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire, a standard tool for measuring how fibromyalgia, a chronic pain condition, affects daily life. The original tool had known flaws after eighteen years of use, and its scoring was cumbersome for clinics. A patient focus group helped shape the revised version, called FIQR.

FIQR keeps three domains, function, overall impact, and symptoms, but adds questions on memory, tenderness, balance, and sensitivity to surroundings, all scored on a simple zero-to-ten scale. In over four hundred respondents, its total score tracked the original closely and separated fibromyalgia patients from arthritis, lupus, depression, and healthy groups well. Patients finished it in about one minute, and scoring took about one minute.
europmc-pmc2771903:
Chomiak and Hu worked out in 2009 the optimal g-ratio for myelinated fibers in the rat central nervous system, using theory rather than measurement. The g-ratio, inner axon diameter over total fiber diameter, indexes how well a fiber is myelinated. A classic speed-based estimate put the optimum near zero point six. That matches some peripheral fibers. Central fibers run higher. Central myelin must also save space and energy and keep signals faithful.

Their approach, built from basic biophysical properties of axon structure and function, puts the central optimum near zero point seven seven. Weakening the volume constraint in the model by about forty percent recovers the peripheral value near zero point six. The result supports the idea that nervous systems are built to an optimized design, tuned differently in center and periphery.
europmc-pmc2821003:
Campos and Vasconcelos reviewed in 2010 how microcystins, toxins from water-bloom bacteria, damage animal cells. These ring-shaped toxins are made by several bloom-forming genera and rank among the most common freshwater poisons. Their main grip is on enzymes called protein phosphatases, which they block strongly.

Blocking those enzymes sets off chain reactions that derail cell signaling, growth control, and even gene activity. The toxins also stir oxidative stress, meaning a flood of reactive oxygen, and they attack mitochondria, the cell's power units, pushing cells toward programmed death. The review covers how animals take up, transform, and excrete the toxins, and which proteins the toxins touch directly along the way.
europmc-pmc2880003:
Cai and Brysbaert built in 2010 a new frequency list for Chinese words and characters drawn from film and television subtitles. Word frequency, how often a word occurs in daily life, is the strongest known predictor of how fast readers recognize words. Chinese researchers had few good lists, so the team counted a subtitle corpus of tens of millions of words.

Their counts explained reading speed in naming and decision tests far better than counts from written texts, repeating a pattern found for English, French, and Dutch. The database is the first for Chinese to add how many different contexts each word appears in, plus good counts for multi-character words and their grammar roles. Subtitles mirror everyday speech, and the list is free for research use.
europmc-pmc2893603:
Mägi and Morris released in 2010 GWAMA, open-source software for pooling genome-wide association studies into one larger analysis. Single studies often lack the sample size to catch genes with small effects on traits like diabetes or obesity. Combining summary results across studies, called meta-analysis, raises that power, but genome-scale files strain ordinary statistics packages.

GWAMA handles the scale with built-in error trapping that catches mismatched strands, alleles, and file formats before they corrupt results. It computes the standard pooled effect measures for both yes-no traits and measured traits, under models that allow effects to vary between studies. Companion scripts format each study's output and draw genome-wide summary plots. The package made rigorous pooling routine for the consortia era of genetics.
europmc-pmc2953403:
Venkatesan and Kim reviewed chitosan composites for rebuilding bone in a 2010 overview. Chitosan comes from chitin in crustacean shells, and bone itself mixes mineral with proteins such as collagen.

Mixed with hydroxyapatite, the main bone mineral, chitosan forms materials the body tolerates, breaks down slowly, and resists bacteria. The blends can be moulded or made porous so growing cells move in and lay down new bone. Adding carbon nanotubes has been tried to stiffen the mix. The authors present these composites as strong candidates for artificial bone and repair scaffolds.
europmc-pmc2982803:
Ochman and colleagues compared gut microbe communities across wild apes and humans in a 2010 study, testing whether microbe makeup mirrors host family history. Gut bacteria arrive from the mother at birth but also shift with diet, place, and health.

Despite that noise, the evolutionary relationships among great ape species were recapitulated in their gut community compositions. Members of one species resembled each other more than outsiders, and the deeper branching pattern matched host ancestry rather than simple diet groupings. The result suggests long co-diversification between apes and their gut residents over evolutionary time.
europmc-pmc2992503:
Gerritsen and co-authors systematically reviewed how tooth loss affects oral health related quality of life in a 2010 study. Losing teeth, usually to oral disease, plausibly harms daily comfort, eating, and confidence, but the pattern needed synthesis.

Searching English papers from 1990 to mid-2009, they kept thirty-five studies for review and pooled the ten with comparable measures. The combined evidence linked more missing teeth with worse quality of life scores, and the position and spread of remaining teeth mattered too, not just the count. Gaps at the front and shortened dental rows carried particular weight.
europmc-pmc2998703:
White and Royston tackled missing data in survival studies using the Cox model in a 2009 methods study. Filling in missing values several times over beats dropping incomplete cases, but survival outcomes complicate what the filling model should include.

Common practice used the event flag plus logged follow-up time, with unclear justification. The authors prove the right ingredients are the event flag and the cumulative baseline hazard, estimated from the data itself. Simulations show the older logged-time recipe biases links toward no effect, while their recipe cuts that bias. They recommend the corrected formula to analysts.
europmc-pmc3077403:
Shi and colleagues built in 2011 the first brain atlases designed specifically for human infants, covering newborns and one and two year olds. Infant brain scans are hard to read because tissue contrast is weak, above all in newborns, and adult atlases fit poorly during the fastest growth period of life. The team followed ninety five healthy infants and scanned each child at all three ages.

From those scans they built average templates, maps of how likely each tissue type is at each spot, and labeled maps of anatomical regions for every age. Links between the age atlases track the same structures as the brain grows. Tests on standard infant tasks showed their atlases beat existing ones. The set was posted freely online. Infant researchers can now align and segment scans against brains the right age.
europmc-pmc3084703:
Kim and colleagues compared in 2011 four viral self cutting peptides used to express several genes from one construct, and found a clear winner. Researchers often need cells to make two or more proteins together. The older linking method is bulky and gives uneven amounts. Short 2A peptides let the cell's protein factory skip a link and restart, yielding separate proteins from one message, but no shared vectors or fair comparison existed.

The team built matching plasmids for all four peptides and tested cutting efficiency in three human cell lines, in zebrafish embryos, and in adult mice. The peptide from a pig virus cut most cleanly in every setting, by both protein blots and microscopy. Their plasmids were made available for others to use. The result gives labs a ready, best in class tool for multi gene experiments.
europmc-pmc3103903:
Fatemeh Madani and co-authors published a 2011 review in the Journal of Biophysics on short peptides that can cross cell membranes. Such peptides, rich in basic building blocks, had raised hopes as carriers for large drug molecules that normally stay outside cells. The authors focus on how entry actually happens.

Two main routes are weighed: direct passage through the membrane and uptake by a process where the cell swallows material inward. The review notes that the route can shift with dose, cargo, and test setup, and that harm to cells remains a concern. It gives drug designers a clear account of what is known and what is still debated.
europmc-pmc3158103:
Karen Seto and colleagues pooled satellite studies of city growth worldwide in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Turning land into urban use is among the least reversible human impacts, eating farmland, warming local climate, and splitting habitats. The team combined more than three hundred mapping studies covering three decades.

Urban land grew by a large measured area between 1970 and 2000. Growth rates ran fastest in India, China, and Africa, while North America added the most total area. Everywhere, land conversion matched or outran population growth, meaning cities are spreading thinner. Income growth drove much of China's expansion but mattered less in India and Africa, where population led. Forecasts to 2030 vary hugely, and much variation defied all their explanatory factors.
europmc-pmc3180703:
Sitao Wu and colleagues launched a web server that assembles the whole metagenomics toolbox in one place in a 2011 paper in BMC Genomics. Reading all DNA in an environmental sample reveals whole microbe communities without culturing, but modern sequencers bury researchers in data needing dozens of separate programs. Few labs can install and maintain that chain.

Their server bundles more than twenty common tools, from gene finding and sequence clustering to quality checks, contaminant removal, species assignment, and function annotation. The tools run in parallel on a computing cluster, so big jobs finish fast, and users can chain them into custom pipelines through a browser or scripts. No login is required. The service is free online.
europmc-pmc3182203:
Smita Majumder and colleagues tested timing in Alzheimer prevention using a mouse model in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Boosting the cell's recycling system had eased early memory problems tied to soluble toxic protein, but established plaques and tangles might be beyond rescue. They fed a recycling-boosting drug to Alzheimer-model mice either from youth or only once brain deposits were entrenched.

Lifelong early treatment switched recycling on, cut plaques and tangles substantially, and preserved cognition. Starting the same drug in old mice with full-blown deposits changed none of those outcomes. The contrast draws a hard line: recycling-based therapy looks valid only early in disease progression, before deposits consolidate, which reshapes how such drugs should be trialled in people.
europmc-pmc3233603:
Debora Marks and colleagues showed that a protein's three-dimensional shape can be computed from its evolutionary history alone, in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Related proteins record millions of natural experiments: positions that touch in the folded structure tend to change together over evolution. The difficulty is telling true partnerships from background noise in those correlations.

Using a maximum-entropy statistical model fitted to alignments of related sequences, the team inferred which residue pairs genuinely co-evolve. The strongest pairs predicted which parts of the protein sit close together. They were accurate enough to fold fifteen test proteins from scratch. The set included a membrane receptor, and no known structures were used as help. Errors were small across most of each chain. The authors foresee surveying unknown protein structures and spotting harmful genetic variants this way.
europmc-pmc3298503:
Augoff, McCue, Plow, and Sossey-Alaoui reported in 2012 on how a protective small RNA gets switched off in an aggressive form of breast cancer. The RNA, called miR-31, normally holds back several steps of tumor spread by reining in genes that drive invasion. Its loss in triple negative breast cancer, a hard to treat subtype, had no clear explanation.

The team found that heavy chemical tagging of the control region, a silencing mark called methylation, shuts down both miR-31 and the longer RNA that hosts it. Drugs that strip these marks switched both back on in lab grown cancer cells. Cell types with the aggressive profile carried the heavy marks, while less aggressive types did not, tying the silencing directly to the disease subtype.
europmc-pmc3315503:
Ziemert and colleagues built a web tool that sorts gene fragments by family history to judge a microbe's drug making potential, describing it in 2012. Many antibiotics and other useful natural compounds are built by two families of giant enzymes in bacteria. Their genes are highly repetitive, which makes them hard to read and compare in the flood of new genome data.

The tool, called NaPDoS, pulls out signature pieces from those enzyme genes in genomes, samples, or raw environmental DNA. It then places each piece on a family tree beside genes whose products are already known. Close matches hint at the rough shape of the compound a strain can make, while pieces on brand new branches flag unknown chemistry worth chasing. Trials on four draft genomes and two environmental datasets showed it gives a fast census of natural product talent.
europmc-pmc3381403:
Overdevest and colleagues reported in 2011 that drug-resistance genes were rife in Dutch chicken meat and matched genes carried by people. They sampled retail chicken and, in the same region, stool samples and blood cultures from four hospitals. The genes studied make bacteria resist a key family of antibiotics.

About four fifths of the chicken meat carried these extended-spectrum resistance genes. The leading genes in meat and in people's stool samples were identical, and they also appeared often in blood infections. The E. coli strains themselves looked closely alike across meat and humans. The authors warn that a loaded food chain could narrow future treatment choices.
europmc-pmc3419203:
Gevers and co-authors described the Human Microbiome Project in 2012, the national effort to catalogue the microbes of the healthy human body. After the Human Genome Project, attention turned to this other genome riding in and on us. Most microbes resist growing in dishes, so the field learned to read community DNA directly.

The paper reviews the field's history, tells how the project came together, and surveys the consortium's first wave of publications. New sequencing let teams census communities across body sites without culturing them. Immunologists meanwhile found microbes shaping the immune system's growth. The project was built as a shared community resource, meant to anchor future work linking our microbes to health and disease.
europmc-pmc3466303:
Choi and colleagues introduced a tool called PROVEAN in PLoS ONE in 2012, built to judge whether a change in a protein is likely to harm its function. Older tools handled only single amino acid swaps, leaving out insertions and deletions. Their method scores a change by how much it lowers the match between the altered protein and its relatives.

Tested on tens of thousands of known human variants, the score sorted disease-linked changes from harmless common ones well. It also worked on variants from other species. Choi's team put the tool online for free use. Because it handles several kinds of change at once, it helps researchers narrow long lists of variants to the few worth lab testing.
