The study gives a concrete case for one of evolution's stranger claims, that selection can favor DNA that looks out only for itself.
plos-pone-0000103:
Jian Li, Samuel M. McClure, and Brooks King-Casas studied economic choices over time in PLOS ONE in 2006. In their game, players adjusted their strategy as conditions changed, much as governments adjust policy in a shifting economy. The authors tracked how people update their approach after wins and losses.

People did not simply chase the last good result. Their adjustments followed patterns that simple learning rules only partly capture. Games like this are the lab bench of neuroeconomics, the study of how brains make value choices. Knowing how strategies drift in dynamic settings matters for real policy too, where each new rule changes the game it governs.
plos-pone-0000203:
Jittima Piriyapongsa and I. King Jordan published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. MicroRNAs are tiny regulators that fine-tune gene activity. The authors identify a family of human microRNA genes that arose from miniature inverted-repeat transposable elements, small pieces of jumping DNA known as MITEs.

Genes born from jumping DNA show how genomes recycle their own clutter into working parts. The paper traces this family's origin and spread in the human genome. It adds to the evidence that transposable elements, often dismissed as junk, are a real source of new regulatory genes.
plos-pone-0000303:
Christian G. Noble and Haiwei Song published this molecular biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. eIF4AIII is an RNA helicase, a motor that unwinds RNA, and a core part of a complex that marks newly made messages. The authors show that the protein MLN51 stimulates that helicase activity.

A stimulator that speeds the motor changes how the marking complex does its job in quality control of gene messages. The paper defines MLN51's role in that machinery. Such detail feeds into the study of diseases where RNA processing goes wrong. Details like these fill in the wiring of a core cellular machine.
plos-pone-0000403:
Abhaya V. Kulkarni, Jason W. Busse, and Iffat Shams asked what makes a medical paper get cited, in a 2007 PLOS ONE study. Citations are the currency of science: a paper that others cite shapes the field, while an ignored one sinks. The team looked for traits of papers that are linked to a higher citation rate.

Knowing which features go with influence helps readers judge a crowded literature and helps researchers report work so it can be found and used. The study is a piece of meta-research, science studying its own habits. Its lessons apply to anyone trying to tell landmark studies from the mass of published work.
plos-pone-0000503:
David C. Nickle and colleagues built statistical models of how HIV proteins change over time, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. HIV evolves fast, dodging immune attack and drugs. Their HIV-specific probabilistic models of protein evolution capture the virus's particular patterns of mutation, which differ from the generic models borrowed from other organisms.

A model tuned to the virus reads its sequences more accurately, spotting which changes are meaningful. That helps in tracing transmission, predicting drug resistance, and designing vaccines against a moving target. The work is infrastructure for HIV research: better math underneath many other studies.
plos-pone-0000603:
Clara S.M. Tang and Richard J. Epstein reported an unexpected division in human DNA structure, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper titled A Structural Split in the Human Genome. The genome is usually described by its sequence of letters; structure here refers to larger-scale organization in how that sequence is arranged.

A split in genome structure, if real, divides the genome into two kinds of territory with different rules. Claims of large-scale order matter because they affect how genes are regulated and how variation is distributed. Short structural papers like this one stake a claim that later genome-wide data can confirm or dissolve.
plos-pone-0000703:
Hiroki Nagai and Guojun Sheng watched two chicken globin genes switch on together, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. The chicken beta globin locus holds four genes. Two of them, called rho and epsilon, are expressed from the earliest stage of primitive hematopoiesis, the first wave of blood formation in the embryo. The pair sits side by side in the genome.

The authors show the two genes' transcription runs in on and off phases. During each on phase, they are cotranscribed, copied together in a shared burst. That coordination raises questions about how neighboring genes share control machinery. Blood development is a classic system for gene regulation, and this adds timing to the picture.
plos-pone-0000803:
Katsuyuki Hotta, Toshio Ogura, Kenji Nishii and colleagues evaluated a blood test for tuberculosis screening in Japanese healthcare students. The whole blood interferon-gamma assay, QuantiFERON-TB-2G, had not been fully evaluated as a baseline screening test in students about to begin clinical contact with patients. Their 2007 PLOS ONE aim was to compare the assay's results with those of the tuberculin skin test.

Baseline screening matters because healthcare workers face TB exposure, and a starting value separates old infection from new. A blood test avoids return visits and reading errors of skin tests. The comparison in a low-risk student population tests the assay where false positives hurt most.
plos-pone-0000903:
Sheila Costford, Nihan Kavaslar, Nadav Ahituv and colleagues studied a human gene change that boosts a key energy enzyme, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The enzyme, AMPK, watches over energy balance in cells and in the whole body. In muscle, switching it on guards against some effects of inactivity and poor diet.

The change they studied, called R225W, sits in the gamma 3 part of AMPK and makes it work harder. The title links it to more glycogen and less fat stored in skeletal muscle. Human cases like this are rare natural tests of what a drug target does. They show both the promise and the reach of AMPK in daily metabolism.
plos-pone-0001003:
Tom Little, Lenny Nelson and Ted Hupp found signs of fast evolution in a stress response protein, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Some cancers grow from a mix of tissue damage, germs and local immune attack. The links in that chain are only starting to be unraveled.

Against that background, the team report a strong signature of adaptive evolution on the DNA sequence of a stress response protein. A sequence that changed faster than chance suggests it was shaped by real pressure, not drift. Which pressure, infection or damage, becomes the next question. The find ties an evolutionary pattern to a protein with a foot in cancer biology.
plos-pone-0001103:
Hiroyuki Kurata, Takayuki Tanaka and Fumitaka Ohnishi worked out how to find the critical reactions in a feedback rich cell model, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Computer simulations are needed to see how biochemical networks stay robust under stress or mutation. Sensitivity analysis links that robustness to network structure, but it usually gives only local answers.

The authors present a mathematical method to identify critical reactions in the interlocked feedback model, a standard test network full of loops. Reactions that carry robustness are the ones drugs and mutations hit hardest. A method that finds them reliably helps modelers spend experiments where they count.
plos-pone-0001203:
Knowing which genes are on in each tissue is basic reference data for biology. Henrik Hornshøj and colleagues built such a reference for the pig in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Using gene expression microarrays, they profiled 20,000 genes across 23 healthy porcine tissues.

Most microarray studies chase genes tied to a disease or a stimulus. A catalogue of normal expression across many tissues is a different kind of resource: the baseline against which abnormal patterns stand out. Pigs are also a major model for human medicine and a food animal, so the profiles serve several fields at once.
plos-pone-0001303:
Knocking out a gene in a mouse and measuring which other genes change activity is a standard way to find a protein's targets. Luis Valor and Seth Grant report a caution about that method in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Using tissues from multiple lines of knockout mice, they found that gene expression changes cluster around the targeted gene's location.

Changes near the manipulated locus may reflect the engineering itself rather than the missing protein's function. The authors describe these clustered changes flanking targeted gene loci. Their warning affects how thousands of microarray studies in mutant organisms should be read.
plos-pone-0001403:
Ludovic Tailleux and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study that reads both sides of a TB infection at once. Gene chips let labs watch many genes switch on or off in a sample. The team used them on the TB germ and on the human cells it infects. No prior study had read both partners in this paired way.

Their paired reads map the cross talk as germ and host react to each other. Some host genes rose while germ genes shifted to meet the new state. A two sided map like this can reveal weak points on both sides. Those weak points may yield new drug or shot targets for a disease that still kills widely.
plos-pone-0001503:
Hilde Krol and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a class of brain ills tied to a stretched protein tract. In these ills, a tract of one building block grows too long in a protein. Brains show clumps of the stretched protein, which were thought to drive harm. The team tracked one such protein, ataxin-1, live in cells.

They found the stretched protein moves faster, not slower, in cells. It also did not form clumps in their tests. That breaks the simple clump tale for this protein. Harm may come from the free protein's acts, not from clumps, which shifts drug aims.
plos-pone-0001603:
Heungjeong Woo and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a mouse model of salmonella gut ill. Mice fed salmonella by mouth do not get diarrhea as people do. A dose of germ drugs first makes them prone to gut inflammation, but gene prone mice die of body wide infection first. The team built a model in hardy mice that get the gut ill.

Their mice show diarrhea with the gut harm, much like human cases. A model that mirrors the human course lets labs test vaccines and drugs with more faith. It also helps sort gut harm from body wide spread, two ills with unlike needs.
plos-pone-0001703:
Koichi Iijima, Hsueh-Cheng Chiang, Stephen A. Hearn, and their co-authors used fruit flies to test Alzheimer's-linked protein variants in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Clumping of the amyloid-beta-42 peptide in the brain is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, and stopping clumping is a proposed treatment. Yet the peptide can form several kinds of assemblies, not all equally harmful.

The team made Aβ42 mutants with different aggregation profiles and expressed them in Drosophila. Different variants induced distinct pathologies in the flies, per the paper's title. The full text gives the variants, the fly brain damage, and the behavior effects. Separating which assemblies hurt most sharpens the target for anti-amyloid drugs, a field with many failed trials.
plos-pone-0001803:
Takeshi Nagashima, Takahiro Suzuki, Shinji Kondo, and their co-authors profiled gene activity in breast cancer cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Heregulin beta-1 is a signal that activates MAPK and PI3K/Akt pathways through ErbB receptors. Those pathways can add phosphate tags to the estrogen receptor at one site, Ser-118. That raises the question of how much the estrogen receptor matters in the response.

Their gene activity analysis shows heregulin can drive genes without the estrogen receptor in MCF-7 cells. The full text gives the gene sets and the pathway tests. If heregulin drives genes without the estrogen receptor, hormone blocking breast cancer drugs may leave this route open, which matters for resistant tumors.
plos-pone-0001903:
Jenia Semyonov and colleagues asked which gene families survive genome doubling, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. At rare points in the past, whole genomes were copied at once, leaving most genes in pairs. Most spare copies are lost with time, yet some families keep theirs far more often than chance would suggest.

The team reports that genes for G protein-coupled receptors, a huge family of cell signal catchers, are kept at high rates after such doublings. That bias hints that extra copies of signal genes paid off in survival. The work helps explain how complex signal webs grew, and why some gene families are so large today.
plos-pone-0002003:
Elie Aoun and co-authors pooled past studies to decode a gene risk in a pancreas illness, in a 2008 PLOS ONE meta-analysis. Chronic pancreatitis is long-term inflammation of the pancreas with lasting harm. One gene form, the SPINK1 N34S haplotype, marks high risk, but how it interacts with trypsin-driven injury and alcohol-driven injury was undefined.

The team set out a model in which the illness can arise by several paths, then tested it against pooled data. Sorting paths matters, since care for an alcohol-driven case may differ from care for a gene-driven one. The study gives doctors a frame for a mixed-cause illness.
plos-pone-0002103:
Sara Thomas and co-authors read the genome of a versatile soil bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Anaeromyxobacter dehalogenans strain 2CP-C is a delta-proteobacterium found in many soils and sediments. Its ribosomal RNA gene groups it with the myxobacteria, social bacteria with striking traits, yet its genome is a mosaic of pieces from many sources.

As the title states, that mosaic suggests an aerobic common ancestor for the delta-proteobacteria, a group now rich in oxygen-shunning forms. A patchwork genome can record a past way of life that the modern cell has left behind.
plos-pone-0002203:
Isabelle George, Hugo Cousillas, and Jean-Pierre Richard looked for the brain basis of sound grouping in songbirds, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Sorting sounds into classes is basic to thought, but finding where the brain does it is hard. Songbirds are a good test case because they sort songs and calls and learn them socially.

The team searched for a neural substrate, a brain area whose activity matches the sorting of complex acoustic signals into functional classes. A songbird that treats some calls as one kind and others as another must have circuitry that draws those lines. Locating it would link animal communication to the wider science of categorization.
plos-pone-0002303:
Thilo Lange, Kyu Kwang Kim, Rakesh Singh, and co-authors tested an iron-based compound against hard-to-treat ovarian cancer cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Some ovarian cancers resist platinum drugs, the standard chemotherapy, leaving few options. The compound, iron(III)-salophene, is an organometallic molecule, built around a metal atom.

In this first study of its biological activity, the team measured its effects on viability, shape, growth. Cell cycle in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer cell lines. The compound showed selective cytotoxic and anti-proliferative effects, killing cancer cells more than ordinary ones. Early selectivity like this is what drug hunters look for before animal tests.
plos-pone-0002403:
Painter joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Corrie A. Painter, Anthony Cruz, Gustavo E. López, among others. Its subject is model for the Peptide-Free Conformation of Class II MHC Proteins. Major histocompatibility complex proteins are believed to undergo significant conformational changes concomitant with peptide binding, but structural characterization of these changes has remained elusive.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002503:
Ma led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Yanqing Ma, Craig C. Malbon, David L. Williams, among others. Its subject is altered Gene Expression in Early Atherosclerosis Is Blocked by Low Level Apolipoprotein E. Mice deficient in apolipoprotein E (apoE −/−) develop atherosclerosis.

The possible linkage between expression of adhesion molecules/cofactors and atherosclerosis was probed at the level of mRNA and protein expression. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002603:
Fishman and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Yelena Fishman, Eliahu Zlotkin, Daniel Sher, among others. Its subject is expulsion of Symbiotic Algae during Feeding by the Green Hydra – a Mechanism for Regulating Symbiont Density?. Algal-cnidarian symbiosis is one of the main factors contributing to the success of cnidarians, and is crucial for the maintenance of coral reefs.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002703:
Xincheng Zheng and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was modulation of NKT cell development by B7-CD28 interaction: an expanding horizon for costimulation. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Xincheng Zheng, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. It has been demonstrated that the development of NKT cells requires CD1d. It goes on to note a further point. The contribution of costimulatory molecules in this process has not been studied. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002803:
Qingfa Wu and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on poly A- transcripts expressed in HeLa cells. The catalog record names Qingfa Wu first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Transcripts expressed in eukaryotes are classified as poly A+ transcripts or poly A- transcripts based on the presence or absence of the 3′ poly. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002903:
Kamija Phiri, Job Calis, Brian Faragher and colleagues followed Malawian children after severe anaemia in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Severe anaemia is common in African children admitted to hospital and often proves fatal. What happens to survivors over the long term was unknown when the study began.

Early reports had warned that survivors might face later illness and death. The team tracked outcomes to test that concern with real follow-up data. Child health programs in Africa can use such results to decide whether care should extend well past discharge from hospital. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003003:
Suraiya Rasheed, Jasper Yan, Alex Lau and co-authors profiled proteins in HIV-infected cells in 2008. People with HIV develop metabolic problems including insulin resistance, fat redistribution, and abnormal blood lipids. These were tied to antiretroviral drugs, yet infected individuals also showed changes beyond drug effects.

Using proteomics, the team reports HIV replication itself raises free fatty acids, low density lipoproteins, and many key lipid metabolism proteins. Published in PLOS ONE, that shifts part of the blame from drugs to the virus. It may change how metabolic care for HIV patients is planned. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003103:
Ching-Shan Chou, Qing Nie and Tau-Mu Yi modeled yeast cell polarization under spatial gradients in 2008. Cells polarize by localizing internal components to specific locations in response to external signals. Yeast, for example, forms a mating projection toward the source of mating pheromone, a chemical gradient.

Polarization raises specific challenges in robustness: cells must aim accurately despite noise. The model weighs tradeoffs between robustness goals, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, those tradeoffs are general design principles for any cell that must sense a faint gradient, from immune cells to neurons. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003203:
Jacqueline Chevalier and co-authors track a drug pump in hospital germs in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Deaths from infectious disease are set to rise as germs evolve resistance to antibiotics faster. Each new defence germs gain wears down the drugs doctors can use. Pumps that throw drugs out of the cell are one such defence.

The team compare the pump in strains of Enterobacter aerogenes taken from patients in 1995 and in 2003. Readers see how the pump changed over eight years of drug use. That record shows how treatment itself can breed harder infections.
plos-pone-0003303:
Paul C. Sereno, Ricardo N. Martinez, Jeffrey A. Wilson and colleagues report a new predatory dinosaur from Argentina in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Living birds possess a unique heterogeneous pulmonary system composed of a rigid, dorsally anchored lung and several compliant air sacs that operate as bellows, driving inspired air through the lung. Evidence from the fossil record for the origin and evolution of this system is essential.

The authors present evidence for avian intrathoracic air sacs in this new dinosaur. Readers see the bird breathing system traced into a meat-eating dinosaur. That supports a deep origin of bird-style breathing before flight itself evolved.
plos-pone-0003403:
Harparkash Kaur and colleagues checked malaria drug quality across Tanzania in this 2008 survey. Malaria care depends on pills that truly contain the stated drug. Weak or fake pills fail patients and breed drug resistance. The team bought antimalarial drugs from retail shops across the country.

Each sample was tested for what was really inside. The nationwide results showed how often buyers got poor-quality medicine. Substandard drugs are a direct threat to malaria control in hard-hit regions. The survey gave health officials hard numbers to act on. Shops, not hospitals, were where many patients actually bought their malaria pills.
plos-pone-0003503:
Hanneke K. M. Meeren and co-authors timed early vision in this 2008 study. Sorting sights into categories was thought to start well after first sight. The first hundred milliseconds were seen as an even, unsorted stage. Flipping images upside down disrupts face and object processing in known ways.

Using that inversion trick, they found category-specific activity very early. Brain responses differed by category within the first hundred milliseconds. Early vision thus begins sorting sooner than the old view allowed. The finding reshapes models of how perception builds. Faces are the test case here, but the timing claim reaches all vision.
plos-pone-0003603:
Joseph L. Mankowski and co-authors studied brain protection in virus-infected monkeys in this 2008 paper. HIV often causes neurologic disease even under treatment. Certain MHC class I alleles have been tied to AIDS outcomes. Their role in restricting brain disease was less clear.

In SIV-infected macaques, one MHC class I allele was neuroprotective. Monkeys carrying it resisted lentiviral disease of the central nervous system. Host genetics can thus guard the brain specifically. The finding may guide HIV neurology research. SIV in monkeys is the main lab stand-in for HIV in people.
plos-pone-0003703:
Raúl Y. Tito, Simone Macmil, Graham Wiley, and colleagues published this microbiome study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The microbes living in the human gut differ between people and shape health in many ways. Modern samples alone cannot show what those communities once looked like. The team turned to ancient material.

They typed the microbes in two ancient human microbiomes and studied what those microbes could do. The census maps which organisms lived in people long ago and what jobs they performed. It sets a baseline for judging how modern guts, and their ills, have changed.
plos-pone-0003803:
Kaw Bing Chua, Kenny Voon, Gary Crameri, and colleagues published this virus study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Reoviruses were found in the early 1950s and named orphan viruses because no disease was linked to them. The group's earlier work had isolated the Melaka virus from a patient with acute respiratory disease.

Here they identify and characterize a new orthoreovirus from patients with acute respiratory infections. The virus expands a family once thought harmless to humans. Its characterization puts a new suspect on the board for respiratory illnesses that routine tests cannot explain.
plos-pone-0003903:
Krishnamurthy N. Rao, Stephen K. Burley, and Subramanyam Swaminathan solved shapes of ancient microbe proteins in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns a protein family found only in archaea. Archaea are microbes distinct from bacteria, and many of their proteins remain unknown. The family, called UPF0201, had no known job.

The team used X-ray methods to get the structures of four family members. Their shapes look like proteins that bind RNA, the cell's message copies. Tests still suggested these proteins are unlikely to bind RNA themselves. The work shows how shape alone can mislead about a protein's task.
plos-pone-0004003:
Eva Gross, Birgit Busse, Matthias Riemenschneider, and co-authors linked a gene variant to drug harm in cancer care in 2008. Some chemotherapy drugs, called fluoropyrimidines, can cause severe side effects. Patients with faults in the DPYD gene face high risk from them. The gene makes an enzyme that clears those drugs.

Their PLOS ONE article reports a strong link for one common variant. Testing patients before treatment could flag those at risk. Avoiding severe toxicity saves lives and hospital time. The study supports wider genetic screening before fluoropyrimidine therapy. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004103:
Kuniaki Sano, Mary Miyaji-Yamaguchi, Kimiko M. Tsutsui, and co-authors studied a DNA enzyme in neurons in 2008. Topoisomerase II passes one DNA duplex through a break in another. Late stages of neuron development need its beta form active. The enzyme seems to aid the transcription of long genes.

Their PLOS ONE article reports topo II beta activates a set of neuronal genes. Those genes sit in AT-rich stretches that normally repress them. The enzyme thus frees specific genes from a silencing environment. That role explains why developing neurons fail without it. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004203:
Kresten Lindorff-Larsen and Jesper Ferkinghoff-Borg published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. Comparing the shapes of proteins tells scientists about function and evolution. Many scores exist to measure how alike two protein conformations are, the most common being the root mean square deviation.

The authors review and test similarity measures for protein ensembles, sets of shapes rather than a single structure. Their aim is to show which measures stay trustworthy when proteins flex and wobble. Choosing the right measure matters, because a bad one can make two different shapes look the same.
plos-pone-0004303:
Heather Cameron and Warren Foster published this toxicology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Breast cancer is the most common cancer in Western women, and environmental factors are thought to play a role. Dieldrin, an organochlorine pesticide that persists in the environment, is suspected of raising breast cancer risk.

The team exposed Her2/neu transgenic mice, a breast cancer model, to dieldrin during development and lactation. They examined whether that early exposure alters mammary tumour development later in life. Testing exposure in the cradle, not just in adults, matches how such chemicals actually meet people.
plos-pone-0004403:
Air travel carries infections across the world in hours. Modelers who forecast spread must include flights in their math. Full flight data are rich but heavy to compute with. Justin Lessler, James Kaufman, Daniel Ford, and co-authors asked what simpler models lose. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper compares detailed air travel models with simplified ones. The question is practical: how much accuracy does simplification cost?

Disease models must balance detail against speed and computing limits. Too much detail can make a model unwieldy or over-set. The authors compared what the two approaches predict for long-distance spread. Their results guide modelers choosing data for outbreak forecasts. Every epidemic plan built on such models depends on that trade-off.
plos-pone-0004503:
Two forms of a human immune protein are tracked from gene to function by Robert Eagle, Gillian Flack, Anthony Warford, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is ULBP5, also called RAET1G. It is a ligand, a signal flag read by a receptor named NKG2D on natural killer cells and some T cells.

That receptor helps the immune system attack tumors and virus-infected cells. The ligands it reads are varied, and this one comes in two isoforms, two versions from the same gene. The team describes where each version is expressed, how it travels inside cells, and what it does. Knowing which version appears on a cell helps explain when the immune system will treat that cell as a threat.
plos-pone-0004603:
A rice gene that arose from scratch, with no ancestor, dampens the plant's defense against pathogens, report Wenfei Xiao, Hongbo Liu, Yu Li, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. How defense genes originated remains an important problem. It is generally held that new genes evolve from ancestral genes, often by duplication followed by change.

The team shows a different route: a gene of de novo origin, born from previously non-gene DNA. Stranger still, this newborn gene negatively regulates the pathogen-induced defense response. A new gene that restrains immunity seems paradoxical, but restraint can prevent the plant from harming itself with overreaction. The finding widens the known ways genomes invent new working parts.
plos-pone-0004703:
Florian Altermatt, Ilmari Pajunen, and Dieter Ebert studied how drying shapes rock pool water flea groups, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rock pools fill and dry in cycles, so life there faces sharp swings. For small crustaceans, drought is the most harsh break, since water can vanish for long spans.

The team asked how often pools dry and how that sets which fleas persist. They tracked a linked set of pools as one shared system. Their work shows how harsh timing, not just place, sorts species. It also helps predict what more drought under climate change may do.
plos-pone-0004803:
Johan Bollen and colleagues showed that clickstream data yields high resolution maps of science, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Intricate maps of science have been created from citation data to visualize the structure of scientific activity. However, most scientific publications are now accessed online, and scholarly web portals record detailed log data at a scale exceeding all existing citation counts combined.

Reader trails reveal which fields actually connect in practice. The team built maps from journal clickstreams across many institutions. Usage based maps complement citation maps with fresher signals. They can guide libraries, funders, and readers through science.
plos-pone-0004903:
Feriel Hacini-Rachinel led a team that tested a probiotic drink against skin inflammation in mice for PLOS ONE in 2009. Probiotics are live bacteria taken by mouth for health. They are said to ease allergic and inflamed skin, yet how they act on the T cells that drive skin flares was still poorly known. The team used the well known strain Lactobacillus casei DN-114 001 for its tests.

Oral doses of the bacteria eased skin flares in the mice. The effect ran through both kinds of T cells: the ones that drive flares and the ones that calm them. A gut microbe can thus tune skin immunity from afar. That gives probiotic claims a clear test path in people.
plos-pone-0005003:
High blood pressure runs in families. The gene WNK1 helps the kidneys balance salt and water. It was already a strong candidate for inherited hypertension. Stephen Newhouse and colleagues tested it further in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used tag SNPs that capture the gene's common variation. They measured blood pressure and urinary potassium in their subjects.

Variants in WNK1 were linked to blood pressure differences. They were also linked to how much potassium appears in urine. The gene flags part of the inherited risk for hypertension. The finding sharpens the search for blood-pressure genes. It also connects a kidney salt pathway to everyday blood pressure variation.
plos-pone-0005103:
Most mammalian genes lack the classic TATA signpost at their start. Their promoters often have several possible start sites. How transcription begins there was poorly known. Ramakrishnan Anish and colleagues studied TATA-less promoters in PLOS ONE in 2009. They characterized the DNA elements these promoters use. They also tested which factors the elements require.

They identified a new core promoter element, XCPE2. The element helps start transcription without TATA. That fills a major gap in the gene-start story. Over eighty percent of protein-coding genes use such promoters. A new element in this system matters widely. It may explain start-site choice in many genes. Textbook accounts of transcription can now be more complete.
plos-pone-0005203:
Hospitals now store vast amounts of patient data in electronic health records. Genomics faced a data flood earlier and built enrichment methods to find real patterns in gene lists. Hanauer and colleagues borrowed those methods for clinical records in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Doctors keep short problem lists for each patient, much like gene sets in a lab. Applying omics-style enrichment to those lists can reveal links between conditions that no one had joined up. The crossover shows that tools built for one data flood can help tame another. The tools were built for gene data, yet they fit the clinic well, and that fit may help doctors spot links they would miss by eye.
plos-pone-0005303:
G-CSF is a growth factor best known for making blood cells, but it also protects neurons and fights cell death. Diederich and colleagues paired it with cognitive training in PLOS ONE in 2009 and looked for combined effects in the hippocampus.

Together, the drug and training improved spatial learning more than either alone. More newborn hippocampal neurons also survived. A synergy between a drug and mental exercise is attractive for brain repair, since training is cheap, safe, and easy to add to care. Mind drills alone help some stroke and brain injury cases, and a cheap drug alone helps a bit too. So a pair that boosts each other is a strong lead for care.
plos-pone-0005403:
Neutrophils, the first immune cells to reach infection, polarize and crawl toward chemical cues. Their front and rear ends carry different membrane domains. Rossy and colleagues tracked proteins called flotillins during that polarization in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Flotillins interact with PSGL-1, a surface protein on neutrophils. Upon stimulation, they rapidly organize into membrane domains that later accumulate in the uropod, the cell's rear. Mapping that choreography shows how a crawling cell sorts its machinery between front and back. A cell that crawls must know its front from its back at each step,. The quick sort of these proteins is one way it paints that map anew each time it turns toward food or harm.
plos-pone-0005503:
Eunha Shim and Alison Galvani modelled bird flu control in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. The H5N1 flu virus keeps spreading in birds and sometimes infects people. Killing flocks in an outbreak, called culling, is the main defence used worldwide.

Their model asked how culling changes the virus itself over time. Wiping out birds can favour strains that spread faster or hit harder before the flock is culled. Weighing that risk helps officials design control plans that cut danger now without breeding a worse virus for later. The study is a model of how a sound control policy must count long-term effects, not just short-term case numbers.
plos-pone-0005603:
Shinichi Hayashi and co-authors studied a rhythm gene in mouse embryos in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. As a vertebrate embryo grows, blocks of tissue called somites form one after another at steady intervals. A clock-like set of gene waves in the tail tissue sets that rhythm.

The team showed that a gene called Sprouty4, which brakes a growth signal, pulses on and off under the clock's control. Its pulses help time where each new block forms. Somites later become vertebrae and muscle, so the clock shapes the spine itself. Faults in this clock are linked to spine defects, so its parts are studied with care.
plos-pone-0005703:
Thomas Watts, Tamara Haselkorn, Nancy Moran, and co-authors surveyed wild fruit flies in 2009 for a heritable germ called Spiroplasma. This bacterium passes from mother to offspring in many insects. In some hosts it kills males, skewing the sex ratio toward females.

The team checked many natural Drosophila groups and species for the infection. Rates varied widely from place to place and species to species. That patchiness raises questions about what lets the germ spread or fade. Tracking such hidden partners helps explain insect numbers, sex ratios, and even pest control ideas based on germs.
plos-pone-0005803:
Anna Grochot-Przeczek and co-authors showed in 2009 that an enzyme called HO-1 speeds skin wound healing in mice. HO-1 protects cells, calms inflammation, and promotes new blood vessels. It surges in injured tissue, peaking a few days after a wound.

The team clarified what that surge does for closing a wound. Mice with more HO-1 activity healed faster in their tests. Faster closure means less infection risk and less scarring. Wounds that stall, as in diabetes, are a major burden, so any natural accelerator is worth mapping. The study defines where HO-1 helps in the healing sequence.
plos-pone-0005903:
Timothy Radstake and co-authors profiled a newly recognized T cell pattern in systemic sclerosis in 2009. This autoimmune disease hardens skin and can scar inner organs. Debate had long centered on whether Th1 or Th2 immunity dominates.

The team found a pronounced Th17 profile, a third arm of T cell response, in patients. They also measured two signals inside cells that together distinguish disease subtypes, limited and diffuse. A clear immune fingerprint could help predict the course of disease and choose therapy well. The study redirects an old debate toward the Th17 arm.
plos-pone-0006003:
India makes a large share of the world's medicines, yet quality control rests with its states. Roger Bate, Richard Tren, Lorraine Mooney and colleagues ran a pilot check of essential drug quality in two major Indian cities in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper samples basic medicines and tests whether they meet the standard buyers assume.

Each state enforces its own rules, and the levels do not always match. A pilot study in two cities can flag where the system leaks before a wider check is run. The findings matter well past India, since its drugs ship worldwide; weak pills in one market can mean failed treatment for patients on other continents.
plos-pone-0006103:
Front-page medical news reaches millions, so its quality deserves a check. William Lai and Trevor Lane ran that check in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper searched a news database for medical research reported on newspaper front pages, and recorded the studies' sources, judging each by research maturity and level of evidence.

Placement on a front page is meant to seize attention, which raises the stakes on what gets chosen. If front pages favor early, weak findings, public hope and fear will swing on shaky ground. The audit gives editors and readers a record of what the front page actually amplifies, and a basis for doing it better.
plos-pone-0006203:
Skin scarring after a transplant can look strikingly like scleroderma, a disease that hardens skin and organs. Jo Nadine Fleming and colleagues compared the two conditions in a 2009 PLOS ONE study of chronic graft-versus-host disease. Recent work had found odd blood vessel changes and vessel loss in scleroderma skin.

The transplant skin lacked those vessel faults, the team reports, despite similar scarring. Looks, in other words, can mislead: two similar scars arise by different routes. Telling the conditions apart matters because treatments differ. The study gives doctors tissue signs that separate graft disease from true scleroderma.
plos-pone-0006303:
The algae living inside corals contain puzzling crystals of uric acid. Hiroshi Yamashita, Atsushi Kobiyama, and Kazuhiko Koike ask whether those deposits work as eye-spots in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The algae, zooxanthellae of the genus Symbiodinium, power tropical reefs through their partnership with corals.

Eye-spots in other single-celled algae sense light direction. Crystals inside the coral symbionts could serve a similar light-related role. How host and symbiont interact physiologically is still poorly understood. Testing odd structures like these crystals is how that picture gets filled in.
plos-pone-0006403:
Salmonella in chicken litter can carry over to doom the next flock raised in the same house. Victoriya Volkova, Hartford Bailey, and Robert Wills studied litter contamination and farm soil properties in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. In the southern United States, broiler houses are built primarily on local soils.

Contamination of litter before placement predicts the flock's later contamination down the production line. Soil properties at the farm location relate to that persistence. Knowing which ground holds the germ longest guides cleaning and site choices. Food safety begins before the chicks arrive.
plos-pone-0006503:
Young-Il Jeong and co-authors found a surprising protective role for a known molecule in PLOS ONE in 2009. Platelet-activating factor, or PAF, has long been linked to harmful processes during septic shock. Sepsis is a runaway response to infection that can kill. The team present novel activities for PAF that cut the other way.

Their title reports that PAF protects mice against endotoxic shock caused by lipopolysaccharide, a bacterial toxin. A molecule cast as villain may also be a defender, depending on timing or dose. The result warns against simple stories in sepsis biology. It may also suggest new angles for treating shock.
plos-pone-0006603:
Stefania Mattiussi and co-authors studied a stress kinase in blood vessel cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Smooth flow of blood sends one of the strongest guard signals to the cells that line vessels. That flow signal is called laminar shear stress. Some physical and chemical agents can block its guard effect. The team studied a kinase called HIPK2 in these lining cells.

Their title says that when HIPK2 is switched on, the cells respond less well to smooth flow. A stress-driven kinase may thus undo the good that flow does. That path could add to vessel disease where flow is rough or disturbed. It also marks HIPK2 as a point where drugs might step in.
plos-pone-0006703:
Carole L. Galligan and co-authors applied a detailed cell test to early rheumatoid arthritis in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rheumatoid arthritis attacks the joints and can disable patients. Its exact starting mechanisms are still unknown. Early symptoms are often vague, which delays diagnosis and treatment. Doctors also lack reliable ways to predict which drugs will help a patient.

The team used multiparameter phospho-flow analysis on lymphocytes. That method reads signaling activity inside many immune cells at once. Comparing early patients with controls can reveal early warning patterns. Such patterns might support faster, more confident diagnosis. They might also help doctors monitor whether a drug is working.
plos-pone-0006803:
Vitor Hugo Teixeira and his team read gene use in blood cells of arthritis patients in PLOS ONE in 2009. The illness is rheumatoid arthritis, in which the body attacks its own joints. Blood cells carry traces of that fight. Reading all their gene use at once can map the fight. The team sought genes tied to defense and immunity.

Blood came from the arm veins of patients. The team logged which genes were on and which were off. Fresh defense genes stood out in the logs. A blood-based map could aid diagnosis without joint taps. It may also point to paths that new drugs could block.
plos-pone-0006903:
Matthew L. Rizk and James C. Liao modeled aromatic chemical production in engineered bacteria in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ensemble modeling is a newer method for metabolic modeling. It uses enzyme tuning data to refine production models. Aromatic products include building blocks for drugs and materials. E. coli is the usual factory organism for such work.

The authors investigated aromatic production in E. coli with the ensemble approach. Multiple plausible models are carried together rather than one. Their spread shows which predictions are robust. Robust predictions guide which enzymes to tune in the cell factory. Better models mean fewer failed engineering rounds in industrial biotechnology.
plos-pone-0007003:
Darko Bosnakovski, Randy Daughters, Zhaohui Xu, and colleagues studied a muscular dystrophy gene in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy, or FSHD, follows shrinkage of repeat DNA at one chromosome tip. A gene inside each repeat, DUX4, is a prime suspect. The mouse carries a conserved relative of that gene, called mDUX.

The team examined what mouse DUX does to muscle. Its effects came in two phases, a biphasic myopathic pattern. Studying the mouse version helps test whether DUX proteins truly harm muscle. That question sits at the center of how FSHD begins.
plos-pone-0007103:
Min Hua Jen, Alex Bottle, and Azeem Majeed tested a hospital folklore claim in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many in England assume early August is a risky time for hospital admission. Newly qualified doctors start work in NHS hospitals on the first Wednesday of that month. The team checked whether death rates rise in that first week.

They compared in-hospital mortality right after the new doctors started with other weeks. Hard data beat anecdote on a question staff and patients worry about. Their analysis informs how hospitals supervise and support new doctors during the changeover period.
plos-pone-0007203:
Robert L. Snyder, Katy H. Frederick-Hudson, and Johannes Schul mapped the family history of katydids in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their genus is Neoconocephalus, with more than twenty-five species. These insects live across the Neotropics and North America and sing with a prominent acoustic communication system.

Many earlier studies used this group to study calling, body function, and evolution. The authors build a molecular phylogeny, a family tree based on DNA. They then trace how temperate life histories evolved within the group. Their tree gives future behavior studies a firmer evolutionary frame.
plos-pone-0007303:
Valentina Gallo, Evelin Schwarzer, Stefan Rahlfs, and colleagues presented a case study linking an inherited enzyme defect to malaria in 2009. Inside malaria-infected red blood cells, an enzyme called glutathione reductase renews a key antioxidant. That renewal is essential for defense against oxidative damage inside the infected cell during malaria.

The enzyme uses fuel made by another enzyme, G6PD, in red blood cells. The authors study inherited glutathione reductase deficiency alongside Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Their case shows how host genetics and parasite needs collide. The parasite depends on the same antioxidant system that protects its host.
plos-pone-0007403:
Keehoon Jung, Jung-Eun Lee, Hak-Zoo Kim, and colleagues designed a decoy molecule to block sepsis in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Lipopolysaccharide, or LPS, is a glycolipid on gram-negative bacteria. It induces sepsis through interaction with a partner protein and Toll-like receptor 4 on immune cells, triggering overwhelming inflammation in patients.

Blocking that interaction could prevent septic shock. The authors designed and generated a Toll-like receptor 4 decoy, called TOY. They report it attenuates gram-negative bacterial sepsis. A decoy that soaks up the trigger offers a different strategy from antibiotics, which kill bacteria but can release more LPS.
plos-pone-0007503:
Anna Rignell-Hydbom and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 asking whether a pesticide breakdown product raises the risk of type 2 diabetes. Long-lived pollutants such as PCBs and DDT residues have often been found alongside diabetes. Cross-sectional studies cannot tell which came first. This case-control study was designed to test the direction of the link. Exposure to p,p'-DDE, the main DDT metabolite, was the focus.

Exposure measured before disease onset was tied to later diabetes. That ordering supports the pollutant as a risk factor rather than a bystander. The finding matters because DDE persists in bodies and food chains for decades. Even where DDT is banned, its residue remains a health question. The study strengthens the case that chemical exposure belongs in diabetes prevention thinking, beside diet and weight.
plos-pone-0007603:
Frederik Staikowsky and colleagues published a clinical study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on chikungunya, a mosquito-borne virus that re-emerged explosively. During 2005 and 2006 it caused a massive outbreak on the island of La Réunion in the Indian Ocean. The virus had adapted to a widespread mosquito species, widening its reach. The team ran a prospective study, following patients through the acute phase of infection as the outbreak unfolded.

Following patients forward in time gives a cleaner picture than looking back. The study documents the symptoms and course of acute chikungunya in detail. Fever and severe joint pain are its hallmarks. A reliable clinical picture helps doctors recognize the disease in new regions. It also helps separate chikungunya from look-alike fevers like dengue. The outbreak was a warning; this record is part of the preparation for the next one.
plos-pone-0007703:
Elizabeth Yan Zhang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It looks at a skin reaction in mice caused by a chemical called dinitrochlorobenzene. The reaction, a form of contact dermatitis, was long viewed as driven by cells, not antibodies.

The authors tested whether specific antibodies and B cells help drive the rash. Their results give antibodies a real role in how the disease develops. That shifts the standard picture of this allergy model. It may also change how researchers use the model to test new skin treatments.
plos-pone-0007803:
Philippe Georgel and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It catalogs the variety found in a family of human immune genes. The genes make Toll-like receptors, the sentinels of the innate immune system. Together they detect a wide range of germs and body signals.

Knowledge about these receptors had grown at an explosive pace. The authors describe the heterogeneous allelic repertoire of the genes. In plain terms, people carry many differing versions of them. That variety shapes who resists infection well. It may also shape who develops inflammatory disease.
plos-pone-0007903:
Alun Salt published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It revisits a deceptively simple question about ancient Greek temples. Were their alignments chosen with the sky in mind? Scholars had reached no consensus on whether temple orientations reflect astronomical intentions.

Salt surveyed archaic and classical Greek temples in Sicily. He compared their alignments with those of temples elsewhere in the Greek world. Patterns in the Sicilian set stood out from the comparison group. The study gives the astronomy case hard numbers to stand on. It also shows how landscape and cult practice may have shaped sacred building.
plos-pone-0008003:
Roy Navon and colleagues built a new way to hunt cancer-linked microRNAs in PLOS ONE in 2009. MicroRNAs are short strands that tune gene use, and their levels shift in many cancers. One snag is that levels vary a lot from person to person, which buries true signals.

Their rank-based method sorts the shifts in a way that resists that noise. Applied across several cancer types, it surfaced microRNAs whose shifts look real and shared. A cleaner hit list gives labs fewer false leads to chase and a better shot at markers that hold up in the clinic.
plos-pone-0008103:
Ayce Yesilaltay and colleagues removed a cholesterol helper in mice and saw heart attacks follow in PLOS ONE in 2009. The helper, PDZK1, steadies the receptor that pulls in good cholesterol. Mice without it already showed odd cholesterol readings on plain diets.

On a fatty diet, and lacking a second gene that guards arteries, the mice clogged their coronary arteries and suffered heart attacks. That grave outcome from one missing helper shows how much quiet work it does. The result adds a new name to the list of heart disease players.
plos-pone-0008203:
Alejandro J. Moyano and Andrea M. Smania studied bacterial change in cystic fibrosis in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, turning mucoid marks a point of no return in lung infection. The main route to that state runs through faults in the mucA gene. Many faults are small deletions in a simple repeat stretch of DNA.

The authors examined how those repeats bias mucA mutation. They worked with strains that lack normal mismatch repair, the system that fixes copying errors. Their findings explain why mucoid forms arise so often in these patients. That helps track how chronic lung infection becomes entrenched.
plos-pone-0008303:
Xavier Fant, Vlastimil Srsen, and Aude Espigat-Georger studied muscle cell fusion in PLOS ONE in 2009. As myoblasts differentiate into muscle, their inner skeleton reorganizes. Fibers that once radiated from the centrosome align along the cell's long axis. Centrosome proteins also move to the outer surface of the nucleus. The team fused non-muscle cells with these differentiating myoblasts.

Nuclei from the non-muscle cells began binding centrosome proteins after fusion. The muscle cell environment thus reprogrammed foreign nuclei. That shows differentiation signals dominate over a nucleus's origin. The result informs how cell identity is controlled.
plos-pone-0008403:
Seongcheol Kim and colleagues traced blood clotting evolution in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Hemostasis is the defense that stops bleeding after injury. The team had established that major mammalian clotting factors are conserved in early vertebrates. Fish gills, though, are highly vascularized and face strong water flow. That raises special challenges for stopping bleeding there.

Their work examines how primary hemostasis first evolved in early vertebrates. Knowing which parts are ancient shows the core of the system. Later additions can then be spotted by comparison. The study grounds human clotting biology in deep evolution.
plos-pone-0008503:
Irena Lavelin and co-authors screen for new proteasome blockers in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Proteasomes are large complexes that break down damaged proteins. They also break down key signaling proteins to control them. Blocking proteasomes is a proven strategy in some cancers. But new blockers with fresh traits are still needed. The team build a high-content cell-based screening system.

Their system watches many cell features at once in each well. It can flag compounds that block proteasomes inside living cells. Hits from the screen are novel inhibitor candidates. The method may speed drug discovery for cancer and other diseases.
plos-pone-0008603:
Jari Heikkila and co-authors test a virus vector against brain tumors in mice in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. VA7 is an alphavirus vector based on a weakened Semliki Forest virus. It is neurotropic, meaning it favors nerve tissue. The team had shown VA7 kills human melanoma grafts in mice. Here they ask if intravenous delivery can eradicate glioma grafts. The gliomas grow orthotopically, in the brain itself, in nude mice.

Intravenous VA7 eradicates those human glioma xenografts in their model. A blood-delivered virus reaching and clearing brain tumors is a strong result. It supports oncolytic virus therapy for glioma, a cancer with few options.
plos-pone-0008703:
Isabel Fuentes-Calvo, Ana Blázquez-Medela, Eugenio Santos, and coworkers looked for a cancer-linked protein in an odd place. Their article ran in PLOS ONE in 2010. K-Ras is a switch protein that helps control cell growth. Textbooks place Ras proteins at the cell membrane, where they switch on. Reports of Ras inside the nucleus were rare and doubted.

Working with fibroblasts and kidney mesangial cells, the team used antibodies and cell fraction tests. Their methods separated the nucleus cleanly from other parts. K-Ras showed up in the nucleus after all. A nuclear role would widen what scientists think this growth switch can do.
plos-pone-0008803:
Peter Taylor, Grant Betts, Sarah Maroulis, and colleagues asked where a gene breaks predicts thinking problems. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Duchenne muscular dystrophy weakens muscles through a broken dystrophin gene. Many boys with the disease also face learning difficulties. The gene makes several protein forms, some used in the brain. Breaks that remove brain forms might cost more thinking skill.

Standard intelligence tests were compared with each boy's mutation type and position. Mutation location indeed tracked with cognitive risk. Families can gain earlier warning of learning support needs. The results refine counseling for newly diagnosed boys.
plos-pone-0008903:
Qiang Zhang, Suvobrata Chakravarty, Dario Ghersi, and colleagues profiled the reading tastes of yeast gene-tag readers. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Genes are packed on spools called histones. Chemical tags on those spools help switch genes on or off. Bromodomain proteins read one class of those tags. Each reader's exact taste decides which genes it can affect. The yeast family offered a complete test set.

Binding assays mapped which tags each bromodomain preferred. The family's members proved choosy in distinct ways. A taste map helps predict which genes each reader controls. Yeast results guide thinking about similar readers in human cells.
plos-pone-0009003:
Myoung Sook Kim and co-authors studied a nerve protein that goes missing in throat cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The cancer is oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, which grows aggressively. Such cancers often feed on sugar oddly and have faulty power plants in their cells. In many tumour samples the gene for neurofilament heavy polypeptide was silenced.

The gene was shut down by methylation, a chemical tag that mutes DNA. With the protein gone, a growth pathway through Akt and beta-catenin ran hotter. Restoring the protein calmed that pathway in the team's tests. The protein looks like a brake whose loss helps this cancer grow.
plos-pone-0009103:
Akiko Iwata and co-authors found a cell-death protein moonlighting as a danger signal, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When blood flows back into starved tissue, the injury often gets worse instead of better. That damage pattern follows heart attacks, strokes, shock, and organ transplants. Cell suicide, also called apoptosis, is a major part of the harm done.

BCL2 proteins normally work inside cells, where they govern that suicide choice. Outside cells, the team found, they act as danger signals to nearby tissue. In mouse models of this injury, those signals reduced the tissue damage. An alarm that protects instead of harming could inspire a new kind of treatment.
plos-pone-0009203:
Adelheid Soubry and co-authors published this cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It examines Kaiso, a protein known for switching genes off. Kaiso was first found through its binding to another protein, p120ctn. Where Kaiso sits inside a cell turns out to depend on what the cell is doing.

Looking at cell lines and at normal and cancerous human tissue, the team tracked Kaiso's location across the cell cycle. During division, Kaiso moves to the mitotic spindle, the machine that pulls chromosomes apart. It also forms part of the material around the centrioles that anchor that machine. The finding gives this gene-silencing protein an unexpected second job in cell division.
plos-pone-0009303:
Mihalis Verykokakis and co-authors published this mouse immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. T cells come in two main families, alpha-beta and gamma-delta. Some gamma-delta cells act like innate defenders, striking fast without prior training. Their development depends on a signaling adaptor called SLAM-associated protein.

The team studied a brake protein called Id3, which restrains E protein transcription factors. In mice, Id3 limits how many of these innate gamma-delta T cells develop through the SLAM pathway. Removing or weakening that limit changes the mix of T cells the mouse produces. The finding shows how a single regulator tunes the balance of immune cell types.
plos-pone-0009403:
Margret Shirinian and co-authors published this fruit fly study in PLOS ONE in 2010. C3G is a helper protein that switches on small G proteins of the Rap family. Those switches help cells stick, move, and hold their shape. The team studied what happens in fly larvae when C3G is missing.

Without C3G, the integrity of larval muscles broke down. The muscles could not keep their structure as the larvae grew and moved. That shows a signaling helper, easy to overlook, is load-bearing for muscle. Fly larvae give genetics a fast way to find such hidden supports before testing them in larger animals.
plos-pone-0009503:
Takahiro Kawabe, Nobu Shirai, and Yuji Wada studied how babies judge space in PLOS ONE in 2010. In adults, the time gap between two flashes can warp how far apart they look. That illusion is called the tau effect. Beeps played with the flashes can strengthen it. The team asked whether infants show the same effect.

Babies looked in ways that showed the illusion at work. Sound timing shifted their sense of where flashes fell. So even very young brains blend sight and sound into one picture of space. The result shows that this blending starts early in life, not after years of learning.
plos-pone-0009603:
Zhisong He and co-authors predicted drug targets by computer in PLOS ONE in 2010. Finding which proteins a drug touches takes long, costly lab work. The number of possible drug and protein pairs is huge. The team built a method that forecasts those interactions from data already known. It used the functional groups of chemicals and known traits of proteins.

The forecast network highlights pairs most likely to interact in real life. Drug makers can then test those pairs first, instead of searching blindly. A good forecast list saves years of bench work. The study shows how computation can stand in front of the lab and narrow the field.
plos-pone-0009703:
Northern white rhinos are among the rarest large animals on Earth. Colin Groves, Prithiviraj Fernando, and Jan Robovský took a fresh taxonomic look at them in PLOS ONE in 2010. Taxonomy is the science of naming and grouping living things.

The authors argue the northern form is not a subspecies of the white rhino at all. They say it stands as a full species of its own, the sixth living rhino species. While southern white rhinos recovered to thousands, the northern form neared extinction. Species status, they argue, sharpens the case for saving it.
plos-pone-0009903:
Type 2 diabetes runs in families, but single genes rarely explain the risk alone. Rosalind Neuman and colleagues looked for pairs of genes that raise risk together. Their study of an Ashkenazi Jewish population appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Gene-gene interactions mean two variants matter mainly when they appear in the same person. The team found combinations that lead to higher risk for developing the disease. Ashkenazi populations have a shared ancestry that makes such hunts sharper. Interaction effects may explain why single-gene scans miss part of inherited risk.
plos-pone-0010003:
The authors were Cathy Jensen, Jim Stankovich, Anneke Van der Walt, and others. Their 2010 genetics study covered multiple sclerosis in Australian patients. Earlier work had found several gene variants that raise the risk of getting the disease. The open question was whether those same variants also make the disease worse once it starts.

The group checked severity measures against the known risk variants. Those variants sit near genes such as IL2RA, IL7R, and CD40. Their answer, stated in the title, was no clear effect on severity. That split between risk and course matters for prognosis and for choosing targets for new treatments.
plos-pone-0010203:
The authors were Thomas Spiesser, Christian Diener, Matteo Barberis, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study asked what sets DNA copying speed in budding yeast. Copying starts at sites called origins, where enzymes unwind the DNA. The moving points of active copying are called replication forks, and starts are sparse when the cell begins.

The team weighed which factors influence how fast replication proceeds in this yeast. Yeast is a favorite model because its copying system mirrors that of larger organisms. Knowing what limits speed helps explain how cells finish copying in time and avoid damage.
plos-pone-0010303:
The authors were Jean-Pierre Etchegaray, Elizabeth Yu, Premananda Indic, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used mouse brain clock tissue grown in dishes. An enzyme, casein kinase 1 delta, sets the length of the daily circadian cycle. It plays a bigger role than its close sibling enzyme in tissues like liver, yet mice lacking it die soon after birth.

That early death blocked study of the brain's master clock, the suprachiasmatic nucleus. Working in vitro, the team showed the enzyme regulates that clock's period length. Clock period decides whether our daily cycle runs short, long, or near twenty-four hours.
plos-pone-0010403:
Michael Parsons and Daniel Blumstein tested whether kangaroos learn to ignore false predator alarms, in PLOS ONE in 2010. They spread dingo scent in areas where kangaroos feed. At first, such scent should warn of danger and drive animals away. Over time, with no dingoes ever appearing, animals might stop caring. Understanding that fading response matters for using scents to protect crops or stock.

The kangaroos kept avoiding the scented areas, though. Familiarity did not breed contempt here; the wariness lasted. A scent that keeps working is more useful for wildlife managers. The result also questions simple rules about animals habituating to cues. When the cost of a mistake is death, caution may never fade. A fake alarm, for prey, may always be worth heeding.
plos-pone-0010503:
Rogerio Castilho and colleagues showed a protein called Rac1 is essential for skin and mouth stem cells during healing in PLOS ONE in 2010. Skin renews itself constantly and repairs wounds using stem cells. Several stem cell pools contribute, in the hair follicle and between follicles. Rac1 helps cells move and divide, making it a candidate control. The team removed Rac1 in mice and watched healing and daily upkeep separately.

Without Rac1, wound healing in skin and mouth lining suffered badly. Normal tissue upkeep, though, carried on without it. That split is useful: a target that affects healing but not rest state could be tuned safely. The study clarifies which stem cell jobs need Rac1. It informs both wound care and cancer, where Rac1 is often overactive.
plos-pone-0010603:
Liselotte Petersen, Per Kragh Andersen, and Thorkild Sørensen separated nature from nurture in infection risk, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Family studies had long hinted that genes affect who catches infections. Genes might instead affect who dies once infected, a different question.

Using registry and family data, the team estimated each effect on its own. Inherited factors shaped both catching an infection and surviving it, but not equally. Shared home environment played a smaller role than many expected. Splitting the two risks helps researchers hunt the right genes and design fairer studies of infection outcomes.
plos-pone-0010703:
Michael Dieterle and colleagues identified two long-mystery mutations in a bread mold, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neurospora crassa has served genetics for over fifty years. Some of its mutants die at warm temperatures but grow at cool ones, a handy trait for study. Two such mutants, called un-7 and png-1, had never been matched to genes.

Careful crosses and sequencing tied each cold-loving trait to a single gene. One gene helps build ribosomes, the cell's protein factories. Naming the genes ends decades of guesswork. It also lets new students use these classic mutants with full knowledge of what is broken.
plos-pone-0010803:
María Laura Tondo and colleagues studied a protective enzyme in the citrus canker germ, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The germ Xanthomonas axonopodis causes citrus canker, a leaf and fruit disease fought on several continents. Plants blast invaders with hydrogen peroxide, and the germ must survive that blast to infect.

One of its four catalase genes, katE, makes an enzyme that breaks peroxide down. Germs without working katE caused far milder disease on citrus plants. The enzyme is therefore a shield the germ cannot do without. A shield this vital is a target: sprays that block it could protect orchards with less antibiotic use.
plos-pone-0010903:
Selina Bopp, Vandana Ramachandran, Kerstin Henson and co-authors published this malaria genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Why one malaria patient recovers and another dies depends partly on inherited genes. The authors used laboratory mice infected with a rodent malaria parasite to hunt for the genes that tip that balance.

They first infected more than thirty inbred mouse strains and found that simple survival separated resistant from susceptible lines best. Linking survival to genetic variation across the genome pointed to a spot on chromosome 6 holding just two genes. One of them, Ppar-gamma, was already suspected in malaria, and the result strengthens its claim. Bopp and colleagues show how mouse genetics can shortlist human-relevant defense genes for a disease that kills hundreds of thousands each year.
plos-pone-0011003:
Gloria Lin, Yuanqing Liu, Thanuja Ambagala and co-authors published this cancer immunotherapy study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Antibodies that stimulate the immune receptor 4-1BB can shrink tumors in mice, expanding both T cells and innate immune cells. Depletion experiments could not say which cells must receive the signal directly, so the authors designed a study around memory T cells.

They found that memory T cells re-activated outside the body controlled an established tumor better than resting memory cells. The activated cells kept dividing and entered the tumor, and testing which cells truly need the 4-1BB signal refines how the therapy works. Lin and colleagues narrow the list of essential cellular targets. Precise targets mean future agonist drugs can be tuned to the cells that actually deliver the cure.
plos-pone-0011103:
Mowat, Luhmann, Smith and colleagues wrote about the eye in PLOS ONE in 2010. When blood flow to the retina drops, cells sense low oxygen through two related proteins. The team asked whether both proteins switch on in the same cells at the same time.

They found the two oxygen sensors act in distinct groups of retinal cells. That split response shows the eye does not react to low oxygen as one uniform tissue. Each cell group may need its own treatment approach. The map of who responds, and how, could guide new care for eye disease linked to poor blood flow.
plos-pone-0011203:
Fu, Tong, Cai and colleagues solved a toxin receptor structure in PLOS ONE in 2010. Anthrax toxin enters human cells by grabbing a surface protein that acts as its handle. The team determined the shape of the outer part of that handle, called TEM8, at fine detail.

The structure shows the exact surface where toxin docks. A blocker fitted to that surface could stop the toxin before it enters cells. That is a clear target for defense related drug design. Structural knowledge also helps explain why this receptor serves the toxin so well in the first place.
plos-pone-0011303:
Wu and Paulson studied anemia recovery in mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. After acute blood loss, the spleen helps make emergency red blood cells. Low oxygen, sensed by the body during anemia, was tested for its control of a growth signal in the mouse spleen.

Low oxygen did regulate that signal, called BMP4, during recovery from acute anemia. The signal helps launch the spleen's emergency blood making program. Understanding this stress response informs hematology, the study of blood. It may improve anemia treatment by supporting the body's own rapid response rather than replacing it.
plos-pone-0011403:
Johanna Scheper and co-authors pursued in 2010 a different way to drug cell processes: block proteins from gripping each other. Most medicines jam a single protein's active pocket, but many key steps depend on two proteins holding together. One such step builds unusual chains of ubiquitin tags that decide a protein's fate inside the cell.

The team developed blockers aimed at the grip itself, stopping the unusual tagging without shutting the proteins down entirely. A grip blocker can be more selective than a pocket drug, since the contact surface is unique to that pair. The work opens a route to processes once called undruggable. It also gives chemists a test case for designing grip blockers against other protein pairs involved in disease.
plos-pone-0011503:
Ling Li and co-authors presented in 2010 a method to map where the synapses of a single neuron fall across the mouse brain. One neuron can contact thousands of partners, and knowing the full pattern of its outputs is key to understanding circuits. Earlier tracing methods were slow and often caught only part of one cell's connections.

Their approach visualizes the distribution of synapses from individual neurons at brain-wide scale, turning an abstract wiring diagram into a concrete map. With it, neuroscientists can see exactly where one cell talks to the rest of the brain and compare cell types fairly. Circuit science advances by such tools: every claim about how regions connect rests on maps, and better maps make every later experiment sharper.
plos-pone-0011603:
Emanuela Screpanti and colleagues screened for chemicals that jam cell division, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When a cell divides, structures called kinetochores must grip spindle fibres and pull sister copies of DNA apart. Blocking that grip triggers a safety checkpoint that halts division and often kills the cell.

The screen searched for compounds that disrupt the kinetochore grip. It turned up new chemicals that attack tubulin, the protein the spindle fibres are built from. Such compounds are valuable leads for cancer research, because rapidly dividing tumour cells depend heavily on a working spindle to keep multiplying.
plos-pone-0011703:
Song Ling and co-authors pinpointed a docking site linked to rheumatoid arthritis, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A short protein motif called the shared epitope is a major risk factor for severe rheumatoid arthritis. It sits on an immune molecule, but how it raises susceptibility and severity at the molecular level was unclear.

The team identified where this motif binds on calreticulin, a helper protein inside cells. Mapping that binding site reveals a concrete molecular handshake behind the genetic risk. A defined contact point gives drug designers and immunologists a specific interaction to probe and possibly to block.
plos-pone-0011803:
Federica Collino and co-authors studied tiny bubbles released by human stem cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cell-derived microvesicles are a newly recognised channel of cell-to-cell communication. Once taken up by a target cell, they can deliver genetic information in the form of small RNAs that adjust gene activity.

Comparing vesicles from bone marrow stem cells and tissue-specific stem cells, the team found they shuttle a selected pattern of microRNAs, not a random sample. Chosen cargo implies a deliberate postal service for gene control between cells. Such vesicles may mediate some benefits of stem cell therapy.
plos-pone-0011903:
Eliot Friedman and colleagues described in 2010 a hidden stickiness in the brain's switch between sleep-like anesthesia and waking. How the brain crosses between conscious and unconscious states remains a major open question, and anesthetics give doctors a controlled way to study the crossing. Going under is usually blamed on drug effects across the whole brain.

The evidence points to a behavioral state barrier: the brain resists leaving whichever state it is in, an effect the authors call neural inertia. That resistance helps explain why waking lags after the drug is stopped. It also suggests anesthesia depth is not a simple dial reading of drug level, which matters for safer surgery.
plos-pone-0012003:
Nathalia Vitureira and co-workers showed in 2010 that a kidney protein also does real work in the growing brain. The protein, podocalyxin, was known from the kidney, where its sugar coat keeps filter cells from sticking in the wrong way. In the brain, a sugary cell-surface protein called PSA-NCAM has long been tied to growth and change in nerve links.

The team found podocalyxin in the brain wearing the same kind of sugar coat, and taking part in the growth of nerve cells and in the forming of the links between them. A protein first met in the kidney thus turns out to help wire the brain. Work like this warns labs that a protein's first known job is rarely its only one.
plos-pone-0012103:
Florian Wegwitz, Mark-Andreas Kluth, Claudia Mänz, and co-authors studied a mouse breast tumor cell line for PLOS ONE in 2010. A popular theory holds that tumors grow from a small set of stem-like cancer cells that feed the rest, much as normal stem cells feed a tissue. Those stem-like cells should be rare and locked into a one-way path of growth.

The mouse cells they studied did not fit that picture neatly. The line seemed able to renew its own mix of cell types, more like a self-balancing system than a strict ladder. Findings like this push cancer science to test its favorite theory against odd cases, since treatment plans built on the theory depend on it being right.
plos-pone-0012203:
Gregory Hather, Winston Haynes, Roger Higdon, and co-authors took the measure of American science funding in PLOS ONE in 2010. To judge the country's commitment to research, they compared federal research spending over six decades against the size of the whole economy and against what industry spends. Their span covers the space race, the Cold War's end, and the rise of global research competition.
