Tracking science money against the economy shows whether research kept pace with national wealth or quietly shrank as a share of it. Those long curves give today's funding debates a baseline that single-year budget fights lack. For a country that leads in discovery, the trend line is the argument both sides will use.
plos-pone-0012303:
Will Fischer, Vitaly Ganusov, Elena Giorgi, and co-authors read thousands of HIV genomes from the first weeks of infection, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Using ultra-deep sequencing on samples from three newly infected people, they focused on the virus regions that killer T cells attack. Earlier work had suggested most infections start from a single virus genome, so the earliest changes should show the immune system's first pressure and the virus's first escapes.

Their models follow that escape in near real time, mutation by mutation. Knowing how fast and by which routes HIV dodges the first attack tells vaccine designers what the virus cannot easily change. The first weeks are the one moment the infection might still be stoppable, which makes their detail precious.
plos-pone-0012403:
Johannes Hov, Verena Keitel, Jon Laerdahl and co-workers scanned a bile sensor gene in patients with a scarring bile duct disease, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The disease, primary sclerosing cholangitis, slowly destroys bile ducts and often ends in transplant. The receptor TGR5 senses bile acids and calms inflammation, making its gene a prime suspect.

The team cataloged mutations in the gene among patients and compared them with healthy people. They found variants, some new, that may change how the receptor works. Each candidate variant gives researchers a lead to test in cells, and together they test whether bile sensing gone wrong helps drive this puzzling disease.
plos-pone-0012503:
Cheryl Chun and Hiten Madhani studied a copper transporter in a deadly fungal pathogen, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Cryptococcus neoformans causes a large share of HIV-related deaths worldwide. It wraps itself in a sugar capsule that shields it from immune attack, and it must gather copper to build defenses. The transporter Ctr2 moves that copper.

The team linked Ctr2 to capsule formation and to the fungus's ability to resist being eaten by immune cells. A transporter that arms both shield and survival is an attractive drug target. Fungal infections have few good drugs, so each such dependency is precious.
plos-pone-0012603:
Jarvikivi, Vainio and Aalto studied how listeners sort speech sounds in real time. Some languages mark meaning with tone, the rise and fall of pitch. Others use length, how long a sound lasts, to set words apart. Their 2010 paper compares these two kinds of language as the brain hears them.

Using timed tests of listening, they found evidence that the two systems work much alike under the surface. That unity suggests the brain treats pitch and length with shared tools, even when languages seem far apart. The result informs how scientists think speech perception grows and varies.
plos-pone-0012703:
Bartlett, Dobeck, Tye and co-authors removed a linking protein in mice and watched tooth enamel fail to form properly. Enamel is built by a sheet of cells called ameloblasts that sit against the growing tooth. The protein p120-catenin helps hold such cell sheets together and shapes their behaviour.

Their 2010 targeted deletion shows enamel development breaks down without it. Teeth are a clean model for how organs build hard tissue in stages. The finding may also explain some human enamel defects and guide dental repair research.  The mouse work isolates this one protein cleanly.
plos-pone-0012803:
Edwards, Phan, Abendroth and co-authors solved the shape of a bacterial grappling hook's head. Harmful bacteria stick to host cells with surface proteins called trimeric autotransporter adhesins. Their 2010 structure comes from Burkholderia pseudomallei, a soil bacterium that causes the dangerous disease melioidosis.

The head is the part that first meets the host cell surface. Knowing its exact shape shows where blocking drugs or vaccine antibodies could grip. Adhesion is the first step of infection, so a good map of it is a practical asset.  Several related structures were compared to confirm the pattern.
plos-pone-0335703:
Davood Fereidooni and Matloob Hejazifar built prediction models for two properties that decide how sandstone behaves in tunnels and foundations: how much squeezing it withstands and how stiff it is. Both normally need destructive crushing tests. The team measured twenty sandstones from four Iranian formations with simpler tests, including density, porosity, and a spring hammer that bounces off the rock surface.

Density predicted strength best, while porous rock was reliably weaker. Among the computer methods tried, a neural network forecast both properties most accurately, ahead of two rival techniques. The hammer bounce proved the single most useful quick measurement. Because the best inputs are cheap and non-destructive, engineers could estimate a rock face's strength on site before committing to a design, a practical gain for mining and construction.
plos-pone-0336003:
Abdullah Al Mamun and colleagues report the first detection in Bangladesh of the Burkholderia cepacia complex, a group of bacteria that can cause serious infections in vulnerable people and animals. The bacteria are notorious in patients with cystic fibrosis and can cause udder infection and abscesses in goats and sheep. The team tested forty goats, most with breathing symptoms and a history of abortion.

Eight samples from sick goats grew related bacteria, while healthy control goats grew none, and gene tests plus sequencing confirmed the group's presence in several. A first national report matters because it puts the pathogen on the map for veterinarians. Goat keepers and animal health services now know to include it when investigating abortion and lung disease.
plos-pone-0339503:
Jorge Yepez and Sara Caria studied how the old rule that a husband should out-earn his wife shapes women's work in Ecuador. If the norm held, women poised to earn more than their husbands should pull back from the labor market. The data showed the opposite: women with higher potential relative income participated more, not less.

The twist was in job quality. Highly educated women shifted toward informal or part-time, more precarious work rather than increasing participation, and women with secondary schooling gained participation at the price of more precariousness too. Only the least educated, lowest-income women gained participation without added precariousness. The pattern suggests economic vulnerability, not the breadwinner norm, is what bends women's choices.
plos-pone-0341403:
Jorge Hernández-Bello and co-authors explored whether blood markers tied to a cattle germ might help doctors spot rheumatoid arthritis. The germ, a relative of the one behind tuberculosis, makes two proteins that help it survive inside immune cells. The team measured antibodies against both proteins in one hundred Mexican patients with the joint disease and one hundred healthy people.

Antibodies against one protein were clearly higher in patients, rose with worse disease, and alone separated patients from healthy people fairly well. Combining both antibody tests sharpened the separation a great deal. The findings hint that this germ may play a part in the disease for some patients, and that a paired blood test could support earlier, surer diagnosis.
plos-pone-0346003:
Yangzi Zhang and three colleagues interview administrative staff at Chinese vocational colleges about working with generative artificial intelligence, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Sixteen staff from three colleges in Henan Province spoke in depth about tools that draft text and answer queries. The team read their answers through a classic technology-acceptance framework covering usefulness, ease, social pressure, and working conditions.

Staff agreed the tools could speed work, standardise workflows, and improve service to students. But they worried about complexity, scarce resources, unclear rules, privacy, blame when the machine errs, and their own job security. The authors say colleges need governance and trust in place before the technology can take root.
plos-pone-0346503:
Mohamed S. Abd El-baki and colleagues taught cameras and a neural network to judge tomato plants' thirst and predict harvest under different watering regimes. Field plots over two seasons received varied irrigation, and ordinary colour photographs were taken at flowering and fruit ripening alongside direct measurements of biomass, leaf water, chlorophyll, soil moisture, and final yield.

Colour indices that include the green channel tracked plant condition almost perfectly, while one ratio ignoring green failed entirely. The neural network predicted traits and yield with very high accuracy. The authors present cheap camera-based monitoring as a practical route to save water while protecting tomato production in dry conditions.
plos-pone-0347303:
Shucheng Feng, Wei He, Li Jiang, and Manlin Chen built an explainable computer system for diagnosing diabetes. Doctors face patients who differ widely, and black-box algorithms that hide their reasoning are hard to trust at the bedside. Their 2026 model instead reasons through a library of belief rules, which state in plain form how combinations of symptoms point toward a diagnosis.

To keep the rule library lean, the team first ranked which measurements matter most, then pruned redundant rules using a neighbourhood method, and finally tuned the remaining parameters with an evolutionary search. The paper walks through this construction in detail, aiming at diagnoses that are both accurate and open to inspection.
plos-pone-0347603:
Zongheng Xu and colleagues investigate two storm events that set off clusters of landslides in Changning County, Yunnan, China, in this 2026 PLOS ONE geology paper. They mapped two hundred fifty-five slides, combining satellite-scale pattern analysis, field inspection, and rock testing to ask why the failures bunched where they did.

Slides lined up along river valleys, clustering at mid-to-high elevations on moderate slopes, mostly on south to southeast faces in certain layered schist rocks. Curiously, slopes far from roads failed more densely than those near roads, hinting the pattern is driven by geology and rainfall rather than road cuts alone. Such maps help local officials judge which hillsides to watch when the next heavy rain arrives.
plos-pone-0348203:
Eleonore Segard and her team judged a bold school plan in a French district. There, kids with brain-based growth gaps learn in plain schools, with pro help at hand. The team used a style of review that asks what works, for whom, and when. They took two schools, one for young kids and one for teens. Talks reached sixty-three folk in all.

The team found one hundred sixty-two parts at play and boiled them down to fifteen keys. These keys switch on five gains in the kids: calm, true place in class, use of their aids, and will to learn and to mix. Gains in self rule and peer life came in train. The keys can guide new districts.
plos-pone-0348403:
Inès Sartori, Véronique Régnier Denois, and co-authors picked apart a French school health program to find which parts must travel intact when the program moves to new schools. The Alliance for Health program trains teachers and after-school staff to build healthier school environments, and it had already run in about one hundred schools with promising results. Their 2026 study used interviews with staff and officials plus structured exchanges between program leaders and researchers.

Seven core functions emerged across four themes: backing from institutions, staff empowerment through training and resources, fitting the program to local needs and limits, and tight coordination. Activities delivering those functions can bend to local context, but the functions themselves should stay fixed. The authors offer the list as a practical guide for scaling the program without hollowing it out.
plos-pone-0348503:
Mohammad Islam and his team checked the true name of a quince shrub grown in Pakistan. The plant, Chaenomeles japonica, is grown for its blooms and fruit. It is easy to mix up with its kin by eye. So the team took fresh leaves from a garden in the Hazara area. They read four short stretches of the plant's DNA.

Each stretch copied with ease. All four matched known samples of this species near word for word. The kin tree also placed the plants with true samples from China, Japan, and the United States. The team says such DNA tags can name garden plants with trust.
plos-pone-0348603:
Jessica Chin and colleagues checked whether a new eye treatment idea could harm the cornea, the clear front layer of the eye. Their lab has built tiny magnetic particles, steered by a rotating magnet, to strip harmful deposits from the lens in a form of glaucoma. The 2026 safety study exposed layers of pig cornea cells to the particles and the spinning field for up to three hours.

The cells kept their membranes intact, stayed metabolically active, and held onto a key protein that seals the layer's tight junctions, both right after treatment and later. Nothing in the tests suggested damage at the doses used. The authors take this as early support for trying the approach against the disease.
plos-pone-0348803:
Ambika Bansal and co-workers ask whether the view at the edge of vision changes how far people feel they have traveled. Earlier seated studies found that motion shown only in the far edges made trips feel longer. Their 2026 study repeats the test while people stand and walk on a treadmill, sometimes blindfolded, using a huge wraparound screen.

Edge-only flow still stretched felt distance, both standing still and while walking with matching visuals. Blindfolded walking alone also inflated felt distance in one task. A second task, adjusting a marker instead of walking to it, showed no clear differences. Adding body movement cues did not cancel the edge effect, which matters for training simulators and virtual worlds.
plos-pone-0348903:
Saeid Karimi and Zahra Kosari Honarmand surveyed students at a public university in Iran about whether they hope to start their own businesses. Their 2026 PLOS One paper looks at two possible drivers: courses that teach business skills, and a mindset open to spotting chances and taking risks.

Answers from about one hundred ninety students showed that a positive attitude and a sense of personal control most strongly predicted the wish to found a business. What classmates and family think mattered only indirectly. Business courses raised students' sense of control but did not lift intentions on their own. The authors argue for hands-on, practice-based teaching.
plos-pone-0349103:
Shayna L Hilburg, Alfredo Alexander-Katz, and co-authors simulated how single protein-like polymer chains behave when they meet each other in water. These folded chains, called single-chain nanoparticles, are prized as stand-ins for natural proteins, but whether they stick together into clusters was unclear. Their 2026 molecular dynamics study watched random mixed-building-block chains interact and catalogued what happened at the contact points.

Two outcomes dominated: chains either latched onto each other through side-chain contacts, much as proteins do, or brushed past with only brief touches. Small water-loving building blocks gathered at lasting contact points, and greasy blocks anchored prolonged sticking. Surprisingly, a chain's folded shape mattered more for clustering than its exact recipe, since shape varied as much within one recipe as across recipes.
plos-pone-0349203:
Anita Stefoska-Needham and co-workers check how often sorghum actually appears in grain foods sold in China and Australia. Sorghum is a hardy grain with possible health perks, yet shoppers may rarely meet it. Their 2026 audit records ingredients for more than sixteen hundred products in big supermarkets in Shenzhen and the Illawarra region.

Sorghum turned up in only a small share of breakfast cereals and snack bars in both countries. It was missing from all flours, pastas, and noodles checked in Australia. Where present, it seldom led the ingredient list. Rates barely differed between the two countries. The authors argue that shoppers cannot choose sorghum foods they never see, so makers and stores have room to expand them.
plos-pone-0349303:
Aswath Krishna Muthuraman and colleagues reviewed what general practices have tried to cut heart disease risk in people with severe mental illness, who die early from cardiovascular causes at striking rates. Ten studies from the primary care literature were gathered and read for themes covering the interventions themselves, how they were put in place, teamwork structures, barriers, and what participants thought of them.

Attempts ranged from tailored behaviour coaching and a patient-centred medical home model to clinician tools and staff training. Well-trained staff, structures that link services together, and peer support stood out as promising ingredients. Getting such programmes running and keeping them running proved the hard part. The authors map the field for practices that want to act, while noting how thin the tested evidence remains.
plos-pone-0349403:
Pála Björk Kúld and colleagues asked kin and care staff to weigh the good and bad sides of ways to help the most disabled people steer their own lives. Those they serve have deep learning limits plus other health needs, and they speak few words or none, so staff must guess and support each choice with care. Ten kin and thirteen staff took part in four rounds of a Delphi poll, which builds shared views step by step.

The group reached shared views on most of the themes raised. Both sides praised trust built both ways, shared learning, and one joint way of working. They said good support lifts health, daily life, and say in one's own days. The weak points were the things that must be in place first, such as the same staff each day, which real care often lacks.
plos-pone-0349603:
Amanuel Yoseph and co-authors asked how often women in one southern Ethiopian district end a pregnancy, and what personal and neighborhood factors line up with that outcome. Their 2026 PLOS One survey covered more than three thousand five hundred women who had been pregnant in the previous year.

About one pregnancy in five or six ended in abortion. Odds ran higher for women without schooling, women whose pregnancy was unplanned, and women with little say in household decisions. Living in the countryside, living far from a health facility, and hearing little from radio or other media also raised the odds. The authors urge services and outreach aimed at these gaps.
plos-pone-0349803:
Yuan Ma and co-authors designed a solar assisted heat pump system in 2026 that aims to run a full day on no net electricity. Industry needs high temperature heat, usually from fossil fuels, and the design targets that gap.

Solar panels that make both power and heat drive a carbon dioxide heat pump, while a hot water tank stores energy and feeds the pump's cold side. A dynamic model of a typical day in Xi'an tested the setup at steady high heat output. Panel count, tank size, and starting temperature all swayed the balance. The authors frame net zero daily operation as both an engineering and an ethics goal.
plos-pone-0350103:
Nikhil Sharma and colleagues studied how proteins from a bacterium carried by eyelash mites affect the surface cells of the human eye. The bacterium, Bacillus oleronius, can provoke inflammation, and mite-related proteins are suspected in some eye surface disease. The team also tested the salty stress that occurs in dry eye, alone and combined with the proteins.

Eye cells grown in dishes lost viability as protein dose rose, with the higher dose clearly worse than the lower one. Adding strong salt stress deepened the damage. The results support a two-hit picture: mite-carried bacterial proteins plus the salt imbalance of dry eye together strain the eye's surface, which may help explain symptoms in patients with heavy mite loads.
plos-pone-0350403:
Schröder and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask what really drives support for the far-right AfD party in Germany: worry about immigration, or economic deprivation. The party rose from a euroskeptic movement to the second force in the federal parliament, and the losers-of-modernization story, that left-behind voters fuel it, is widely told. The team used a long-running German household panel spanning a decade.

Concern about immigration alone explained about three quarters of the explainable variation in AfD support, and even more of actual voting for the party. Deprivation measures added little beyond it, and barely distorted the immigration link itself. The authors argue this undercuts the deprivation story twice over: it is weaker than the cultural explanation, and it may add almost nothing at all. They are careful to speak of explanation in survey data, but the challenge to a favorite theory is plainly stated.
plos-pone-0350803:
Kazuhiro Omori and colleagues in Japan published a trial plan in 2026 for preventing sore mouth during breast cancer chemotherapy. Mouth sores are common, painful, and hard to prevent, and creams wear off fast and ignore rubbing from teeth. No results are reported yet.

About one hundred fifty patients will be split at random between usual mouth care and care plus a soft mouth protector made to shield the lining. Sore severity, pain, and quality of life will be tracked through treatment. A simple shield that works could spare many patients one of chemotherapy's most miserable side effects.
plos-pone-0351303:
Finding every study about transgender and gender diverse people is harder than it sounds, because wording varies widely. Ryn Gagen and colleagues built and validated ready-made database searches, called hedges, for two major medical and psychology indexes, in this 2026 PLOS One paper.

Two librarians assembled keyword and subject term sets building on earlier work, then tested them against a gold standard of one hundred forty-four known relevant articles. The final searches caught every one. A sample of results was screened by international experts to measure how much noise the searches admit. Freely shared hedges should make future evidence reviews on this population faster and more complete.
plos-pone-0351403:
Sooah Kim and colleagues tested whether spit chemistry can tell apart three conditions that all cause mouth sores. Behcets disease, Sjogrens syndrome, and ordinary recurring mouth ulcers can look alike at first glance. Spit was collected from forty three patients after fasting, and dozens of small molecules were profiled with lab instruments.

Patterns split the three groups cleanly in sorting analyses. Seven molecules stood out as drivers of the split. Two of them, malonic acid and aspartic acid, ran clearly higher in Behcets samples than in the other two groups. A spit test will not replace clinical judgement, but a distinct chemical fingerprint could speed referral and spare patients long diagnostic detours.
plos-pone-0352103:
Yaacov Schul, Yoav Ganzach, and Asya Pazy published a study in PLOS ONE re-examining a lively political psychology debate: do liberals and conservatives dislike their opponents equally? A recent within-person study had argued yes, finding that as party identity strengthens, animosity rises similarly on both sides, supporting a symmetric view. Schul and colleagues raise conceptual and methodological doubts, propose a different model, and run it on the original data plus a second large dataset.

In their reanalysis, the effect of identity strength on outgroup animosity differed between Democrats and Republicans, favoring the asymmetric view that the two camps are not mirror images. The authors are careful to frame this as evidence within these datasets and models, not a universal law. The paper doubles as a methods lesson: how a model separates identity direction from identity strength can quietly decide the symmetry question before data speak.
plos-pone-0352203:
Xiujing Zhao, Whitley Atkins, and Brendon McDermott tested a simple habit in this 2026 PLOS ONE trial: adding one litre of plain water a day for six weeks. Thirty-eight healthy young adults were handed two bottles daily and otherwise left to eat and drink as they pleased. Food and fluid diaries, plus urine tests, tracked what changed at the start, middle, and end.

Plain water drinking did rise and stayed higher at the end. Total fluid intake rose at the halfway point but not by week six, and sugary drink habits barely moved. Calorie intake dipped modestly by the final check. The study suggests a small daily water routine can stick, with only gentle effects on diet.
plos-pone-0352503:
Haynes, in a 2026 data study, maps signaling genes in the brain region that dies back in Parkinson's disease. Massive gene studies of this region, the substantia nigra, produce lists too long to read plainly. Haynes narrows the lens to genes for a big family of cell receptors, their activators, and the machinery that carries their signals.

Across nine older data sets and two newer ones, many strongly used signaling genes had shifted in patients. They include the enzyme that makes dopamine, several growth signal components, and genes for cell sticking and immune talk. In the pigmented nerve cells that actually die, thirty-two receptor and signaling genes had changed, and nearly all were turned up. The pattern points to a stress pathway being switched on. Haynes reads this as a deficit of feedback signals: surviving cells shout louder, perhaps because calming return signals are missing.
plos-pone-0352703:
Liam Wietzorrek and four colleagues record what operating teams say during heart surgery, and how hard they are working. Their 2026 study covers twenty-four cardiac operations and over one hundred hours of surgery. Every spoken exchange from incision to closure was annotated. Team members wore heart monitors, giving a physiological workload trace. The analysis links talk patterns to surgical phases and personal strain.

Case-relevant talk peaked at critical moments. Starting and stopping the heart-lung bypass machine drew the densest relevant communication. Off-topic chat peaked during the final closing phase. Individuals slipped into irrelevant talk when their own workload dipped. Crucially, one person's quiet moment was often another's peak load. Chat therefore does not always signal a relaxed room. The findings support designing communication habits around phases and roles, not blanket rules about silence.
plos-pone-0352903:
Ruana Costa Rodrigues and seven colleagues published this 2026 PLOS One study of the bacteria living in coalho cheese, a traditional raw-milk cheese from Brazil's dry Caatinga region. The cheese is made by spontaneous fermentation, so its microbes reflect local farms, methods, and climate. The team collected samples from eight towns in the Seridó area and sequenced bacterial DNA to map the community.

Lactic acid bacteria dominated the cheese, led by Enterococcus at about a quarter of the community, with Lactococcus, Streptococcus, and Leuconostoc also prominent. These are the microbes that sour the milk, build flavor, and keep the cheese stable. As the first survey of its kind for this region's coalho, the study gives producers a baseline for quality work and future food-safety research.
plos-pone-0353203:
Ho and Nguyen built a learning system that reads breathing from a fingertip light sensor in a 2026 study. The sensor, already common for pulse checks, carries breathing clues in how its wave rises and falls. Earlier systems estimated only breathing rate or only the wave shape, never both at once.

Separate branches read each kind of clue, then merge to produce both outputs together. Stepwise training, where the system adapts from one reference signal type to another, beat all other strategies. Mixing reference types carelessly hurt both outputs. Short sensor windows thus can track breathing fully, if training respects which reference the labels came from.
plos-pone-0353303:
Nasreldein, Riehl, and Obłuski studied plant remains from Old Dongola in Sudan in a 2026 paper. The city was a Christian kingdom's capital before power shifted and Islam spread through the region between the fourteenth and eighteenth centuries. Seeds from every dug layer of the citadel gave a rare, even record of farming change.

Crop mixes shifted across the transition, reflecting wider economic and cultural change. The authors caution that plant evidence alone cannot prove the shifts were caused by migration or conversion. Even so, the record enriches a thin archive for early modern Sudan, showing daily farming life through a deep political and religious turning point.
plos-pone-0353503:
Li Zhu, Long Tang, and Huaqing Mao published a study on machine reading of Chinese handwriting, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Judging whether two samples were written by the same person is hard in Chinese, with thousands of characters and wide personal style. Their system compares samples at the level of single characters.

Zhu's team built paired networks with an attention step, so the model focuses on the strokes that matter most. Trained this way, it learns what makes writing samples match or differ. Forensic examiners and archivists could use such a tool as a tireless second opinion on disputed documents. It would not replace human judgment, but it can sort large sets of samples quickly.
plos-pone-0353903:
Miriam López-Teros and co-authors examine in 2026 the built in abilities that support healthy ageing among older adults in Mexico. They used a national survey of people aged fifty and above and scored five areas, covering movement, senses, memory, mood, and energy. Social hardship was counted through a combined index of unmet needs.

Impairment was very common, with most people affected in two or more areas. Older age, many long term illnesses, low schooling, and trouble getting food all linked to lower ability. Greater social hardship linked steadily to worse scores. The authors see the combined score as a useful early warning tool.
plos-pone-0354103:
Chingiz Nurimanov and co-authors set out in 2026 a study plan for patients in Kazakhstan whose main neck artery to the brain is fully blocked. The plan follows people having a bypass that joins a scalp artery to a brain artery. Care takes place at the national neurosurgery centre, with follow-up over six months.

The main question is how often a stroke occurs after surgery. Scans of blood flow, checks of thinking, and standard nerve tests are taken before and after the operation. As a protocol, the work reports no outcomes yet; its value lies in joining anatomy, flow, and function to guide safer choices.
plos-pone-0354203:
Shaik Irfan Sadaq and five colleagues blend natural and synthetic fibres into layered plastic sheets and test how strong the blends are, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Jute fibre is cheap and renewable but modest in strength; carbon and glass fibres are strong but costly and petroleum-based. The team hand-built three six-layer combinations and pulled, crushed, and bent standard samples of each.

Adding carbon to jute raised strength by nearly ninety percent on average, and glass by over half. The carbon-and-glass pairing without jute was strongest overall on all three tests. Computer simulations matched the bench results closely. Such hybrids could put greener materials into car parts and panels without surrendering performance.
plos-pone-0354303: Sorbus tianschanica seedlings — Tian Shan rowan — respond to light quality. This paper measured growth and photosynthetic effects. The findings guide nursery practice for a mountain tree — light recipes for healthy seedlings.
plos-pone-0354603:
Whyunyoung Choi, a single author, published this 2026 study of generative artificial intelligence scoring the pronunciation of foreign language learners. Sixty students in a twelve-week program produced speech samples that three trained human raters and an AI system scored on the same seven-point rubric across eight features, from single sounds to fluency.

The AI agreed moderately with humans, best on fluency and worst on individual sounds, but it marked everyone higher across the board. Interviewed raters blamed its thin sense of context and learners' first-language habits. Choi recommends a hybrid model pairing machine speed with human judgment.
plos-pone-0354703:
Yuan Cheng and Yanting Sun used molecular dynamics simulations to pull apart trigraphene, a three-atom-thick carbon sheet, and watch how cracks with different angles and lengths destroy it. Their 2026 study stretched the material along its two crystal directions across a wide temperature range, recording stiffness, breaking stress, and toughness as the virtual cracks grew.

Failure depended heavily on direction. Pulling one way produced clean, brittle splits straight from the crack tip, while pulling the other way deflected cracks toward the edges and tolerated more damage, though heat punished that direction more. Rising temperature softened everything. For engineers dreaming of graphene in flexible electronics or armor, such maps of weak directions are essential design data.
plos-pone-0354803:
Shi, in a 2026 paper, proposes a new way to control permanent magnet motors, a workhorse of modern machines and vehicles. Standard predictive control works well only when its model of the motor matches the real thing. When motor values drift, as they do with heat and wear, control quality falls and current turns rough.

The proposed method drops the fixed model and instead learns the motor's behavior from live data. A nonlinear model tracks past inputs and outputs, and an adaptive step updates it while the motor runs, forgetting old data at a changing rate. In computer simulations with badly mismatched motor values, current distortion fell by clear margins compared with two standard methods. Performance also held up under added noise and sudden load changes. The author presents the approach as a sturdier option for drives that must cope with shifting conditions.
plos-pone-0354903:
Berrak Itır Aylı, Mehmet Emin Demir, Arzu Akgül, and Hatice Şahin published this 2026 analysis of the environmental cost of dialysis in Türkiye. Kidney dialysis saves lives but drinks water and power and produces much waste. Combining registry data, published figures, and measurements from two Turkish centers, they scaled the footprint to millions of yearly sessions nationwide.

Measured Turkish water use ran meaningfully below international estimates, showing why local numbers matter. Sloppy waste sorting and fossil-heavy electricity stood out as the biggest fixable burdens. The authors chart practical cuts for a sector that cannot simply shrink.
plos-pone-0355103:
Kexin Zhu and five colleagues published this 2026 study of how the COVID-19 pandemic bent the recorded rates of three immune diseases in the United States. Using a large insurance claims database from 2018 to 2022, they built seasonal groups and compared new diagnoses of asthma, eczema, and multiple sclerosis with pre-pandemic rates.

Recorded diagnoses dropped sharply in spring 2020, most steeply for children, teenagers, and older adults. Zhu reads the dip as missed and delayed care rather than truly fewer cases. The authors warn researchers to treat pandemic-era diagnosis counts with care in any study.
plos-pone-0355203:
Yibo Huang and co-authors propose a new flow meter method in 2026. It measures three phase flow at drilling sites with gamma rays. Grime on the sensor, interference, and heat drift corrupt readings there. Their method joins a smart filter with a small neural network. The filter handles curved physics without flattening it. The network has physics rules built in.

State tracking covers gas, liquid, and solid shares. It also tracks the dirty layer on the sensor. A matching plan keeps the filter gain well tuned. Field data from a drilling platform tested the method. Phase shares were predicted with strong accuracy. The design may suit other harsh measuring jobs.
plos-pone-0355303:
Shubo Liu and co-authors develop a vesicle collection method in 2026. Vesicles are tiny parcels shed by cells into nearby fluid. The team took them from liver tumour tissue and nearby tissue. Blood vesicles lack close ties to one tumour site. Gentle enzyme digestion freed the tissue vesicles first. Staged spinning then cleaned and sorted them.

Checks by sizing, imaging, and protein tests confirmed the parcels. RNA cargo inside them was then measured. A shortlist of candidate RNAs was tested by a gene method. Several long and short RNAs were enriched in tumour parcels. A mixed signature sorted tumour from nearby tissue very well. It joined blood measures with two RNA markers.
plos-pone-0355403:
Jun'an Lei and co-authors optimised a protective spray coat that helps loose-stone road surfaces last longer. Chip seals shed stones over time, and a sand-bearing fog seal can lock them in, but the recipe involves trade-offs. Their 2026 study used a statistical surface method to vary asphalt amount and sand ratio against grip, texture, and stone loss.

More asphalt strengthened bonding but dulled skid resistance. More sand raised grip yet thinned texture depth. Best recipes differed for fine and coarse stone sizes, and both are stated as practical numbers for crews. The optimised coats sealed water well and opened to traffic in reasonable time. Lei and colleagues offer the design as a durability upgrade for low-cost roads.
plos-pone-0355503: The Changshan waterway — how many vessels can it safely pass? This paper researched its vessel passing capacity. The capacity analysis informs the shipping schedules and infrastructure investments that keep this aquatic artery flowing.
plos-pone-0355603:
Amira Abdelwahab and Mohamed Salama propose a hybrid active learning system that picks which unlabelled texts are worth paying humans to annotate. Labelling is the bottleneck of text classification, especially in mixed, messy collections. Their 2026 framework pools four classic classifiers into an ensemble and loops: label a little, retrain, then ask for the most informative next examples.

Texts were converted to numbers four ways, from word counts to modern contextual embeddings, so representation choices could be compared fairly. Benchmarks came from healthcare, finance, spam, and shopping domains. Abdelwahab and Salama argue the ensemble-plus-selection loop reaches useful accuracy with far fewer labels than labelling everything, a practical gain for small teams.
plos-pone-0356003:
Hubert Amu, Theodora Yayra Brinsley, and Joshua Oppong publish a protocol in 2026 for a systematic review of how chronic disease care can be folded into primary healthcare across sub-Saharan Africa. Diseases such as diabetes and hypertension now account for a growing share of deaths, worst in poorer countries. The World Health Organization urges integration into primary care, yet African programs still show persistent gaps. The review asks which implementation strategies have actually been tried and how they fared.

Following standard protocol guidance, the team will search peer-reviewed and grey literature in English from 1990 through 2025. They will appraise study quality with a tool designed for mixed designs, and synthesize results narratively where statistics cannot be pooled. Any changes to the plan will be logged in the public registry record. The authors intend the synthesis to guide ministries aiming for universal coverage.
plos-pone-0356103:
Negin Kordi and colleagues tested whether treadmill exercise can calm the heart inflammation that methamphetamine causes in rats. Their 2026 study ran 104 rats through eight combinations. The combinations mixed drug exposure, withdrawal, and six weeks of moderate endurance training. The team then measured heart damage enzymes in blood. It also measured three inflammatory messengers in heart tissue.

Methamphetamine raised every damage and inflammation marker. Simply withdrawing the drug lowered them. Pairing withdrawal with training lowered them further. That held for the cell-death switch caspase-1 and two interleukin signals. Training during continued use helped less clearly than training after quitting. The results position supervised exercise as a plausible, drug-free therapy for repairing stimulant-damaged hearts, at least in animals.
plos-pone-0357003:

Sudan's war has battered its health system. TB remains the world's deadliest single-pathogen infection. Their 2026 cross-sectional study scored knowledge, attitudes, and self-reported preventive habits. The students ranged from third to sixth year.

Knowledge landed in the middle. Nearly everyone knew TB's cause and airborne spread. But under a third knew latent TB cannot infect others. Only about a quarter said they always masked up around suspected patients. Knowledge barely tracked attitudes and did not predict protective practice. The authors argue Sudan's future doctors need teaching that converts facts into bedside habits before they meet patients.
plos-pone-0357103:

Candidates were filtered through machine learning, accuracy testing, and single cell data from heart tissue. Blood tests in a handful of patients and controls finished the chain.

Three genes survived as biomarkers. Analyses tied them to immune activity around the heart. They mapped the cell types where the genes switch on. They predicted regulatory partners and candidate drugs, checking fit by simulation. Protein levels in patient serum matched the genetic signal. The authors present the trio as a foundation for tests and treatments. The tiny validation group warns how early it is.
plos-pone-0357203:

When an error harms a patient, the staff involved can become second victims, traumatized and often unsupported. The team ran a scoping review of what those workers endure.

Costa's synthesis maps the repercussions for healthcare workers and which support actually helps them recover. Hospitals that ignore second victims lose experienced staff and risk repeat errors from shaken clinicians. The review gathers scattered evidence into one picture managers can act on. Supporting staff after errors is not softness; it is part of patient safety, since the next patient needs a clinician who can still function.
plos-pone-0357303:
Bruna Medeiros Gonçalves de Veras led a team of eight authors who measured the burden of RSV in older adults in Brazil, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. RSV is a common lung virus, best known for harming infants, but it also sends many older people to hospital. The team mined a national surveillance database covering more than a decade.

Veras and her colleagues counted hospital stays for adults aged sixty and older across those years. A firm count of that burden matters now that vaccines for older adults exist. Health officials can use these numbers to judge who should be offered protection first and what hospital demand to expect each virus season.
plos-pone-0357403:

Mites are sensitive markers of soil health. The team grew grass mixes over repeated seasons in two soil types inside half-open field containers, comparing emptied soil with lightly disturbed soil while tracking moisture, plants, and other conditions.

Some mite groups bounced back within a season, helped by fast breeding and easy travel, and they thrived where plant growth was lush. Another group, the slow armored mites, recovered poorly and often incompletely, faring better in rich dark soil than in sand. Gergócs-Winkler and Flórián say recovery depends on the animal's lifestyle as much as on the soil.
plos-pone-0357803:

Acne's mental toll is well known, but formal psychiatric diagnoses of phobia in acne clinics were rarely counted. A psychiatrist assessed patients using international diagnostic criteria, and the team modeled which factors traveled with a phobia diagnosis.

About one patient in four met criteria for a phobic anxiety disorder, and social phobia accounted for nearly all of those cases, with specific phobias in about one in eleven. In adjusted analysis, diagnoses tracked with a personal tendency toward anxiety, other physical illness, acne scarring, and poor response to acne treatment. They did not track with how severe a clinician rated the acne itself. Dermatology services, they say, should screen for social fear, not just skin severity, pending larger prospective studies.
plos-pone-0357903:

The pneumococcus lives harmlessly in many children's noses and throats, yet it can cause meningitis and pneumonia, so tracking which strains circulate shows whether conjugate vaccines are working. Brazil gives the ten-valent vaccine in infancy; the team swabbed four hundred healthy children aged two to five at ten schools and typed the bacteria found.

Nearly two children in five carried the pneumococcus despite vaccination. Strain typing and drug-sensitivity testing mapped what the vaccine has and has not cleared. In adjusted analysis, one factor stood out: white children had lower odds of carriage than mixed-race children, while many other candidates showed no firm links. Carriage this high, they say, keeps transmission alive and justifies continued surveillance.
plos-pone-0358103:

Sentiment classification decides whether a text glows with praise or grumbles with complaint, and businesses pay for accuracy. The team optimized a hybrid model joining an improved Senti-BERT with a BiLSTM network and an attention step.

Zhang's architecture squeezes more accuracy from the models behind review analysis and social listening. Small gains matter at scale, where millions of posts are sorted daily. The hybrid design pairs the strengths of two model families rather than betting on one. For researchers, the paper offers a tested recipe; for users of sentiment tools, it promises fewer glaring misreads of sarcasm and mixed reviews.
plos-pone-0359303: Lei and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on solving a hard class of finance equations.
