Labs use miRBase names and sequences as a shared reference, which keeps studies across the world easy to compare.
pmc-5388903:
The GBD 2015 Mortality and Causes of Death Collaborators reported in 2016 on life expectancy and causes of death worldwide. Extending life in every population takes timely, robust local data on who dies, of what, and how that changes. Without such evidence, health policy flies blind.

The study assesses deaths overall and by cause, for hundreds of causes, across the years from 1980 to 2015. It estimates life expectancy at global, regional, and national levels. The results show where gains are fastest and where causes such as conflict or epidemics reverse them. These figures anchor global health planning and funding decisions.
pmc-6145203:
Jayanta Patra, Gitishree Das, Leonardo Fraceto, and a large team reviewed nano drug delivery systems in 2018. Nanomedicine uses particles of tiny scale to carry drugs or imaging agents. Controlled release at a chosen site is the central promise.

The review surveys particle types, from lipids and polymers to metals, and how each is made. It weighs gains in targeting and dose control against safety and manufacturing hurdles. Many systems work well in animals yet stall before human use. Readers get both the excitement and the sober list of what must still be solved.
pmc-6323903:
John Tate, Sally Bamford, Harry Jubb, and coauthors described the COSMIC cancer mutation catalogue in 2018. COSMIC collects somatic mutations found in human cancers. It is the most detailed resource of its kind.

The release described here holds millions of coding mutations drawn from tumor samples and curated papers. Users can browse by gene, cancer type, or single mutation and see drug links. Expert curation keeps entries tied to real evidence rather than raw dumps. Drug developers consult COSMIC early when judging whether a mutation is worth targeting. A genome browser view lets users move from a mutation to its surrounding genes in one step.
pmc-7199903:
Yasunori Watanabe, Joel Allen, Daniel Wrapp, and coauthors analyzed the sugar coat of the SARS-CoV-2 spike in 2020. Vaccines focus on the spike, the protein that starts infection. Each of its three parts carries many sites where sugar chains attach.

The team mapped which sites actually carry sugars and what those chains look like. The coat shields much of the protein surface from antibodies, but leaves the receptor-binding area fairly open. That pattern is hopeful for vaccine design, since key targets stay reachable. The maps became a reference for antigen engineering.
pmc-7201103:
Jian-Min Jin, Peng Bai, Wei He, and coauthors compared COVID-19 severity between the sexes in 2020. The new outbreak recalled the SARS outbreak years earlier, where men fared worse. The authors set out to test whether the same pattern held.

Pooling case series and public data from China, they find men develop severe disease and die at higher rates than women. The gap persists after broad age patterns are considered. Possible reasons include smoking rates, other illnesses, and immune differences. The analysis helped establish sex as a routine factor in COVID-19 risk reporting.
pmc-7205903:
Bo Diao, Chenhui Wang, Yingjun Tan, and coauthors studied T cells in COVID-19 patients in 2020. T cells are central to antiviral defense. Their numbers and working state in the new disease were still unknown when the study began.

Blood tests on patients in Wuhan showed sharp drops in T cell counts, above all in severe cases and older patients. Remaining cells carried markers of exhaustion and worked poorly. The pattern tracks with worse outcomes, suggesting immune collapse helps drive severe disease. The findings pushed T cell support into early treatment discussions.
pmc-7312803:
Giuseppe Genchi and co-authors reviewed in 2020 the health effects of cadmium, a toxic metal that human and animal bodies have no use for. Cadmium reaches people mainly through food, drink, and tobacco smoke, and it also enters air, soil, and water from farms and industry. Once inside the body it leaves only very slowly, so exposure builds up over a lifetime.

The review describes how cadmium damages the kidneys, bones, lungs, and other organs, and how it can help set cancer in motion. The authors also cover where exposure comes from and which workers and communities face the most of it. Their summary is a reference for doctors and safety officials who must judge how much cadmium is too much.
pmc-7447603:
Jesus Banales and a broad team of specialists reviewed in 2020 where research on cholangiocarcinoma stands and where it should go next. These are cancers that arise somewhere along the bile ducts, the network that carries bile from the liver. They form a varied group of tumors, their numbers are rising worldwide, and they now account for a notable share of primary liver cancers.

The authors survey what is known about how these cancers develop, how they are found, and how they are treated. They also map the open questions, from earlier detection to drugs matched to each tumor's molecular traits. For a cancer that is often caught late and resists standard therapy, the review sets a shared agenda for the next wave of work.
pmc-8450103:
Patricia Chan and colleagues released tRNAscan-SE 2.0 in 2021, an improved version of the standard tool for finding transfer RNA genes in genome sequences. Transfer RNAs are the small molecules that carry amino acids to the protein building machinery, and spotting their genes is a basic step in reading any genome. The original tool had served for over twenty years, since the first genomes were decoded.

The update handles the flood of newer genomes, which are far more numerous and come from a far wider range of species. It also classifies the genes it finds by their likely function. The authors show the gains in accuracy and speed that justify the new version's place in annotation pipelines.
poe-works-raven-edition-1903:
Edgar Allan Poe's works fill this Raven Edition volume, edited by Stedman and Woodberry in 1903. The landmark set of 1902 to 1903 was the first scholarly complete Poe in print. This volume gathers the great tales and the Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym as well.

Readers find tales of horror, detection, and wild fancy in Poe's best-known prose pieces here. The Pym narrative sails to mutiny, shipwreck, and a strange white world at the pole. Poe's poems and essays in the full set show his theory of beauty and effect. Editors' notes trace his hard life and the texts' tangled printing history in detail. For a century this edition anchored Poe study in schools and libraries alike.
prof-cavanagh-s-phrenological-chart-1903: Prof. Cavanagh's Phrenological Chart, 1903. The professor's chart. This book preserves that chart. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: The third volume follows Constant through the Consulate years. Napoleon rises to supreme power while the valet keeps his quiet post. Ceremony grows grander and the court more splendid. A servant's-eye view of history turning.
rousseau-confessions-1903:
Jean-Jacques Rousseau wrote his Confessions late in life, and the book appeared after his death, in 1782 and after. The English text here is the Aldus Society edition of 1903, in an unsigned translation. Rousseau promised to show a man in all the truth of nature, himself, without excuse.

Across twelve books he tells of his boyhood in Geneva, his thefts, lies, and shames. He recalls masters, lovers, patrons, and the making of his famous books. Sweet scenes of youth sit beside acts he plainly regrets. Rousseau hides little, and that candor was new in life writing. The Confessions founded modern autobiography and shaped how later writers told the truth about themselves.
royce-outlines-psychology-1903:
Outlines of Psychology, published in 1903, is Royce's short treatise on the mind, written for students. An idealist among laboratory men, he treats mind as purpose at work in experience: attention, habit, and will shaping a world of meanings.

The book covers sensation, perception, memory, feeling, and choice in Royce's clear lecture style. Throughout, he resists reducing mind to mere mechanism, insisting that purpose is the key idea. The book served Harvard classrooms in the years when James and Royce made its psychology famous. It remains a readable record of that school at its most confident.
russell-principles-mathematics-1903:
Bertrand Russell published The Principles of Mathematics in 1903, his first major work of philosophy. Russell defends logicism, the view that mathematics rests on logic alone. He studies number, quantity, order, and infinity with fresh rigor. A famous appendix discusses the paradox that bears his name.

The book launched analytic philosophy as a movement. Russell's clear style set a new standard for argument in English. Work with Whitehead on Principia Mathematica grew from this start. Mathematicians and logicians still respect its bold program, even where later results limited it. It remains a landmark of modern thought.
savigny-recht-des-besitzes-1803:
Savigny's Law of Possession, published in German in 1803, was his first masterwork, written when he was only twenty-four. Possession, the simple fact of holding a thing, looks like the plainest topic in law. Savigny showed it was one of the deepest, since rights themselves grow out of protected possession.

He argues that possession is guarded by law because disturbing it wounds the person, not just the property. The argument rebuilds Roman doctrine on possession from the sources with a young man's daring and a scholar's patience. The book made its author's European fame at once and announced the historical school of law. Roman law seemed reborn through historical genius, and law students across the continent had to learn the new method. The treatise is still read as a model of legal reasoning.
scheible-das-kloster-vol03:
Cells nine through twelve make up band three of Das Kloster, which Johann Scheible brought out in 1846. By then his cloister of print had won a steady public. Each band added rooms, so to speak, stocked with the worldly and spiritual print of old Germany.

Spell books and grimoires anchor the stock, with Faust books close at hand. The feared Höllenzwänge appear in complete reprints, word for word, not cut down for safety. Around them gather folk charms and the small chapbooks sold at fairs for pennies. Band three shows the set at full stride: a working library of magic as common folk once bought it.
schiller-bride-of-messina-1803:
The Bride of Messina, Schiller's tragedy of 1803, is Englished here in A. Lodge's translation. Schiller set out to revive the chorus of Greek tragedy on the modern stage. Two brothers in Messina love the same unknown girl, who proves to be their own lost sister.

An old curse on the ruling house drives the brothers toward fratricide. The chorus comments, warns, and mourns in the ancient manner between the scenes. Schiller added his essay On the Use of the Chorus in Tragedy to the play. The experiment puzzled many playgoers yet showed his daring as a craftsman. The appended essay remains a key statement of his dramatic theory.
schiller-humanism-1903:
Oxford philosopher F. C. S. Schiller gathered his program in Humanism, a set of philosophical essays from 1903. Schiller called his view humanism, a British cousin of American pragmatism. The essays state what that view means and why he held it. Each piece takes up a live dispute of the day.

Across the set he argues that truth grows from human use and human testing. Mind, on his account, shapes the world it knows rather than copying it passively. He writes with wit and picks fights with rival schools. The volume marks the public launch of his system. Later books kept refining the same core claim.
schopenhauer-basis-morality-1903:
A learned society in Denmark set the prize question that drew Schopenhauer's essay on the basis of morality in 1840. A. Bullock translated the German prize essay into English in 1903. Schopenhauer asked what truly moves a person to act well toward others. His answer cut against the moral theories of his age.

True moral worth, he argued, rests on compassion, the felt sharing of another's pain. Egoism drives most acts, and abstract duty alone moves no one. From compassion flow justice and loving kindness, the two cardinal virtues of his ethics. The essay states his moral thought at its clearest. It remains widely read.
serge-panine-volume-03: The third volume of Serge Panine tightens the net remorselessly. The adventurer's clever deceptions approach their inevitable and terrible crisis. His frightened victims begin to see the truth. Stage-worthy suspense maintained to the very final page.
shakespeare-hamlet-1603:
William Shakespeare wrote Hamlet, first printed in 1603, the tragedy of the Prince of Denmark. No play in the world has been staged more often. Hamlet learns from a ghost that his uncle killed his father, the king.

Hamlet feigns madness while he tests the ghost's tale and plots revenge. His delays, doubts, and sharp soliloquies fill the court with dread. Ophelia goes mad, and duels and poison end the royal house. The play asks what thought, grief, and duty do to a mind. To be or not to be still echoes in speech everywhere today.
shaw-man-and-superman-1903:
George Bernard Shaw published Man and Superman in 1903, calling it a comedy and a philosophy. Shaw rarely got his longer plays staged whole in those years, so he wrote for readers as much as actors. The play carries his ideas about what he called the Life Force.

Jack Tanner, a rich radical, flees across Europe from the determined Ann Whitefield, who means to marry him. The chase runs through the Sierra Nevada with brigands and motor cars. In the famous dream scene, Don Juan debates the Devil in Hell about love, war, and progress. Shaw argues that women drive evolution by choosing mates. The play is one of his most argued-over works.
spr-proceedings-vol17-1901-1903:
Parts forty two through forty five fill volume seventeen, covering 1901 to 1903. The Society for Psychical Research spreads its work across four parts in these years. Thought transference trials continue beside studies of hypnotic and trance states. The Piper sittings reach some of their most discussed sittings in this period.

Cross references between sittings let investigators hunt for a guiding intelligence. Apparition cases still come in, each with its chain of witnesses. The society's internal skeptics keep the tone honest and dry. Volume seventeen is a generous cut of the central archive. It shows the debate widening beyond its founders. Later writers drew on it heavily.
stidger-kgc-treason-history-1903:
Felix G. Stidger worked as a Union secret agent during the Civil War. He joined the Knights of the Golden Circle from inside and sent reports to the army. His 1903 book tells the story of that group, later called the Order of Sons of Liberty. Stidger writes as a spy who sat in its secret rooms.

He lays out the group's signs, oaths, and plans to aid the South and free war captives by force. Names, dates, and trial facts fill the later pages. The book gives a rare inside view of a real plot, told by the man sent to break it.
tarde-laws-imitation-parsons-1903:
Gabriel Tarde's The Laws of Imitation appears in Elsie Clews Parsons's translation of 1903. Tarde, a French judge and thinker, argues that society is built on imitation. Inventions arise rarely; imitation spreads them like rays from a center. Fashions, crimes, languages, and laws all follow its laws.

Tarde rivaled Durkheim in French sociology, though Durkheim's school won the universities. Later readers revived Tarde as a founder of the study of memes and social networks. His micro view starts from person-to-person copying, not vast structures. Parsons, an American sociologist, gave the work its English form. The book feels fresh again in the age of viral media.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau: The third volume of the Confessions idylls at Les Charmettes. Rousseau's happy years with Madame de Warens glow ever brightly. Sweet nature, love, and music fill the gentle pages. The precious calm before life's great storms.
the-red-lily-volume-03: The third volume of The Red Lily deepens Therese's painful dilemma. Love and stern convention pull her in opposite directions. Anatole France's cool irony never falters for a moment. A masterpiece of French subtlety and grace.
the-thirty-years-war-volume-03: Volume three centers on the dramatic years of Wallenstein's ascendancy and Gustavus Adolphus's intervention — the war's most brilliant and terrible phase. Schiller, himself a dramatist, gives these larger-than-life figures their full Shakespearean stature. History at its most gripping.
the-wandering-jew-volume-03: Eugène Sue's Wandering Jew, volume three: the plot thickens. The Jesuits close in. Suspense and sensation. The serial's early act, sue's plot thickens in volume three, the Jesuits close in, suspense grows, Sue's serial.
thompson-devils-evil-spirits-babylonia-v:
R. Campbell Thompson, a British Museum scholar of cuneiform, published The Devils and Evil Spirits of Babylonia at London in 1903. This first volume covers the Utukki Limnuti series, spells against evil spirits. Thompson gives English renderings with the texts spelled out and his own notes.

The spells name the demons blamed for sickness and bad luck, then order them out in the names of the gods. Priests used them at bedsides and in houses thought to be haunted. Thompson's set made Babylonian demon lore open to English readers for the first time.
thomson-bible-1808-vol-03:
Prophets and Apocrypha fill the third volume of Charles Thomson's 1808 translation of the Bible. Thomson worked from the Greek Septuagint, the version of the Jewish scriptures made in Alexandria. Jane Aitken printed the set at Philadelphia, the first English Bible published in America.

Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel speak here in the longer Greek form, with the twelve minor prophets after them. Then come the books the King James Bible set apart: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, and the Maccabees among them. For many of these, Thomson gave American readers their first native version. The Greek wording often expands the Hebrew in striking ways.
tob-0003:
Hindus call their oldest scriptures the Vedas, a word meaning knowledge. Composed in Sanskrit more than three thousand years ago, they were kept by exact oral memory long before writing held them. Hymns to Agni the fire god, Indra the storm king, and the dawn fill the oldest layers.

Four Vedas stand at the root of Hindu worship, law, and thought. Priests still chant verses that herdsmen of the Punjab first sang. The evidence notes that no public-domain English text has yet been attached to this entry; what is described here is the scripture itself. No account of world religion can leave the Vedas out.
tob-0103:
Practice fills book two of the Sacred Magic of Abramelin. Where book one told Abraham's story, this volume gives the working system: the long retreat of prayer and the oratory's arrangement. Then come the rites by which the magician meets his Holy Guardian Angel.

Then come the famous squares of letters, word grids said to grant powers when used after the angel is won. Spirits, once commanded, are bound to serve through those squares. Crowley modeled his own great retreat on this plan. The entry rests on a verified pre-1930 edition. Together the two books form Western magic's most demanding manual.
tob-10803:
Magnus Maclean surveyed the literature of the Celtic peoples, from Irish sagas and Welsh triads to Scottish Gaelic ballads. His span runs from the earliest bards to the modern Celtic revival. Conquest, famine, and language loss shadow the whole story, yet the tradition survived.

Maclean traces how poetry, tale, and song carried memory for peoples often ruled by others, and introduces the major texts and figures in each branch. English readers who know only Arthur may be surprised by the depth on the Irish and Scottish sides. The volume serves as a learned guide to a literature most anglophone readers never meet in school.
tob-13503:
L. W. de Laurence, a Chicago occult publisher, edited this edition of the Goetia, the first part of the Lesser Key of Solomon. Medieval in origin, the grimoire catalogs seventy-two demons with their seals, ranks, offices, and the rites said to summon and command them. It is the most notorious spellbook in Western magic.

Entries describe each spirit's appearance, legions, and specialties, from teaching sciences to revealing treasures. De Laurence's commercial editions carried such texts to mail-order occultists across America. Modern readers are best advised to treat the volume as a document in the history of magic; V1 evidence notes plainly that the operations are not recommended.
tob-14503:
J. M. Rodwell translated the Koran, the scripture of Islam, into English in the nineteenth century. His edition stands out for one bold choice: he placed the chapters, called suras, in the order he judged they were revealed. Most editions keep the standard order, longest first.

Rodwell added notes from the standpoint of a Victorian scholar of the East. English readers of his day often met Islam first through his pages, and the version stayed in print for decades. The style now feels dated, and Muslim readers prefer other versions, but Rodwell's experiment with order remains of real interest.
tob-3003:
Beowulf is the oldest surviving epic in English, composed around the year 1000 in alliterative verse by an unknown Anglo-Saxon poet. A Geatish hero crosses the sea to Denmark, where King Hrothgar's hall is terrorized by the monster Grendel. Beowulf fights Grendel barehanded, then faces Grendel's mother in her underwater hall.

Fifty years later, an aged King Beowulf meets his last enemy, a dragon guarding cursed gold. Loyalty, boasts, gift-giving, and funerals frame the fighting, opening a window onto a pagan heroic world becoming Christian. Terror and doom run through all 3,182 lines, ending with a people mourning the king who protected them and fearing what comes next.
tob-4003:
Sir Thomas More published Utopia in 1516, coining a word every perfect-society plan has used since. Cast as a traveler's report in dialogue, the book describes an island commonwealth with no private property, six-hour workdays, communal meals, and unusual religious tolerance for its century. Raphael Hythloday, the traveler, praises it; More's character listens, skeptical.

The satire cuts both ways: Utopia exposes England's enclosures, hangings for theft, and proud nobles by contrast, yet its own regimentation looks uneasy too. Whether the island is a model, a warning, or a joke at the reader's expense remains genuinely open. That doubleness is why the little book still starts arguments.
tob-4203:
F. W. Burger devoted a 1907 monograph to Janus, the two-faced Roman god of doors and beginnings. January bears his name; his temple's gates stood open in war and shut in peace. Burger traces the god through Roman life and cult with a specialist's patience.

Rites, coins, temples, and the god's place in prayer and calendar all come under review. Janus looks backward and forward at once, which made him the natural lord of thresholds and new years. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. Burger's study remains a compact guide to one of Rome's oldest and oddest gods.
tob-9803:
Longus, a Greek writer of the Roman era, told the love story of Daphnis and Chloe, two foundlings raised by shepherd families on the island of Lesbos. Thornley's old English translation is the version named here. Few ancient novels survive whole, and this is the most loved of them.

Brought up side by side, the boy and girl fall in love slowly, without at first knowing what the feeling is. Pirates, rivals, and city visitors test them before the truth of their birth comes out. Later writers copied its mix of nature, innocence, and desire for centuries, and it shaped pastoral romance in Europe.
un-ga-res-303:
Jerusalem should belong to no single state, ruled the General Assembly in Resolution 303, adopted on 9 December 1949. The text recalls the 1947 partition vote and the 1948 vote that set up a Conciliation Commission for Palestine. Reports of that commission had been studied. The principles of the past votes, the Assembly holds, still mark a just and fair settlement of the question.

The city is to stand as a separate body under a lasting world regime. That regime must guard the Holy Places, in the city and beyond it, as the 1947 plan set out. The record's catalog year of 1947 is off; the vote is of 1949, after Israel's war of birth had left the city split in two.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 303 (IV), adopted on 9 December 1949, restated the Assembly's plan for Jerusalem. The Assembly stood by its 1947 and 1948 resolutions. It studied the Conciliation Commission's reports. It held that its earlier line still offered a just and fair settlement for the city and its holy places.

The text confirms that Jerusalem should stand as a separate body, a corpus separatum, under a lasting world regime run by the United Nations. The Trusteeship Council was told to finish the city's statute at its next meeting. It was to drop parts that no longer fit and make it more democratic. It was to put it into effect without delay.
un-sc-res-103:
Resolution 103 sets the terms for San Marino to join the Statute of the International Court of Justice. The Council adopted it on 3 December 1953. It acted for Japan on the same day. The vote was ten to none. The Soviet Union abstained. San Marino was a small republic. It was not a UN member at the time.

San Marino would join once it filed a signed statement with the Secretary-General. The statement also had to be ratified under its own law. In it, the republic would accept the Statute in full. It would accept the duties in Article 94 of the Charter. It would also agree to pay a fair share of the Court's costs. The Assembly would set that share after talks with its government.
un-sc-res-1203: Resolution 1203 stands in the official record of the United Nations Security Council, catalogued here with a 1998 date. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1303:
Cyprus's force was renewed for six months in June 2000. On 14 June 2000 the Security Council extended UNFICYP until 15 December 2000. The Secretary-General had reported on the operation in May. He again raised the fate of missing persons from the island's conflicts. Cyprus's government agreed the force should stay. The Council restated its Cyprus resolutions, with 1251 of 1999 in the lead.

A report on the use of the resolution was due by 1 December. Turkish Cypriot leaders faced the usual demand to free the force's movement. That demand sharpened weeks later when new limits were placed on UNFICYP. The text also welcomed health work among peacekeepers. The renewal itself followed the mission's long-set form.
un-sc-res-1403: The United Nations Security Council issued Resolution 1403 as one of its formal decisions, and the catalog carries it under the year 2002. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them.
un-sc-res-1503:
The two war crimes tribunals are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1503, adopted on 28 August 2003. The courts for the former Yugoslavia and for Rwanda had convicted many suspects since the 1990s. Both still faced heavy trial loads and fugitives at large. The Council wanted each court on a clear path to finish.

The text locks in a shared completion plan. Investigations end by 2004, first trials by 2008, and all work by 2010. Lesser cases move to national courts, which need help to handle them. States must arrest and hand over the remaining fugitives. The Rwanda court also gains its own prosecutor, ending the shared post held since 1994.
un-sc-res-1603:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1603, adopted on 3 June 2005. The parties had signed the Pretoria Agreement on 6 April 2005. They set the presidential vote for 30 October 2005. A deal on disarmament followed in May. Safety and relief conditions in the west kept getting worse.

The Council backs the Pretoria deal and warns that breaking it will bring targeted sanctions. It creates a High Representative for the elections, apart from the peacekeeping mission, to verify each stage of the vote. The mission and the French forces stay until 24 June 2005, ahead of a seven-month renewal. Militias must disarm and break up at once across the country.
un-sc-res-1703: Timor-Leste was in turmoil in the summer of 2006, with foreign troops back on its streets. The United Nations office there, UNOTIL, was about to close. On 18 August 2006 the Security Council extended its mandate by one week. The new end date was 25 August 2006. The pause gave the Council days to design a larger follow-on mission. That mission was created the day the extension expired.
un-sc-res-1903: From 2009, Resolution 1903 is a Security Council decision kept in official-record wording via a Wikisource transcription. The members behind it acted on a peace and security question within the Council's Charter brief. Their full text is the entry: the facts as they stated them, then the measures they voted into being.
un-sc-res-2003: Resolution 2003 carries a round landmark number in the Security Council's sequence, and its official text is preserved here via Wikisource. The act itself follows the standard pattern of its kind: grounds stated, prior decisions recalled, new steps ordered in numbered form. The entry preserves the pattern and the particulars together, complete and unabridged.
un-sc-res-203: Catalogued with a 1965 date, Resolution 203 forms part of the Security Council's official record at the United Nations. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording.
un-sc-res-2803:
Resolution 2803 gave the Council's ruling on Gaza, adopted on 17 November 2025. A ceasefire plan dated 29 September 2025 had been accepted by the parties. Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye, and the United States had helped broker the halt. The Strip lay in ruins after two years of war.

The Council endorses the peace plan in full. It welcomes a Board of Peace as a temporary administration to frame and fund Gaza's rebuilding. A Palestinian technocratic committee will run daily services under its watch. The Council authorizes an International Stabilization Force to deploy with power to use all necessary measures. The force will secure borders, demilitarize armed groups, and guard civilians. Both bodies stay authorized until the end of 2027.
un-sc-res-303:
Deadlock in the Security Council sent the India-Pakistan war to the General Assembly on 6 December 1971. The Council had met twice on the question, at its 1606th and 1607th meetings. Its permanent members could not agree, so the Council could not carry out its main duty for international peace and security. The fighting in South Asia went on while the vetoes held.

The Council decided to refer the question to the General Assembly at its twenty-sixth session. It acted under Assembly resolution 377 A (V) of 3 November 1950, the Uniting for Peace text. That procedure lets the Assembly take up a peace question when the Council is blocked by lack of unanimity among its permanent members. The referral is the whole of the resolution. It is one of the rare times the Council handed a live war to the Assembly because its members could not act together.
un-sc-res-403:
Botswana's case against Rhodesian attacks opened the Council's year in January 1977. Botswana's letters of 22 December 1976 and 12 January 1977 told of hostile acts by the illegal minority regime in Southern Rhodesia. Lives had been lost and property destroyed. Botswana still sheltered refugees fleeing the regime, a stance the Council praised. Its security needed urgent strengthening.

The Council strongly condemned every act of provocation and harassment by the Rhodesian regime, from raids and murder to arson and kidnapping. It demanded an immediate and total end to hostile acts against Botswana. The cost to Botswana of diverting development funds to defense was formally noted. The Council accepted Botswana's invitation to send a mission to assess its needs. United Nations bodies and all states were asked to help Botswana, guided by the mission's report. A report on the text's working was due by 31 March 1977.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 103 was adopted on 3 December 1953, by 10 votes to none with one abstention. It recommends the terms on which the Republic of San Marino could become a party to the Statute of the International Court of Justice. San Marino would deposit an instrument accepting the Statute and the Charter's Article 94 obligations. It would undertake to pay an equitable share of the Court's expenses. The General Assembly assesses that share after consulting San Marino's government.

Security Council resolution 1203, adopted on 24 October 1998 under Chapter VII, concerns Kosovo and the compliance of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with resolutions 1160 and 1199. The Council endorses two agreements signed in Belgrade that month. One, of 16 October 1998, gives the OSCE a verification mission in Kosovo. The other, of 15 October 1998, gives NATO an air verification mission over it.

The Council demands full and prompt implementation of the agreements and of its earlier resolutions by Belgrade. It demands the same compliance from the Kosovo Albanian leadership. It insists on safety and freedom of movement for the verification missions. It insists on urgent dialogue toward a negotiated settlement. It insists on action to avert a humanitarian catastrophe. It insists on the right of refugees to return home. It insists on prompt investigation of atrocities against civilians, in full cooperation with the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.

Do not trust the shelf tag that ties this text to Western Sahara. Its land is Cyprus. The isle had been split since 1974. UNFICYP troops kept the green line still. The host state agreed the force should stay past June. The chief's report of 26 May 2000 backed the stay. Resolution 1303 passed on 14 June 2000.

The force won six months more, to 15 December 2000. The old call for the lost folk of the war rang out again. Both sides had to face the fate of the missing with speed and care. A health clause marks the age of the text. The UN's drive to teach peace staff how to guard against HIV won a warm note. Word on the work was due by 1 December.

Days earlier, the Council had called for a Middle East ceasefire and an Israeli withdrawal from Palestinian cities. By 4 April 2002 it judged that resolution 1402 had not been carried out, and that the situation on the ground had grown worse. This short text is its answer.

Implementation of resolution 1402 without delay is demanded. The mission of the United States Secretary of State to the region is welcomed, as is the work of other envoys, including those from Russia, the European Union, and the United Nations. The Secretary-General is asked to follow events closely and keep the Council informed as the crisis continues.

The two war-crimes tribunals are put on a deadline by Resolution 1503, adopted unanimously on 28 August 2003. The Yugoslavia tribunal's completion strategy aimed to end investigations by 2004, first-instance trials by 2008, and all work in 2010. It focused on the most senior leaders and sent lesser cases to national courts. Rwanda's tribunal was urged to adopt the same model. Many indictees were still at large.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council calls on both tribunals to meet the completion deadlines. It calls on states to cooperate fully, work with Interpol, and consider travel bans and asset freezes against people helping fugitives evade justice. It backs a new War Crimes Chamber in Bosnia's State Court to take transferred cases. It also splits the prosecutor's job the two tribunals had shared: the Rwanda tribunal's statute is amended so it gets its own prosecutor, to be nominated by the Secretary-General.

Côte d'Ivoire's peace deal gains an election referee in Resolution 1603, adopted on 3 June 2005. The Pretoria Agreement of 6 April 2005, reached under African Union mediation, had restarted it. A disarmament agreement followed on 14 May. The first presidential round was set for 30 October 2005. Security and humanitarian conditions kept deteriorating.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council endorses the Pretoria Agreement and demands full implementation, warning that breaches will trigger the targeted sanctions of Resolution 1572 (2004). It creates a High Representative for the elections, separate from UNOCI, to verify every stage — voter register, voter cards, the work of the electoral commission and Constitutional Council. The Representative is to report any difficulty that could block free and fair elections. It extends UNOCI and the French forces to 24 June 2005 ahead of a seven-month renewal, and demands militias disarm and be dismantled at once.

Timor-Leste slipped back into unrest in 2006, and the UN's small political office there, UNOTIL, was nearing its end just as the Council debated a bigger follow-up presence. Resolution 1703, adopted on 18 August 2006, kept UNOTIL alive for one extra week, until 25 August 2006.

The stopgap mattered because the Secretary-General had just delivered two reports, one on the situation generally and one on justice and reconciliation for past abuses. Leaders in Dili had also written asking for continued UN help. The one-week extension held the mission in place while members finished negotiating the larger mission that would replace it.

Liberia was slowly rebuilding after its civil war when the Security Council adopted Resolution 1903 on 17 December 2009. The resolution renewed the sanctions that were still in place on the country. The Council noted real progress since 2006, including better control of the timber trade. Liberia had also joined the Kimberley Process, which tries to keep diamonds from war zones off the world market.

The Council kept the travel ban on listed people and kept the arms embargo in force. Arms could still reach Liberia's government, but only with advance notice and clear marking. A panel of experts was given until 20 December 2010 to check how the rules were followed. The panel also had to watch assets once held by the former president. Its reports covered timber, diamonds, and money from natural resources.

Darfur, in western Sudan, is the subject of Resolution 2003, adopted on 29 July 2011. A joint peacekeeping mission of the African Union and the United Nations, called UNAMID, was working there. Security had worsened in places. Rebel attacks, government bombing, and tribal fighting had driven tens of thousands of people from their homes.

The Council extended UNAMID's mandate for twelve months, until 31 July 2012. Protecting civilians across Darfur was named the mission's top priority. Keeping aid routes open came with it. The text welcomed a peace document signed in Doha that month. Sudan's government and one armed movement had signed it. All armed groups were told to join a lasting cease-fire and a full settlement without delay.

Fighting in the Dominican Republic drew a quick response from the Council on 14 May 1965. Resolution 203 was adopted unanimously, and it is very short, with only three points. The Council said it was deeply concerned at the grave events in the country. It called for a strict cease-fire at once. The Secretary-General was invited to send a representative to the Dominican Republic as an urgent step. That envoy had to report back on the situation. Everyone involved was called on to cooperate with the envoy in that work.

Gaza's post-war order is set by Resolution 2803, adopted on 17 November 2025. It endorses the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict of 29 September 2025 and the 13 October 2025 declaration that sealed the ceasefire.

The Council welcomes a Board of Peace as a transitional administration coordinating redevelopment funding until the Palestinian Authority completes its reform programme and resumes control. After that, a pathway to Palestinian statehood may open. It authorizes Board entities, including a technocratic Palestinian committee for administration, demands resumption of humanitarian aid kept from armed groups, and authorizes an International Stabilization Force, using all necessary measures. The force is to secure Gaza's borders, demilitarize the territory by destroying infrastructure and decommissioning non-state weapons, protect civilians, and train vetted Palestinian police. Israeli forces withdraw as milestones are met, save for a security perimeter. The arrangements run to 31 December 2027, with Board reports every six months.

A blocked Council hands a war to the General Assembly in Resolution 303. It passed on 6 December 1971, with eleven votes in favor and four members not voting either way. India and Pakistan were at war over East Pakistan. The big-power members could not agree on a reply. The text admits that this split stopped the Council from doing its main job: guarding world peace.

So the Council sent the question to the Assembly's session that year. It used the Assembly's 1950 peace plan for such deadlocks, made for times when vetoes freeze the Council. The Assembly took up the war the next day.

Botswana's plight fills Resolution 403, passed in January 1977. Thirteen members backed it, and two did not vote either way. Botswana's foreign chief told of raids by the white-led rebel regime in Rhodesia, its neighbor. Rhodesian troops crossed the line to hunt men who fought for Zimbabwe's freedom. The raids had cost lives and wrecked homes and goods.

The Council condemned the raids and the threats to Botswana's safety and welfare. It praised Botswana's calm and its care for those who fled Rhodesia. It then moved from words to help. A team would go to Botswana to size up the aid it needed to stand firm. That team's report drove a full aid plan months later.

A Pacific trust land took its own seat by way of this line of 1991. On 9 August, the Council adopted Resolution 703 without a vote. The Federated States of Micronesia had run its own affairs since 1986. A compact tied it closely to the United States. The old UN trust status was winding down at the time.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Micronesia. Admission followed that September. The step was part of a small Pacific wave of the era. Former trust lands of the ocean took single seats of their own. Each gained a voice in the Assembly's debates on seas and climate.
voyages-of-samuel-de-champlain-volume-03: The third volume of Champlain's journals covers his later explorations and the consolidation of French power in Canada. Wars with the Iroquois, the hardships of settlement, and Champlain's statesmanship fill these pages. The essential record of New France's founding father.
widger-s-quotations-from-the-project-gut: David Widger gathers the choicest lines from a Project Gutenberg edition. The best passages are set here side by side for easy browsing. Readers can taste the work's flavor in minutes. A handy treasury of fine writing.
yeats-ideas-good-evil-1903:
Yeats's 1903 essay collection is the prose manifesto of the Celtic revival, gathering pieces written while he was founding an Irish national theater. In them he sets out what art should be for a country recovering its own stories.

Key essays include 'The Symbolism of Poetry', 'The Theatre', and 'Magic', the last stating his belief in a great memory of the world that symbols can reach. He argues against dry realism and for drama fed by myth and folk tale. The style is dreamy and commanding at once. These essays shaped a generation of Irish writers and the Abbey Theatre they built.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol03:
Volume III of the Journal of Discourses came from Liverpool in 1856, carrying sermons from the Saints' first decade in the Great Basin. The stenographic record preserves Brigham Young and fellow leaders addressing their people face to face. Doctrine here walks beside counsel on crops, conduct, and holding a scattered frontier church together.

Because the talks were printed as delivered, later readers meet nineteenth-century Mormonism without a filter. Belief, discipline, and hope all speak in the cadence of the pulpit. The volume's place mid-set matters too: the Journal was becoming the movement's running memory of its own teaching.
